title: Subgrouping Reduces Complexity and Speeds Up Learning in Recurrent Networks

abstract: Genetic algorithms were used to select and create features and to select reference exemplar patterns for machine vision and speech pattern classi(cid:173) fication tasks. For a complex speech recognition task, genetic algorithms required no more computation time than traditional approaches to feature selection but reduced the number of input features required by a factor of five (from 153 to 33 features). On a difficult artificial machine-vision task, genetic algorithms were able to create new features (polynomial functions of the original features) which reduced classification error rates from 19% to almost 0%. Neural net and k nearest neighbor (KNN) classifiers were unable to provide such low error rates using only the original features. Ge(cid:173) netic algorithms were also used to reduce the number of reference exemplar patterns for a KNN classifier. On a 338 training pattern vowel-recognition problem with 10 classes, genetic algorithms reduced the number of stored exemplars from 338 to 43 without significantly increasing classification er(cid:173) ror rate. In all applications, genetic algorithms were easy to apply and found good solutions in many fewer trials than would be required by ex(cid:173) haustive search. Run times were long, but not unreasonable. These results suggest that genetic algorithms are becoming practical for pattern classi(cid:173) fication problems as faster serial and parallel computers are developed.

paragraphs: The paper uses genetic algorithms to improve classification by changing the information available to a classifier. The search selects existing features, creates new polynomial features, and chooses which reference examples to retain. These applications address both predictive performance and the amount of information needed to achieve it.

For a complex speech task, feature selection reduces the inputs from 153 to 33 without requiring more computation time than traditional selection approaches. On an artificial vision task, newly created features reduce classification error from 19% to almost zero. Neural networks and nearest-neighbor classifiers using only the original features do not achieve similarly low error.

For a ten-class vowel task, the search reduces stored nearest-neighbor exemplars from 338 to 43 without a significant error increase. Across the applications, useful solutions require far fewer trials than exhaustive search. The authors describe runtimes as long but reasonable, supporting genetic search as a practical way to improve representations and compact reference sets for classification.
summary.tldr: Genetic algorithms improve classification by selecting compact feature sets, creating useful features, and reducing stored reference examples.

title: Using Genetic Algorithms to Improve Pattern Classification Performance

abstract: A connection is drawn between rational functions, the realization theory of dynamical systems, and feedforward neural networks. This allows us to parametrize single hidden layer scalar neural networks with (almost) arbitrary analytic activation functions in terms of strictly proper rational functions. Hence, we can solve the uniqueness of parametrization problem for such networks.

This allows us to parametrize single hidden layer scalar neural networks with (almost) arbitrary analytic activation functions in terms of strictly proper rational functions. Hence, we can solve the uniqueness of parametrization problem for such networks.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to describe neural networks mathematically in a way that resolves questions about uniqueness of parametrization. Its setting is scalar feedforward networks with a single hidden layer. The central issue is the relationship between a network's parameter description and the function represented by that description.

The authors connect these networks to rational functions and to realization theory from dynamical systems. Through this connection, they express the relevant networks in terms of strictly proper rational functions. The construction applies to almost arbitrary analytic activation functions, giving the approach a broad activation-function scope within the stated network class.

The resulting framework solves the uniqueness-of-parametrization problem for these networks. Its significance is structural: it provides a mathematical route for understanding when a representation is uniquely specified. The contribution comes from linking areas that describe functions in different ways, allowing tools associated with rational functions and dynamical systems to answer a question about feedforward neural-network representations.
summary.tldr: A connection to rational functions and dynamical-system realization theory resolves parametrization uniqueness for a class of single-hidden-layer networks.

title: Rational Parametrizations of Neural Networks

abstract: We analyse the geometry of eye rotations, and in particular saccades, using basic Lie group theory and differential geome(cid:173) try. Various parameterizations of rotations are related through a unifying mathematical treatment, and transformations between co-ordinate systems are computed using the Campbell-Baker(cid:173) Hausdorff formula. Next, we describe Listing's law by means of the Lie algebra so(3). This enables us to demonstrate a direct connection to Donders' law, by showing that eye orientations are restricted to the quotient space 80(3)/80(2). The latter is equiv(cid:173) alent to the sphere S2, which is exactly the space of gaze directions. Our analysis provides a mathematical framework for studying the oculomotor system and could also be extended to investigate the geometry of mUlti-joint arm movements.

paragraphs: This paper develops a geometric account of eye rotations, with particular attention to saccades. It brings different mathematical descriptions of rotation into a common framework using Lie group theory and differential geometry. This helps relate coordinate choices that otherwise describe the same movement in different forms.

The authors compute transformations between coordinate systems using the Campbell–Baker–Hausdorff formula. They then express Listing's law through the rotation Lie algebra so(3). This representation reveals a direct connection to Donders' law: the allowed eye orientations are described by the quotient space SO(3)/SO(2), which is equivalent to a sphere.

That sphere is precisely the space of gaze directions. The result therefore connects constraints on full eye orientation to the directions in which the eye can look. The paper's contribution is a unified mathematical framework for studying the oculomotor system and the relationship between these laws. The authors also identify the geometry of movements involving multiple arm joints as a possible extension.
summary.tldr: A geometric treatment connects Listing's and Donders' laws by relating constrained eye orientations to the sphere of gaze directions.

title: The Geometry of Eye Rotations and Listing's Law

abstract: Structure in a visual scene can be described at many levels of granular(cid:173) ity. At a coarse level, the scene is composed of objects; at a finer level, each object is made up of parts, and the parts of subparts. In this work, I propose a simple principle by which such hierarchical structure can be extracted from visual scenes: Regularity in the relations among different parts of an object is weaker than in the internal structure of a part. This principle can be applied recursively to define part-whole relationships among elements in a scene. The principle does not make use of object models, categories, or other sorts of higher-level knowledge; rather, part-whole relationships can be established based on the statistics of a set of sample visual scenes. I illustrate with a model that performs unsu(cid:173) pervised decomposition of simple scenes. The model can account for the results from a human learning experiment on the ontogeny of part(cid:173) whole relationships.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a system could discover objects, parts, and smaller subparts from visual experience without already knowing object categories. Its proposed principle compares regularities at different scales: relationships inside a part are more consistent than relationships between different parts of an object. That difference provides a basis for deciding which visual elements belong together.

Applying the principle repeatedly creates a hierarchy of part-whole relationships. A grouping found at one level can participate in a larger grouping at another level. The required evidence comes from statistics across sample scenes, rather than supplied object models or other higher-level knowledge. This makes the approach an account of how hierarchical organization could emerge through unsupervised learning.

The author illustrates the principle with a model that decomposes simple scenes. The model can also account for results from a human experiment concerning the development of part-whole relationships. These findings support the principle as an explanation of that demonstrated learning behavior, while the visual demonstrations themselves concern simple scenes.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes learning visual hierarchies by grouping elements whose internal relationships are more regular than their relationships with other parts.

title: A Principle for Unsupervised Hierarchical Decomposition of Visual Scenes

abstract: Problems in which abnormal or novel situations should be detected can be approached by describing the domain of the class of typical exam- ples. These applications come from the areas of machine diagnostics, fault detection, illness identiﬁcation or, in principle, refer to any prob- lem where little knowledge is available outside the typical class. In this paper we explain why proximities are natural representations for domain descriptors and we propose a simple one-class classiﬁer for dissimilarity representations. By the use of linear programming an efﬁcient one-class description can be found, based on a small number of prototype objects. This classiﬁer can be made (1) more robust by transforming the dissimi- larities and (2) cheaper to compute by using a reduced representation set. Finally, a comparison to a comparable one-class classiﬁer by Campbell and Bennett is given.

paragraphs: The paper considers detecting unusual or novel cases when there is little knowledge about anything outside a typical class. In this setting, learning focuses on describing the domain of normal examples. The authors motivate the problem through applications such as fault detection, machine diagnostics, and illness identification.

They propose a one-class classifier whose representation uses dissimilarities between objects. Describing an object through its proximity to known examples provides a natural basis for specifying the typical class. Linear programming finds an efficient description based on a small collection of prototype objects, making those prototypes central to the learned representation.

The method offers two further adjustments. Transforming dissimilarities can improve robustness, while reducing the representation set can lower computation cost. These changes address different practical properties of the classifier: sensitivity to the dissimilarity representation and the expense of evaluating it. The paper also compares the approach with a related one-class classifier, though the abstract does not state a direction of advantage for that comparison.
summary.tldr: Linear programming learns a compact, prototype-based description of typical objects using dissimilarities for one-class classification.

title: One-Class LP Classifiers for Dissimilarity Representations

abstract: We derive a Bayesian Ideal Observer (BIO) for detecting motion and solving the correspondence problem. We obtain Barlow and Tripathy’s classic model as an approximation. Our psychophysical experiments show that the trends of human performance are similar to the Bayesian Ideal, but overall human performance is far worse. We investigate ways to degrade the Bayesian Ideal but show that even extreme degradations do not approach human performance. Instead we propose that humans perform motion tasks using generic, general purpose, models of motion. We perform more psychophysical experiments which are consistent with humans using a Slow-and-Smooth model and which rule out an alterna- tive model using Slowness.

Our psychophysical experiments show that the trends of human performance are similar to the Bayesian Ideal, but overall human performance is far worse. We investigate ways to degrade the Bayesian Ideal but show that even extreme degradations do not approach human performance. We perform more psychophysical experiments which are consistent with humans using a Slow-and-Smooth model and which rule out an alterna- tive model using Slowness.

paragraphs: Detecting motion involves deciding which observations correspond to one another across time. This paper derives a Bayesian Ideal Observer that addresses motion detection and this correspondence problem together. The authors also obtain the classic Barlow and Tripathy model as an approximation, connecting their formulation to an established account.

Psychophysical experiments show that human performance follows trends similar to those of the ideal observer, but its overall level is much worse. The authors test whether degrading the ideal observer can explain this gap. Even the extreme degradations they investigate do not bring its performance close to the human results.

They therefore propose that people use general-purpose models of motion rather than the task-specific ideal strategy. Further experiments are consistent with a Slow-and-Smooth model and rule out the alternative Slowness model considered. The evidence favors an explanation involving the structure of the motion model people use, while consistency with Slow-and-Smooth remains support for that account rather than proof that it uniquely describes human motion perception.
summary.tldr: Human motion-detection results favor a general-purpose Slow-and-Smooth model over the tested degraded ideal observers and a Slowness-only alternative.

title: Ideal Observers for Detecting Motion: Correspondence Noise

abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), as any other interaction modality based on physiological signals and body channels (e.g., muscular activity, speech and gestures), are prone to errors in the recognition of subject's intent. An elegant approach to improve the accuracy of BCIs consists in a verification procedure directly based on the presence of error-related potentials (ErrP) in the EEG recorded right after the occurrence of an error. Six healthy volunteer subjects with no prior BCI experience participated in a new human-robot interaction experiment where they were asked to mentally move a cursor towards a target that can be reached within a few steps using motor imagination. This experiment confirms the previously reported presence of a new kind of ErrP. These Interaction ErrP" exhibit a first sharp negative peak followed by a positive peak and a second broader negative peak (~290, ~350 and ~470 ms after the feedback, respectively). But in order to exploit these ErrP we need to detect them in each single trial using a short window following the feedback associated to the response of the classifier embedded in the BCI. We have achieved an average recognition rate of correct and erroneous single trials of 81.8% and 76.2%, respectively. Furthermore, we have achieved an average recognition rate of the subject's intent while trying to mentally drive the cursor of 73.1%. These results show that it's possible to simultaneously extract useful information for mental control to operate a brain-actuated device as well as cognitive states such as error potentials to improve the quality of the brain-computer interaction. Finally, using a well-known inverse model (sLORETA), we show that the main focus of activity at the occurrence of the ErrP are, as expected, in the pre-supplementary motor area and in the anterior cingulate cortex."

paragraphs: A brain-computer interface can misread a person's intended command. This paper investigates whether the brain's response to that mistake can provide a verification signal. Six healthy volunteers without prior BCI experience used motor imagination to move a cursor toward a target, while EEG captured both control-related activity and responses to the interface's feedback.

The experiment confirms interaction-related error potentials with negative, positive, and broader negative peaks around 290, 350, and 470 milliseconds after feedback. To make these signals useful during interaction, the authors detect them in individual trials within a short post-feedback window. Average recognition rates were 81.8% for correct trials and 76.2% for erroneous trials; intended cursor commands were recognized at 73.1%.

These results show that useful command information and error-related cognitive signals can be extracted within the same interaction setting. Source localization using sLORETA places the main error-related activity in the pre-supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate cortex. The work supports error-potential detection as a way to inform BCI verification, with separate reported measurements for command recognition and error recognition.
summary.tldr: Single-trial EEG error signals can help verify BCI responses alongside decoding the user's intended commands.

title: EEG-Based Brain-Computer Interaction: Improved Accuracy by Automatic Single-Trial Error Detection

abstract: Cascade detectors have been shown to operate extremely rapidly, with high accuracy, and have important applications such as face detection. Driven by this success, cascade earning has been an area of active research in recent years. Nevertheless, there are still challenging technical problems during the training process of cascade detectors. In particular, determining the optimal target detection rate for each stage of the cascade remains an unsolved issue. In this paper, we propose the multiple instance pruning (MIP) algorithm for soft cascades. This algorithm computes a set of thresholds which aggressively terminate computation with no reduction in detection rate or increase in false positive rate on the training dataset. The algorithm is based on two key insights: i) examples that are destined to be rejected by the complete classifier can be safely pruned early; ii) face detection is a multiple instance learning problem. The MIP process is fully automatic and requires no assumptions of probability distributions, statistical independence, or ad hoc intermediate rejection targets. Experimental results on the MIT+CMU dataset demonstrate significant performance advantages.

paragraphs: Cascade detectors save computation by rejecting examples before every part of a classifier has been evaluated. Training them raises a difficult question: how much rejection should each stage perform? This paper proposes multiple-instance pruning, or MIP, to set thresholds automatically for soft cascades, avoiding the need to choose intermediate detection targets by hand.

The method combines two observations. An example that the complete classifier will ultimately reject can potentially be discarded earlier without changing that final decision. Also, face detection can be treated as a multiple-instance learning problem. Together, these ideas guide threshold selection toward earlier termination while preserving the relevant training-set outcomes.

The stated guarantee is specifically about the training dataset: the selected thresholds do not lower detection rate or raise false-positive rate there. MIP requires neither assumed probability distributions nor statistical independence. Experiments on the MIT+CMU dataset show significant performance advantages. The practical contribution is an automatic way to reduce cascade computation while explicitly protecting the training behavior of the complete detector.
summary.tldr: MIP automatically prunes soft-cascade computation while preserving detection and false-positive rates on the training data.

title: Multiple-Instance Pruning For Learning Efficient Cascade Detectors

abstract: Sampling functions in Gaussian process (GP) models is challenging because of the highly correlated posterior distribution. We describe an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for sampling from the posterior process of the GP model. This algorithm uses control variables which are auxiliary function values that provide a low dimensional representation of the function. At each iteration, the algorithm proposes new values for the control variables and generates the function from the conditional GP prior. The control variable input locations are found by continuously minimizing an objective function. We demonstrate the algorithm on regression and classification problems and we use it to estimate the parameters of a differential equation model of gene regulation.

We describe an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for sampling from the posterior process of the GP model. This algorithm uses control variables which are auxiliary function values that provide a low dimensional representation of the function. At each iteration, the algorithm proposes new values for the control variables and generates the function from the conditional GP prior. The control variable input locations are found by continuously minimizing an objective function. We demonstrate the algorithm on regression and classification problems and we use it to estimate the parameters of a differential equation model of gene regulation.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process posterior functions can be strongly correlated, making direct sampling inefficient. This paper introduces a lower-dimensional set of auxiliary function values to guide the sampling process. Those control variables provide a manageable handle on changes to the full function.

At each Markov-chain step, the method proposes new control-variable values and draws the remaining function from the conditional Gaussian-process prior. Their input locations are optimized continuously through an objective function. The procedure therefore adapts where its compact representation is anchored rather than fixing those locations arbitrarily.

Demonstrations include regression, classification, and parameter estimation for a differential-equation model of gene regulation. The contribution is an inference strategy that combines compact proposals with the full process’s conditional structure. It addresses correlation in function-space sampling while retaining a probabilistic representation of uncertainty, rather than replacing posterior inference with a single fitted function.
summary.tldr: Adaptive control variables make Gaussian-process posterior sampling more efficient by proposing compact function summaries and sampling conditional completions.

title: Efficient Sampling for Gaussian Process Inference using Control Variables

abstract: This paper studies the forward greedy strategy in sparse nonparametric regression. For additive models, we propose an algorithm called additive forward regression; for general multivariate regression, we propose an algorithm called generalized forward regression. Both of them simultaneously conduct estimation and variable selection in nonparametric settings for the high dimensional sparse learning problem. Our main emphasis is empirical: on both simulated and real data, these two simple greedy methods can clearly outperform several state-of-the-art competitors, including the LASSO, a nonparametric version of the LASSO called the sparse additive model (SpAM) and a recently proposed adaptive parametric forward-backward algorithm called the Foba. Some theoretical justifications are also provided.
originalAbstract: This paper studies the forward greedy strategy in sparse nonparametric regression. For additive models, we propose an algorithm called additive forward regression; for general multivariate regression, we propose an algorithm called generalized forward regression. Both of them simultaneously conduct estimation and variable selection in nonparametric settings for the high dimensional sparse learning problem. Our main emphasis is empirical: on both simulated and real data, these two simple greedy methods can clearly outperform several state-of-the-art competitors, including the LASSO, a nonparametric version of the LASSO called the sparse additive model (SpAM) and a recently proposed adaptive parametric forward-backward algorithm called the Foba. Some theoretical justifications are also provided.

paragraphs: The paper studies regression problems with many candidate variables but a sparse underlying relationship. Its focus is nonparametric learning, where the relationship being estimated is allowed more flexibility than a fixed parametric form. The authors investigate whether simple forward greedy strategies can both identify relevant variables and estimate their predictive effects.

They propose two methods for different model settings. Additive forward regression addresses additive models, which combine separate contributions from variables. Generalized forward regression addresses broader multivariate regression. Both perform variable selection and estimation together, bringing a forward-selection strategy into high-dimensional nonparametric learning.

The main evidence is empirical. On simulated and real datasets, the methods can clearly outperform several strong alternatives, including LASSO, the sparse additive model SpAM, and the adaptive forward-backward method Foba. The paper also provides some theoretical justification. These results support greedy nonparametric methods as competitive approaches to sparse learning: flexible estimation and variable selection can work effectively within relatively simple algorithms. The claims concern demonstrated comparative performance, rather than a guarantee of superiority across all sparse regression problems.
summary.tldr: Two greedy nonparametric regression methods jointly select variables and estimate relationships, with strong empirical sparse-learning results.

title: Nonparametric Greedy Algorithms for the Sparse Learning Problem

abstract: The long-standing problem of efficient nearest-neighbor (NN) search has ubiquitous applications ranging from astrophysics to MP3 fingerprinting to bioinformatics to movie recommendations. As the dimensionality of the dataset increases, exact NN search becomes computationally prohibitive; (1+eps)-distance-approximate NN search can provide large speedups but risks losing the meaning of NN search present in the ranks (ordering) of the distances. This paper presents a simple, practical algorithm allowing the user to, for the first time, directly control the true accuracy of NN search (in terms of ranks) while still achieving the large speedups over exact NN. Experiments with high-dimensional datasets show that it often achieves faster and more accurate results than the best-known distance-approximate method, with much more stable behavior.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor search looks for the data points closest to a query, but exact search becomes computationally expensive in high dimensions. Distance-based approximation can provide large speedups while weakening the ordering information that makes a neighbor useful. This paper focuses on accuracy expressed through rank: where a returned result falls in the ordering of distances.

The authors introduce a simple, practical algorithm that lets users directly control rank-based search accuracy while retaining large speedups over exact search. This changes the approximation target from closeness in distance value to closeness in the neighbor ordering. The distinction matters when the purpose of retrieval depends on returning highly ranked neighbors.

Experiments on high-dimensional datasets show that the algorithm often produces faster and more accurate results than the best-known distance-approximate method, with much more stable behavior. The reported advantage is empirical and qualified by how often it occurs. The central contribution is a controllable rank-oriented approximation that aligns the search criterion with ordering quality while addressing the computational cost of high-dimensional retrieval.
summary.tldr: A rank-controlled nearest-neighbor algorithm retains large search speedups and often improves accuracy and stability over distance-based approximation.

title: Rank-Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search: Retaining Meaning and Speed in High Dimensions

abstract: Matching functional brain regions across individuals is a challenging task, largely due to the variability in their location and extent. It is particularly difficult, but highly relevant, for patients with pathologies such as brain tumors, which can cause substantial reorganization of functional systems. In such cases spatial registration based on anatomical data is only of limited value if the goal is to establish correspondences of functional areas among different individuals, or to localize potentially displaced active regions. Rather than rely on spatial alignment, we propose to perform registration in an alternative space whose geometry is governed by the functional interaction patterns in the brain. We first embed each brain into a functional map that reflects connectivity patterns during a fMRI experiment. The resulting functional maps are then registered, and the obtained correspondences are propagated back to the two brains. In application to a language fMRI experiment, our preliminary results suggest that the proposed method yields improved functional correspondences across subjects. This advantage is pronounced for subjects with tumors that affect the language areas and thus cause spatial reorganization of the functional regions.

paragraphs: Matching functional brain areas across people is difficult because their positions and sizes vary. Tumors can make the problem especially pronounced by reorganizing functional systems. Anatomical alignment then has limited value for identifying corresponding functional areas or locating active regions that have shifted from their usual positions.

The authors propose aligning brains in a space defined by patterns of functional interaction. Each brain is embedded in a functional map reflecting connectivity during an fMRI experiment. The maps are registered to one another, and the resulting matches are transferred back to the original brains. This makes connectivity patterns the basis for establishing correspondence between regions.

Preliminary results from a language fMRI experiment suggest improved functional matches across subjects. The apparent advantage is particularly pronounced for people with tumors affecting language areas and causing spatial reorganization. The findings support the possibility that functional interaction geometry can help locate corresponding areas when anatomy alone provides an incomplete guide.
summary.tldr: Aligning connectivity-based brain maps shows preliminary improvements in matching functional areas, especially when tumors have reorganized language regions.

title: Functional Geometry Alignment and Localization of Brain Areas

abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of learning an n x n Kernel matrix from m similarity matrices under general convex loss. Past research have extensively studied the m =1 case and have derived several algorithms which require sophisticated techniques like ACCP, SOCP, etc. The existing algorithms do not apply if one uses arbitrary losses and often can not handle m > 1 case. We present several provably convergent iterative algorithms, where each iteration requires either an SVM or a Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) solver for m > 1 case. One of the major contributions of the paper is to extend the well known Mirror Descent(MD) framework to handle Cartesian product of psd matrices. This novel extension leads to an algorithm, called EMKL, which solves the problem in O(m^2 log n) iterations; in each iteration one solves an MKL involving m kernels and m eigen-decomposition of n x n matrices. By suitably defining a restriction on the objective function, a faster version of EMKL is proposed, called REKL, which avoids the eigen-decomposition. An alternative to both EMKL and REKL is also suggested which requires only an SVM solver. Experimental results on real world protein data set involving several similarity matrices illustrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: Different similarity matrices can describe different relationships among the same data points. This paper studies how to learn a kernel matrix from several such inputs under general convex losses. Earlier algorithms often addressed only one similarity matrix or restricted the choice of loss, motivating methods that accommodate a broader combination of inputs and objectives.

The authors develop several iterative algorithms with convergence guarantees. Their main construction extends mirror descent to collections of positive semidefinite matrices. The resulting EMKL algorithm requires O(m² log n) iterations for m input matrices and an n-by-n learned kernel. Each iteration solves a multiple-kernel-learning problem and performs m eigen-decompositions of n-by-n matrices.

A faster variant, REKL, avoids those eigen-decompositions by imposing a restriction on the objective function. Another proposed alternative requires only an SVM solver. Experiments on a real protein dataset with multiple similarity matrices illustrate the algorithms' effectiveness. The paper thus offers several computational routes, with the faster restricted formulation trading some objective flexibility for cheaper iterations.
summary.tldr: Provably convergent algorithms learn kernels from multiple similarity matrices under general convex losses, with restricted variants reducing computational work.

title: Efficient algorithms for learning kernels from multiple similarity matrices with general convex loss functions

abstract: How humans achieve long-term goals in an uncertain environment, via repeated trials and noisy observations, is an important problem in cognitive science. We investigate this behavior in the context of a multi-armed bandit task. We compare human behavior to a variety of models that vary in their representational and computational complexity. Our result shows that subjects' choices, on a trial-to-trial basis, are best captured by a forgetful" Bayesian iterative learning model in combination with a partially myopic decision policy known as Knowledge Gradient. This model accounts for subjects' trial-by-trial choice better than a number of other previously proposed models, including optimal Bayesian learning and risk minimization, epsilon-greedy and win-stay-lose-shift. It has the added benefit of being closest in performance to the optimal Bayesian model than all the other heuristic models that have the same computational complexity (all are significantly less complex than the optimal model). These results constitute an advancement in the theoretical understanding of how humans negotiate the tension between exploration and exploitation in a noisy, imperfectly known environment."

paragraphs: Repeated decisions under uncertainty require balancing the value of trying alternatives against using what already appears rewarding. This paper studies how people manage that balance in a multi-armed bandit task. The authors compare human choices with models that differ in how they represent uncertainty and how much computation they use to select actions.

The best account of subjects' trial-by-trial choices combines a forgetful Bayesian learning model with Knowledge Gradient, a partially myopic decision policy. This combination fits choices better than the compared alternatives, including optimal Bayesian learning and risk minimization, epsilon-greedy, and win-stay-lose-shift. The finding concerns the observed behavior in the studied task.

The model also comes closest to optimal Bayesian performance among the compared heuristics with the same computational complexity. Those heuristics are all substantially less complex than the optimal model. Together, the behavioral fit and performance comparison suggest that limited-memory learning paired with partially short-sighted planning can help explain effective human exploration without requiring the full computation of optimal Bayesian decision-making.
summary.tldr: A forgetful Bayesian learner with Knowledge Gradient best explains the reported human bandit choices among the models compared.

title: Forgetful Bayes and myopic planning: Human learning and decision-making in a bandit setting

abstract: An incredible gulf separates theoretical models of synapses, often described solely by a single scalar value denoting the size of a postsynaptic potential, from the immense complexity of molecular signaling pathways underlying real synapses. To understand the functional contribution of such molecular complexity to learning and memory, it is essential to expand our theoretical conception of a synapse from a single scalar to an entire dynamical system with many internal molecular functional states. Moreover, theoretical considerations alone demand such an expansion; network models with scalar synapses assuming finite numbers of distinguishable synaptic strengths have strikingly limited memory capacity. This raises the fundamental question, how does synaptic complexity give rise to memory? To address this, we develop new mathematical theorems elucidating the relationship between the structural organization and memory properties of complex synapses that are themselves molecular networks. Moreover, in proving such theorems, we uncover a framework, based on first passage time theory, to impose an order on the internal states of complex synaptic models, thereby simplifying the relationship between synaptic structure and function.

paragraphs: Many theoretical models reduce a synapse to a single number representing its strength. Real synapses contain much richer molecular machinery, raising the question of what that internal complexity contributes to memory. The paper also gives a theoretical motivation: network models with scalar synapses and finitely many distinguishable strengths have sharply limited memory capacity.

The authors instead treat a synapse as a dynamical system with multiple internal molecular states. They develop mathematical theorems connecting the structural organization of these systems to their memory properties. This makes the internal arrangement of a synapse part of the explanation of memory, rather than treating its observable strength as the entire mechanism.

The proofs introduce a framework based on first passage times, which concern how a dynamical system reaches particular states. This framework imposes an order on otherwise complicated internal states and simplifies the connection between structure and function. The stated contribution is a theoretical account of how synaptic organization relates to memory, rather than an experimental identification of a particular molecular implementation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops theorems linking the internal organization of complex synapses to their memory properties.

title: A memory frontier for complex synapses

abstract: For classifying time series, a nearest-neighbor approach is widely used in practice with performance often competitive with or better than more elaborate methods such as neural networks, decision trees, and support vector machines. We develop theoretical justification for the effectiveness of nearest-neighbor-like classification of time series. Our guiding hypothesis is that in many applications, such as forecasting which topics will become trends on Twitter, there aren't actually that many prototypical time series to begin with, relative to the number of time series we have access to, e.g., topics become trends on Twitter only in a few distinct manners whereas we can collect massive amounts of Twitter data. To operationalize this hypothesis, we propose a latent source model for time series, which naturally leads to a weighted majority voting" classification rule that can be approximated by a nearest-neighbor classifier. We establish nonasymptotic performance guarantees of both weighted majority voting and nearest-neighbor classification under our model accounting for how much of the time series we observe and the model complexity. Experimental results on synthetic data show weighted majority voting achieving the same misclassification rate as nearest-neighbor classification while observing less of the time series. We then use weighted majority to forecast which news topics on Twitter become trends, where we are able to detect such "trending topics" in advance of Twitter 79% of the time, with a mean early advantage of 1 hour and 26 minutes, a true positive rate of 95%, and a false positive rate of 4%."

paragraphs: Why can classifying a time series by its nearest known example work so well? This paper develops an explanation based on a latent source model: many observed sequences may arise from a relatively small collection of underlying patterns. Having many examples of those patterns could make simple comparisons effective.

The model leads to a weighted voting rule, in which training examples contribute to a classification decision, and nearest-neighbor classification approximates that rule. The authors establish finite-sample performance guarantees for both methods under their model. These guarantees account for the amount of a sequence observed and the complexity of its underlying sources, connecting early prediction to the assumed structure of the data.

In synthetic experiments, weighted voting reaches the same classification error as nearest neighbors using shorter observations. Applied to Twitter news topics, it detects trends before Twitter 79% of the time, averaging an advantage of 1 hour and 26 minutes. The reported true-positive and false-positive rates are 95% and 4%, respectively. These results demonstrate early forecasting in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: A model with relatively few underlying time-series patterns explains simple classifiers and supports early trend forecasting.

title: A Latent Source Model for Nonparametric Time Series Classification

abstract: Numerous algorithms are used for nonnegative matrix factorization under the assumption that the matrix is nearly separable. In this paper, we show how to make these algorithms scalable for data matrices that have many more rows than columns, so-called tall-and-skinny matrices." One key component to these improved methods is an orthogonal matrix transformation that preserves the separability of the NMF problem. Our final methods need to read the data matrix only once and are suitable for streaming, multi-core, and MapReduce architectures. We demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms on terabyte-sized matrices from scientific computing and bioinformatics."

paragraphs: The paper focuses on nonnegative matrix factorization for nearly separable matrices that have far more rows than columns. Many algorithms already exploit near-separability, but very large row counts create a separate scaling challenge. The authors investigate how to adapt those methods to this tall-and-skinny shape.

A key component is an orthogonal matrix transformation that preserves the separability of the factorization problem. Preserving that property matters because it retains the structural basis on which the existing algorithms operate. The transformation is used within improved methods designed for large data, rather than requiring a completely unrelated factorization formulation.

The resulting methods need only one read of the data matrix and are suitable for streaming, multicore, and MapReduce architectures. Experiments demonstrate their effectiveness on terabyte-sized matrices from scientific computing and bioinformatics. The contribution is therefore both mathematical and computational: a structure-preserving transformation supports implementations that reduce repeated access to large inputs. The stated scope is near-separable tall-and-skinny matrices, which is the setting supporting these scalability claims.
summary.tldr: A separability-preserving transformation enables single-pass, scalable nonnegative factorization methods for near-separable tall-and-skinny matrices.

title: Scalable Methods for Nonnegative Matrix Factorizations of Near-separable Tall-and-skinny Matrices

abstract: Bandit convex optimization is one of the fundamental problems in the field of online learning. The best algorithm for the general bandit convex optimization problem guarantees a regret of $\widetilde{O}(T^{5/6})$, while the best known lower bound is $\Omega(T^{1/2})$. Many attemptshave been made to bridge the huge gap between these bounds. A particularly interesting special case of this problem assumes that the loss functions are smooth. In this case, the best known algorithm guarantees a regret of $\widetilde{O}(T^{2/3})$. We present an efficient algorithm for the banditsmooth convex optimization problem that guarantees a regret of $\widetilde{O}(T^{5/8})$. Our result rules out an $\Omega(T^{2/3})$ lower bound and takes a significant step towards the resolution of this open problem.

paragraphs: The paper addresses bandit convex optimization, an online learning problem evaluated through regret. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage of the learner's decisions relative to a comparison choice. The motivating issue is a gap between achievable upper bounds and known lower bounds: the abstract gives a general upper bound with exponent 5/6 and a lower bound with exponent 1/2.

The authors focus on the special case in which loss functions are smooth. For this setting, they present an efficient algorithm whose regret is bounded by O-tilde(T^(5/8)), improving the previously stated O-tilde(T^(2/3)) guarantee. Here T is the time horizon, and the tilde notation suppresses logarithmic factors. The smaller exponent improves how the guarantee scales over longer runs.

The theoretical consequence is that an Omega(T^(2/3)) lower bound cannot hold for this smooth problem: the new algorithm already achieves a better rate. This narrows the uncertainty about the best possible performance. It is a step toward resolving the gap, with the improvement explicitly tied to smooth losses.
summary.tldr: An efficient algorithm improves the regret guarantee for smooth bandit convex optimization from O-tilde(T^(2/3)) to O-tilde(T^(5/8)).

title: Bandit Smooth Convex Optimization: Improving the Bias-Variance Tradeoff

abstract: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), or particle filtering, is a popular class of methods for sampling from an intractable target distribution using a sequence of simpler intermediate distributions. Like other importance sampling-based methods, performance is critically dependent on the proposal distribution: a bad proposal can lead to arbitrarily inaccurate estimates of the target distribution. This paper presents a new method for automatically adapting the proposal using an approximation of the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true posterior and the proposal distribution. The method is very flexible, applicable to any parameterized proposal distribution and it supports online and batch variants. We use the new framework to adapt powerful proposal distributions with rich parameterizations based upon neural networks leading to Neural Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo (NASMC). Experiments indicate that NASMC significantly improves inference in a non-linear state space model outperforming adaptive proposal methods including the Extended Kalman and Unscented Particle Filters. Experiments also indicate that improved inference translates into improved parameter learning when NASMC is used as a subroutine of Particle Marginal Metropolis Hastings. Finally we show that NASMC is able to train a latent variable recurrent neural network (LV-RNN) achieving results that compete with the state-of-the-art for polymorphic music modelling. NASMC can be seen as bridging the gap between adaptive SMC methods and the recent work in scalable, black-box variational inference.

paragraphs: Particle filtering approximates difficult probability distributions through a sequence of simpler sampling problems. Its accuracy depends heavily on the proposal distribution that generates candidate particles. This paper develops a way to adapt that proposal automatically, using an approximation to the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the posterior and proposal.

The framework accepts parameterized proposal families and supports both online and batch adaptation. Using neural networks for the proposals produces Neural Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo. Richer learned proposals are intended to place particles where they better represent the posterior, linking adaptive particle methods with ideas from scalable variational inference.

Experiments show improved inference in a nonlinear state-space model compared with adaptive proposals including Extended Kalman and Unscented Particle Filters. Better inference also improves parameter learning when the method is used inside Particle Marginal Metropolis Hastings. Finally, it trains a latent-variable recurrent network with competitive music-modeling results. These findings demonstrate benefits both for posterior estimation itself and for learning procedures that depend on those estimates.
summary.tldr: Neural networks adapt particle-filter proposals to improve inference and downstream learning in the evaluated sequential models.

title: Neural Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: We study the problem of reconstructing a mixture of Markov chains from the trajectories generated by random walks through the state space. Under mild non-degeneracy conditions, we show that we can uniquely reconstruct the underlying chains by only considering trajectories of length three, which represent triples of states. Our algorithm is spectral in nature, and is easy to implement.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of reconstructing a mixture of Markov chains from the trajectories generated by random walks through the state space. Under mild non-degeneracy conditions, we show that we can uniquely reconstruct the underlying chains by only considering trajectories of length three, which represent triples of states. Our algorithm is spectral in nature, and is easy to implement.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to reconstruct a mixture of Markov chains from observed trajectories. The observations are sequences of states generated by random walks, while the underlying chains are unknown. The central question is whether these sequences contain enough information to distinguish and recover the separate chains that make up the mixture.

The main result is that trajectories containing just three states can suffice for unique reconstruction. This statement is conditional on mild non-degeneracy assumptions. Those conditions matter because the result establishes recoverability for mixtures satisfying them; it does not assert that every possible collection of chains can be uniquely identified from triples.

The authors provide a spectral algorithm and describe it as easy to implement. The significance of the result lies in the short trajectory length required under the stated conditions: reconstruction need not depend on observing long individual walks. Here, length three refers to the number of states within each trajectory, rather than a claim that three total observations suffice to learn the mixture.
summary.tldr: Under mild non-degeneracy conditions, a spectral algorithm uniquely reconstructs mixtures of Markov chains from three-state trajectories.

title: On Mixtures of Markov Chains

abstract: Concurrent measurements of neural activity at multiple scales, sometimes performed with multimodal techniques, become increasingly important for studying brain function. However, statistical methods for their concurrent analysis are currently lacking. Here we introduce such techniques in a framework based on vine copulas with mixed margins to construct multivariate stochastic models. These models can describe detailed mixed interactions between discrete variables such as neural spike counts, and continuous variables such as local field potentials. We propose efficient methods for likelihood calculation, inference, sampling and mutual information estimation within this framework. We test our methods on simulated data and demonstrate applicability on mixed data generated by a biologically realistic neural network. Our methods hold the promise to considerably improve statistical analysis of neural data recorded simultaneously at different scales.

paragraphs: Neural activity can be recorded simultaneously at several scales, producing measurements with different statistical forms. Spike counts are discrete, while local field potentials are continuous. Analyzing their relationships requires a joint model that can accommodate both kinds of variables and represent interactions between them.

This paper introduces a framework based on vine copulas with mixed margins. The construction allows the individual variables to retain their discrete or continuous character within a shared multivariate probability model. The authors also provide efficient procedures for calculating likelihoods, performing inference, generating samples, and estimating mutual information. These operations make the framework useful for several aspects of statistical analysis, beyond specifying a distribution.

The methods are tested on simulated data and applied to mixed measurements generated by a biologically realistic neural network. These demonstrations establish applicability in the settings examined. The proposed benefit is a richer way to analyze neural measurements collected together at different scales. Broader improvements to the analysis of recorded neural data are presented as a promise of the framework, rather than as an already established result across recording settings.
summary.tldr: Mixed vine copulas provide a joint statistical framework for dependencies between discrete spike counts and continuous local field potentials.

title: Mixed vine copulas as joint models of spike counts and local field potentials

abstract: Optimizing task-related mathematical model is one of the most fundamental methodologies in statistic and learning areas. However, generally designed schematic iterations may hard to investigate complex data distributions in real-world applications. Recently, training deep propagations (i.e., networks) has gained promising performance in some particular tasks. Unfortunately, existing networks are often built in heuristic manners, thus lack of principled interpretations and solid theoretical supports. In this work, we provide a new paradigm, named Propagation and Optimization based Deep Model (PODM), to bridge the gaps between these different mechanisms (i.e., model optimization and deep propagation). On the one hand, we utilize PODM as a deeply trained solver for model optimization. Different from these existing network based iterations, which often lack theoretical investigations, we provide strict convergence analysis for PODM in the challenging nonconvex and nonsmooth scenarios. On the other hand, by relaxing the model constraints and performing end-to-end training, we also develop a PODM based strategy to integrate domain knowledge (formulated as models) and real data distributions (learned by networks), resulting in a generic ensemble framework for challenging real-world applications. Extensive experiments verify our theoretical results and demonstrate the superiority of PODM against these state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: This paper connects mathematical optimization with trained neural networks through a framework called Propagation and Optimization based Deep Model, or PODM. The motivation is that predefined optimization procedures can struggle to reflect complex data distributions, while networks designed through heuristics can be difficult to interpret theoretically. PODM brings these two approaches into a shared framework.

In one use, PODM acts as a learned solver for a mathematical model. The authors provide convergence analysis covering nonconvex and nonsmooth settings, where the optimization problem can have multiple competing solutions or lack ordinary derivatives. This gives theoretical support to the solver formulation rather than relying only on successful experimental behavior.

In another use, the authors relax model constraints and train the system end to end. This combines domain knowledge expressed through mathematical models with patterns learned from data. Experiments support the theoretical results and report advantages over competing approaches. The distinction between the two uses matters: the abstract presents convergence analysis for the solver and a more flexible learned framework for applications.
summary.tldr: PODM connects learned neural propagation with mathematical optimization, providing solver convergence analysis and a flexible way to combine models with data.

title: A Bridging Framework for Model Optimization and Deep Propagation

abstract: Standard neural network architectures are non-linear only by virtue of a simple element-wise activation function, making them both brittle and excessively large. In this paper, we consider methods for making the feed-forward layer more flexible while preserving its basic structure. We develop simple drop-in replacements that learn to adapt their parameterization conditional on the input, thereby increasing statistical efficiency significantly. We present an adaptive LSTM that advances the state of the art for the Penn Treebank and Wikitext-2 word-modeling tasks while using fewer parameters and converging in half as many iterations.

We develop simple drop-in replacements that learn to adapt their parameterization conditional on the input, thereby increasing statistical efficiency significantly. We present an adaptive LSTM that advances the state of the art for the Penn Treebank and Wikitext-2 word-modeling tasks while using fewer parameters and converging in half as many iterations.

paragraphs: Standard neural network layers obtain their nonlinear behavior through simple activation functions applied separately to individual values. The paper identifies this restricted source of flexibility as a contributor to brittle and excessively large networks. It investigates how to make a feed-forward layer more expressive while preserving the layer's basic structure.

The proposed replacements learn to adapt their parameterization according to the input. Consequently, the layer can change how it processes different inputs through its learned parameters. The authors describe these components as simple drop-in replacements and report a significant increase in statistical efficiency. The central design idea is to make the layer's computation itself more adaptable.

The paper demonstrates the approach with an adaptive LSTM for word modeling on Penn Treebank and Wikitext-2. It reports state-of-the-art results while using fewer parameters and reaching convergence in half as many iterations. These findings connect the additional flexibility to better language-modeling performance, a smaller parameter count, and faster convergence in the stated evaluations.
summary.tldr: Input-dependent parameterization makes neural layers more flexible and improves an LSTM's word-modeling results with fewer parameters and iterations.

title: Breaking the Activation Function Bottleneck through Adaptive Parameterization

abstract: Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) is a particle-based inference algorithm that leverages gradient information for efficient approximate inference. In this work, we enhance SVGD by leveraging preconditioning matrices, such as the Hessian and Fisher information matrix, to incorporate geometric information into SVGD updates. We achieve this by presenting a generalization of SVGD that replaces the scalar-valued kernels in vanilla SVGD with more general matrix-valued kernels. This yields a significant extension of SVGD, and more importantly, allows us to flexibly incorporate various preconditioning matricesto accelerate the exploration in the probability landscape. Empirical results show that our method outperforms vanilla SVGD and a variety of baseline approaches over a range of real-world Bayesian inference tasks.

paragraphs: Stein variational gradient descent approximates a probability distribution using particles whose updates use gradient information. This paper extends the method so those updates can also incorporate geometric information about the distribution. The motivation is to help particles explore the probability landscape more efficiently by changing how update directions are scaled and combined.

The key change replaces the scalar-valued kernels of standard SVGD with matrix-valued kernels. This broader construction allows preconditioning matrices, including Hessian and Fisher information matrices, to enter the updates. Rather than providing only a scalar kernel value, the generalized kernel can express directional structure relevant to the inference problem.

The authors present this as a flexible extension supporting different choices of preconditioning, with the aim of accelerating exploration. Empirical evaluations across real-world Bayesian inference tasks show improvements over standard SVGD and several baseline approaches. These findings support incorporating geometry through the kernel itself as a useful way to strengthen particle-based approximate inference, with the reported performance evidence coming from the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Matrix-valued kernels let SVGD incorporate geometric preconditioning and improve empirical performance on Bayesian inference tasks.

title: Stein Variational Gradient Descent With Matrix-Valued Kernels

abstract: Deep neural networks have been embraced as models of sensory systems, instantiating representational transformations that appear to resemble those in the visual and auditory systems. To more thoroughly investigate their similarity to biological systems, we synthesized model metamers – stimuli that produce the same responses at some stage of a network’s representation. We generated model metamers for natural stimuli by performing gradient descent on a noise signal, matching the responses of individual layers of image and audio networks to a natural image or speech signal. The resulting signals reflect the invariances instantiated in the network up to the matched layer. We then measured whether model metamers were recognizable to human observers – a necessary condition for the model representations to replicate those of humans. Although model metamers from early network layers were recognizable to humans, those from deeper layers were not. Auditory model metamers became more human-recognizable with architectural modifications that reduced aliasing from pooling operations, but those from the deepest layers remained unrecognizable. We also used the metamer test to compare model representations. Cross-model metamer recognition dropped off for deeper layers, roughly at the same point that human recognition deteriorated, indicating divergence across model representations. The results reveal discrepancies between model and human representations, but also show how metamers can help guide model refinement and elucidate model representations.

title: Metamers of neural networks reveal divergence from human perceptual systems

abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of how a reinforcement learning agent that is tasked with solving a sequence of reinforcement learning problems (a sequence of Markov decision processes) can use knowledge acquired early in its lifetime to improve its ability to solve new problems. We argue that previous experience with similar problems can provide an agent with information about how it should explore when facing a new but related problem. We show that the search for an optimal exploration strategy can be formulated as a reinforcement learning problem itself and demonstrate that such strategy can leverage patterns found in the structure of related problems. We conclude with experiments that show the benefits of optimizing an exploration strategy using our proposed framework.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent facing a sequence of related problems can potentially reuse more than solutions to individual tasks. It can also reuse experience about how to explore. This paper studies how knowledge gained earlier in an agent’s lifetime can help it gather useful information when a new problem arrives.

The central move is to treat the search for an exploration strategy as another reinforcement learning problem. The original problems are Markov decision processes, and the proposed framework places the choice of how to explore at a higher level. This makes exploration itself something the agent can optimize through experience across related problems.

The authors demonstrate that an exploration strategy learned this way can exploit recurring structure among tasks. Their experiments show benefits from optimizing exploration within the proposed framework. The contribution is therefore a way to transfer experience about learning behavior: earlier tasks can inform how the agent investigates a new task, helping it use similarities between problems while seeking a solution.
summary.tldr: The paper formulates learning how to explore related reinforcement learning tasks as a reinforcement learning problem itself.

title: A Meta-MDP Approach to Exploration for Lifelong Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many machine learning models operate on images, but ignore the fact that images are 2D projections formed by 3D geometry interacting with light, in a process called rendering. Enabling ML models to understand image formation might be key for generalization. However, due to an essential rasterization step involving discrete assignment operations, rendering pipelines are non-differentiable and thus largely inaccessible to gradient-based ML techniques. In this paper, we present DIB-Render, a novel rendering framework through which gradients can be analytically computed. Key to our approach is to view rasterization as a weighted interpolation, allowing image gradients to back-propagate through various standard vertex shaders within a single framework. Our approach supports optimizing over vertex positions, colors, normals, light directions and texture coordinates, and allows us to incorporate various well-known lighting models from graphics. We showcase our approach in two ML applications: single-image 3D object prediction, and 3D textured object generation, both trained using exclusively 2D supervision.

The broader suggestion that understanding image formation may improve generalization remains a motivation, while the demonstrated contribution is the rendering framework and these two applications.
summary.tldr: DIB-Render makes rendering differentiable through weighted interpolation, enabling 3D object learning with exclusively 2D supervision.

title: Learning to Predict 3D Objects with an Interpolation-based Differentiable Renderer

abstract: Flow models have recently made great progress at modeling ordinal discrete data such as images and audio. Due to the continuous nature of flow models, dequantization is typically applied when using them for such discrete data, resulting in lower bound estimates of the likelihood. In this paper, we introduce subset flows, a class of flows that can tractably transform finite volumes and thus allow exact computation of likelihoods for discrete data. Based on subset flows, we identify ordinal discrete autoregressive models, including WaveNets, PixelCNNs and Transformers, as single-layer flows. We use the flow formulation to compare models trained and evaluated with either the exact likelihood or its dequantization lower bound. Finally, we study multilayer flows composed of PixelCNNs and non-autoregressive coupling layers and demonstrate state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10 for flow models trained with dequantization.

This paper introduces subset flows to address that mismatch between the data and the model’s mathematical representation.

Through this formulation, the authors identify discrete autoregressive models such as PixelCNNs, WaveNets, and Transformers as single-layer flows. This supplies a common framework for comparing models trained and evaluated with exact likelihood against those using a dequantization lower bound.

The paper also investigates multilayer flows combining PixelCNNs with non-autoregressive coupling layers. These models achieve the reported state of the art on CIFAR-10 within the category of flow models trained with dequantization. The contribution connects exact discrete modeling with flow architectures while also showing that the resulting perspective can inform competitive multilayer models.
summary.tldr: Subset flows enable exact discrete likelihoods and reveal familiar autoregressive models as single-layer flows.

title: Closing the Dequantization Gap: PixelCNN as a Single-Layer Flow

abstract: Learning to plan for long horizons is a central challenge in episodic reinforcement learning problems. A fundamental question is to understand how the difficulty of the problem scales as the horizon increases. Here the natural measure of sample complexity is a normalized one: we are interested in the \emph{number of episodes} it takes to provably discover a policy whose value is $\varepsilon$ near to that of the optimal value, where the value is measured by the \emph{normalized} cumulative reward in each episode. In a COLT 2018 open problem, Jiang and Agarwal conjectured that, for tabular, episodic reinforcement learning problems, there exists a sample complexity lower bound which exhibits a polynomial dependence on the horizon --- a conjecture which is consistent with all known sample complexity upper bounds. This work refutes this conjecture, proving that tabular, episodic reinforcement learning is possible with a sample complexity that scales only \emph{logarithmically} with the planning horizon. In other words, when the values are appropriately normalized (to lie in the unit interval), this results shows that long horizon RL is no more difficult than short horizon RL, at least in a minimax sense. Our analysis introduces two ideas: (i) the construction of an $\varepsilon$-net for near-optimal policies whose log-covering number scales only logarithmically with the planning horizon, and (ii) the Online Trajectory Synthesis algorithm, which adaptively evaluates all policies in a given policy class and enjoys a sample complexity that scales logarithmically with the cardinality of the given policy class. Both may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper asks how the number of episodes needed to learn a near-optimal policy changes as planning horizons grow. It studies tabular, episodic reinforcement learning with cumulative rewards normalized to the unit interval. This normalization keeps the accuracy target comparable across horizons, rather than letting longer episodes automatically increase the scale of the value being estimated.

The authors prove that the required episode count can depend only logarithmically on the horizon. This refutes a conjecture that a polynomial dependence was unavoidable. The conclusion concerns normalized values and minimax sample complexity measured in episodes; it does not equate an episode's length with its count.

Second, Online Trajectory Synthesis adaptively evaluates a supplied policy class using a number of episodes that scales logarithmically with the class's size. Together, these ideas show that long planning horizons need not impose the previously conjectured growth in episode requirements under the paper's formulation.
summary.tldr: For tabular episodic reinforcement learning with normalized rewards, near-optimal learning can require only logarithmic dependence on horizon in the number of episodes.

title: Is Long Horizon RL More Difficult Than Short Horizon RL?

abstract: Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs) have wide-ranging applications in machine learning and the natural and social sciences. In most of the settings in which they are applied, the number of observed samples is much smaller than the dimension and they are assumed to be sparse. While there are a variety of algorithms (e.g. Graphical Lasso, CLIME) that provably recover the graph structure with a logarithmic number of samples, to do so they require various assumptions on the well-conditioning of the precision matrix that are not information-theoretically necessary. Here we give the first fixed polynomial-time algorithms for learning attractive GGMs and walk-summable GGMs with a logarithmic number of samples without any such assumptions. In particular, our algorithms can tolerate strong dependencies among the variables. Our result for structure recovery in walk-summable GGMs is derived from a more general result for efficient sparse linear regression in walk-summable models without any norm dependencies. We complement our results with experiments showing that many existing algorithms fail even in some simple settings where there are long dependency chains. Our algorithms do not.

paragraphs: Gaussian graphical models describe relationships among variables through a graph. Learning that graph is especially useful when there are many variables but relatively few observations, and the graph is assumed to be sparse. Existing recovery guarantees often require the precision matrix to be well-conditioned, restricting the dependencies the methods can handle.

The paper gives fixed polynomial-time algorithms for two particular families: attractive and walk-summable Gaussian graphical models. They recover structure with a logarithmic number of samples without those conditioning assumptions. This allows strong dependencies among variables within the studied families. The walk-summable result follows from a broader sparse linear regression result that also avoids norm dependencies.

Experiments complement the guarantees by examining settings with long dependency chains. The authors report that many existing algorithms fail even in simple examples of this kind, while their algorithms do not. The contribution is therefore both computational and statistical: it removes an unnecessary conditioning requirement for these model classes while retaining efficient learning and favorable sample requirements.
summary.tldr: Efficient algorithms learn attractive and walk-summable Gaussian graphical models without conditioning assumptions, even with strong variable dependencies.

title: Learning Some Popular Gaussian Graphical Models without Condition Number Bounds

abstract: We consider the phase retrieval problem of reconstructing a $n$-dimensional real or complex signal $\mathbf{X}^\star$ from $m$ (possibly noisy) observations $Y_\mu = | \sum_{i=1}^n \Phi_{\mu i} X^{\star}_i/\sqrt{n}|$, for a large class of correlated real and complex random sensing matrices $\mathbf{\Phi}$, in a high-dimensional setting where $m,n\to\infty$ while $\alpha = m/n=\Theta(1)$. First, we derive sharp asymptotics for the lowest possible estimation error achievable statistically and we unveil the existence of sharp phase transitions for the weak- and full-recovery thresholds as a function of the singular values of the matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$. This is achieved by providing a rigorous proof of a result first obtained by the replica method from statistical mechanics. In particular, the information-theoretic transition to perfect recovery for full-rank matrices appears at $\alpha=1$ (real case) and $\alpha=2$ (complex case). Secondly, we analyze the performance of the best-known polynomial time algorithm for this problem --- approximate message-passing--- establishing the existence of statistical-to-algorithmic gap depending, again, on the spectral properties of $\mathbf{\Phi}$. Our work provides an extensive classification of the statistical and algorithmic thresholds in high-dimensional phase retrieval for a broad class of random matrices.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval reconstructs a signal from measurements that retain magnitudes but lose phase information. This paper studies real and complex signals measured through a broad class of correlated random sensing matrices. Its analysis concerns a high-dimensional limit where the number of measurements and signal dimensions grow together at a fixed-order ratio.

The authors derive sharp asymptotic limits on the smallest statistically achievable estimation error. They identify abrupt changes in weak and full recovery that depend on the sensing matrix's singular values. A rigorous proof supports a result previously obtained through the replica method. Its performance can fall short of the statistical limit, with the gap again depending on spectral properties. The findings distinguish information available in the measurements from information this algorithm can recover, organizing both thresholds by sensing-matrix structure.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes statistical recovery thresholds and approximate-message-passing gaps in high-dimensional phase retrieval through sensing-matrix spectra.

title: Phase retrieval in high dimensions: Statistical and computational phase transitions

abstract: Deep neural networks can empirically perform efficient hierarchical learning, in which the layers learn useful representations of the data. However, how they make use of the intermediate representations are not explained by recent theories that relate them to ``shallow learners'' such as kernels. In this work, we demonstrate that intermediate \emph{neural representations} add more flexibility to neural networks and can be advantageous over raw inputs. We consider a fixed, randomly initialized neural network as a representation function fed into another trainable network. When the trainable network is the quadratic Taylor model of a wide two-layer network, we show that neural representation can achieve improved sample complexities compared with the raw input: For learning a low-rank degree-$p$ polynomial ($p \geq 4$) in $d$ dimension, neural representation requires only $\widetilde{O}(d^{\ceil{p/2}})$ samples, while the best-known sample complexity upper bound for the raw input is $\widetilde{O}(d^{p-1})$. We contrast our result with a lower bound showing that neural representations do not improve over the raw input (in the infinite width limit), when the trainable network is instead a neural tangent kernel. Our results characterize when neural representations are beneficial, and may provide a new perspective on why depth is important in deep learning.
