paragraphs: Gaussian processes produce uncertainty estimates, but those estimates can be miscalibrated and lack frequentist guarantees. Existing calibration approaches enlarge the posterior variance, which can make predictive intervals excessively broad. The paper addresses the challenge of producing uncertainty estimates that satisfy calibration requirements while remaining tight enough to be informative.

The proposed method generates predictive quantiles using a computation inspired by ordinary Gaussian-process posterior variance. It introduces a different set of hyperparameters chosen to satisfy an empirical calibration constraint. This creates more flexibility than variance inflation alone, and the authors optimize that flexibility to obtain tight predictive quantiles.

The paper establishes calibration under reasonable assumptions and reports better sharpness than existing approaches in calibrated regression. Here, sharpness concerns how tightly the predictions express uncertainty, so the improvement addresses the loss of precision that can accompany calibration. The central contribution is a way to adjust uncertainty through a flexible constrained computation, with both a conditional calibration result and empirical evidence of tighter predictions.
summary.tldr: A flexible Gaussian-process calibration method learns predictive quantiles that satisfy calibration constraints while improving sharpness.

title: Sharp Calibrated Gaussian Processes

abstract: Instance detection (InsDet) is a long-lasting problem in robotics and computer vision, aiming to detect object instances (predefined by some visual examples) in a cluttered scene. Despite its practical significance, its advancement is overshadowed by Object Detection, which aims to detect objects belonging to some predefined classes. One major reason is that current InsDet datasets are too small in scale by today's standards. For example, the popular InsDet dataset GMU (published in 2016) has only 23 instances, far less than COCO (80 classes), a well-known object detection dataset published in 2014. We are motivated to introduce a new InsDet dataset and protocol. First, we define a realistic setup for InsDet: training data consists of multi-view instance captures, along with diverse scene images allowing synthesizing training images by pasting instance images on them with free box annotations. Second, we release a real-world database, which contains multi-view capture of 100 object instances, and high-resolution (6k$\times$8k) testing images. Third, we extensively study baseline methods for InsDet on our dataset, analyze their performance and suggest future work. Somewhat surprisingly, using the off-the-shelf class-agnostic segmentation model (Segment Anything Model, SAM) and the self-supervised feature representation DINOv2 performs the best, achieving $>$10 AP better than end-to-end trained InsDet models that repurpose object detectors (e.g., FasterRCNN and RetinaNet).

This differs from recognizing an object category: the target is the specific instance. The paper addresses a shortage of sufficiently large datasets for studying this problem, which has received less attention than category-level object detection.

The authors introduce a dataset containing captures of 100 objects from multiple viewpoints and testing images at 6,000 by 8,000 pixels. Their training protocol combines these object captures with varied scene backgrounds. Pasting object images into scenes produces synthetic training examples whose bounding boxes are available from the construction process.

The benchmark also compares detection approaches. Combining the existing SAM segmentation model with DINOv2 features performs best, exceeding adapted end-to-end object detectors by more than 10 AP. Within this evaluation, that result shows the strength of combining general segmentation and learned visual representations, while providing a concrete reference point for future instance-detection methods.
summary.tldr: A new instance-detection dataset finds that combining SAM and DINOv2 outperforms adapted object detectors by more than 10 AP.

title: A High-Resolution Dataset for Instance Detection with Multi-View Object Capture

abstract: In this paper, we provide a rigorous proof of convergence of the Adaptive Moment Estimate (Adam) algorithm for a wide class of optimization objectives. Despite the popularity and efficiency of the Adam algorithm in training deep neural networks, its theoretical properties are not yet fully understood, and existing convergence proofs require unrealistically strong assumptions, such as globally bounded gradients, to show the convergence to stationary points. In this paper, we show that Adam provably converges to $\epsilon$-stationary points with $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ gradient complexity under far more realistic conditions. The key to our analysis is a new proof of boundedness of gradients along the optimization trajectory of Adam, under a generalized smoothness assumption according to which the local smoothness (i.e., Hessian norm when it exists) is bounded by a sub-quadratic function of the gradient norm. Moreover, we propose a variance-reduced version of Adam with an accelerated gradient complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$.

paragraphs: Adam is widely used to train neural networks, but proving its convergence has often required strong assumptions about the optimization objective. One example is requiring gradients to be bounded everywhere. This paper develops a convergence argument for a broad class of objectives under a more flexible smoothness condition.

The key step is proving that gradients remain bounded along Adam's own optimization trajectory. The generalized smoothness assumption allows local curvature, expressed by the Hessian norm when available, to grow with gradient size according to a subquadratic function. The proof therefore derives the bound needed along the visited path instead of assuming a global gradient bound.

Under the paper's conditions, Adam reaches an epsilon-stationary point with gradient complexity O(epsilon^-4). Such a point has a sufficiently small gradient; the result concerns stationarity rather than a guarantee of a global optimum. The authors also propose a variance-reduced Adam variant with improved complexity O(epsilon^-3). Together, the results strengthen the theoretical foundation of Adam and identify a variant with a faster stated convergence rate.
summary.tldr: Adam provably reaches approximate stationary points under generalized smoothness assumptions, and a variance-reduced variant improves its gradient complexity.

title: Convergence of Adam Under Relaxed Assumptions

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved great success in modeling continuous data modalities such as images, audio, and video, but have seen limited use in discrete domains such as language. Recent attempts to adapt diffusion to language have presented diffusion as an alternative to existing pretrained language models. We view diffusion and existing language models as complementary. We demonstrate that encoder-decoder language models can be utilized to efficiently learn high-quality language autoencoders. We then demonstrate that continuous diffusion models can be learned in the latent space of the language autoencoder, enabling us to sample continuous latent representations that can be decoded into natural language with the pretrained decoder. We validate the effectiveness of our approach for unconditional, class-conditional, and sequence-to-sequence language generation. We demonstrate across multiple diverse data sets that our latent language diffusion models are significantly more effective than previous diffusion language models. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/justinlovelace/latent-diffusion-for-language}.

paragraphs: Diffusion models work naturally with continuous representations, while language consists of discrete tokens. This mismatch has complicated their use for text generation. The paper treats diffusion and pretrained language models as complementary components, using the language model to connect text with a continuous space where diffusion can operate.

The authors first use encoder-decoder language models to learn high-quality language autoencoders efficiently. The encoder supplies latent representations of text, and a continuous diffusion model is trained within that latent space. During generation, diffusion produces a continuous representation that the pretrained decoder converts into natural language. This gives each component a distinct role in the generation process.

The approach is evaluated for unconditional generation, class-conditioned generation, and sequence-to-sequence generation. Across multiple diverse datasets, the authors report significantly better effectiveness than previous diffusion language models. These findings support latent-space diffusion as a way to build on existing language-model capabilities. The reported comparison is specifically with earlier diffusion approaches, rather than a claim of superiority over every language generation method.
summary.tldr: The method generates continuous language representations with diffusion and decodes them using a pretrained language model.

title: Latent Diffusion for Language Generation

abstract: Privacy-Preserving Action Recognition (PPAR) aims to transform raw videos into anonymous ones to prevent privacy leakage while maintaining action clues, which is an increasingly important problem in intelligent vision applications. Despite recent efforts in this task, it is still challenging to deal with novel privacy attributes and novel privacy attack models that are unavailable during the training phase. In this paper, from the perspective of meta-learning (learning to learn), we propose a novel Meta Privacy-Preserving Action Recognition (MPPAR) framework to improve both generalization abilities above (i.e., generalize to *novel privacy attributes* and *novel privacy attack models*) in a unified manner. Concretely, we simulate train/test task shifts by constructing disjoint support/query sets w.r.t. privacy attributes or attack models. Then, a virtual training and testing scheme is applied based on support/query sets to provide feedback to optimize the model's learning toward better generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of the proposed framework compared to state-of-the-arts.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving action recognition transforms videos to hide private information while retaining clues about the actions being performed. A difficult deployment problem is that privacy risks can change: new sensitive attributes or new attack models may appear after training. This paper develops a framework that trains for generalization along both of those dimensions.

The proposed Meta Privacy-Preserving Action Recognition framework uses meta-learning to simulate these changes during training. It constructs separate support and query sets that differ in privacy attributes or attack models. A virtual training-and-testing procedure then measures how learning on one set transfers to the other. That feedback guides the model toward handling the kinds of differences it may encounter later.

Experiments report improved effectiveness and generalization compared with state-of-the-art approaches. The key contribution is making unfamiliar attributes and unfamiliar attackers part of the training objective through simulated task shifts. This supports better adaptation to the tested privacy changes while preserving the action-recognition purpose of the transformed videos; the reported findings do not amount to universal protection against every possible future attack.
summary.tldr: Meta-learning improves video anonymization’s generalization to privacy attributes and attack models absent during training.

title: Joint Attribute and Model Generalization Learning for Privacy-Preserving Action Recognition

abstract: Within a single sniff, the mammalian olfactory system can decode the identity and concentration of odorants wafted on turbulent plumes of air. Yet, it must do so given access only to the noisy, dimensionally-reduced representation of the odor world provided by olfactory receptor neurons. As a result, the olfactory system must solve a compressed sensing problem, relying on the fact that only a handful of the millions of possible odorants are present in a given scene. Inspired by this principle, past works have proposed normative compressed sensing models for olfactory decoding. However, these models have not captured the unique anatomy and physiology of the olfactory bulb, nor have they shown that sensing can be achieved within the 100-millisecond timescale of a single sniff. Here, we propose a rate-based Poisson compressed sensing circuit model for the olfactory bulb. This model maps onto the neuron classes of the olfactory bulb, and recapitulates salient features of their connectivity and physiology. For circuit sizes comparable to the human olfactory bulb, we show that this model can accurately detect tens of odors within the timescale of a single sniff. We also show that this model can perform Bayesian posterior sampling for accurate uncertainty estimation. Fast inference is possible only if the geometry of the neural code is chosen to match receptor properties, yielding a distributed neural code that is not axis-aligned to individual odor identities. Our results illustrate how normative modeling can help us map function onto specific neural circuits to generate new hypotheses.

paragraphs: Identifying odors requires recovering a few active odorants from noisy receptor signals that compress a much larger space of possibilities. This paper models that task as Poisson compressed sensing. It asks how an olfactory-bulb circuit could carry out the computation quickly enough to fit within a single sniff.

The proposed rate-based circuit corresponds to neuron classes in the olfactory bulb and reproduces salient aspects of their connectivity and physiology. It can also sample from a Bayesian posterior to estimate uncertainty about the inferred odors.

A central finding is that fast inference requires the geometry of the neural code to match receptor properties. The resulting representation distributes information across the code rather than aligning its axes with individual odor identities. These are results about the proposed model, which connects a computational objective to circuit organization and generates hypotheses about how biological olfactory processing could work.
summary.tldr: A biologically motivated circuit model decodes sparse odor mixtures within a sniff when its neural code matches receptor properties.

title: Neural Circuits for Fast Poisson Compressed Sensing in the Olfactory Bulb

abstract: The past decade has witnessed the flourishing of a new profession as media content creators, who rely on revenue streams from online content recommendation platforms. The reward mechanism employed by these platforms creates a competitive environment among creators which affects their production choices and, consequently, content distribution and system welfare. It is thus crucial to design the platform's reward mechanism in order to steer the creators' competition towards a desirable welfare outcome in the long run. This work makes two major contributions in this regard: first, we uncover a fundamental limit about a class of widely adopted mechanisms, coined \emph{Merit-based Monotone Mechanisms}, by showing that they inevitably lead to a constant fraction loss of the optimal welfare. To circumvent this limitation, we introduce \emph{Backward Rewarding Mechanisms} (BRMs) and show that the competition game resultant from BRMs possesses a potential game structure. BRMs thus naturally induce strategic creators' collective behaviors towards optimizing the potential function, which can be designed to match any given welfare metric. In addition, the class of BRM can be parameterized so that it allows the platform to directly optimize welfare within the feasible mechanism space even when the welfare metric is not explicitly defined.

Because creators compete strategically, a reward rule also shapes the resulting content distribution and overall system welfare. This paper studies how platforms can design those incentives to guide competition toward desirable long-term outcomes.

The authors identify a fundamental limitation of a class called Merit-based Monotone Mechanisms. Within the studied framework, these mechanisms necessarily lose a constant fraction of the optimal welfare. The result concerns this particular class of reward rules and motivates looking beyond it when designing incentives for competing creators.

The proposed Backward Rewarding Mechanisms generate competition with a potential-game structure: creators' strategic behavior is directed toward optimizing a shared potential function. The authors show that this function can be designed to match any given welfare metric. They also describe a parameterization allowing direct welfare optimization within the feasible mechanism space when the metric is not explicitly defined. This connects reward design to the collective objective the platform wants creator competition to serve.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a welfare limit for merit-based monotone rewards and proposes mechanisms that align creator competition with a chosen welfare objective.

title: Rethinking Incentives in Recommender Systems: Are Monotone Rewards Always Beneficial?

abstract: Analysis of compressible turbulent flows is essential for applications related to propulsion, energy generation, and the environment. Here, we present BLASTNet 2.0, a 2.2 TB network-of-datasets containing 744 full-domain samples from 34 high-fidelity direct numerical simulations, which addresses the current limited availability of 3D high-fidelity reacting and non-reacting compressible turbulent flow simulation data. With this data, we benchmark a total of 49 variations of five deep learning approaches for 3D super-resolution - which can be applied for improving scientific imaging, simulations, turbulence models, as well as in computer vision applications. We perform neural scaling analysis on these models to examine the performance of different machine learning (ML) approaches, including two scientific ML techniques. We demonstrate that (i) predictive performance can scale with model size and cost, (ii) architecture matters significantly, especially for smaller models, and (iii) the benefits of physics-based losses can persist with increasing model size. The outcomes of this benchmark study are anticipated to offer insights that can aid the design of 3D super-resolution models, especially for turbulence models, while this data is expected to foster ML methods for a broad range of flow physics applications. This data is publicly available with download links and browsing tools consolidated at https://blastnet.github.io.

BLASTNet 2.0 provides a 2.2-terabyte collection containing 744 full-domain samples from 34 direct numerical simulations. It covers both reacting and non-reacting flows, supporting research on physical systems relevant to propulsion, energy, and the environment.

The authors use this collection to benchmark 49 variants of five deep learning approaches for 3D super-resolution, which aims to recover finer spatial detail. Their scaling analysis examines how predictive performance changes with model size and computational cost. The comparison includes two scientific machine learning techniques.

Three findings emerge: predictive performance can improve with scale, architecture choices matter substantially for smaller models, and benefits from physics-based losses can persist as models grow. These observations make size only one consideration in designing a super-resolution model. The benchmark provides evidence about architecture and training objectives alongside a public data resource expected to support broader machine learning research in flow physics.
summary.tldr: BLASTNet 2.0 benchmarks 3D turbulence super-resolution, showing how model scale, architecture, and physics-based losses affect performance.

title: Turbulence in Focus: Benchmarking Scaling Behavior of 3D Volumetric Super-Resolution with BLASTNet 2.0 Data

abstract: We propose a new variant of the Adam optimizer called MicroAdam that specifically minimizes memory overheads, while maintaining theoretical convergence guarantees. We achieve this by compressing the gradient information before it is fed into the optimizer state, thereby reducing its memory footprint significantly. We control the resulting compression error via a novel instance of the classical *error feedback* mechanism from distributed optimization in which *the error correction information is itself compressed* to allow for practical memory gains. We prove that the resulting approach maintains theoretical convergence guarantees competitive to those of AMSGrad, while providing good practical performance. Specifically, we show that MicroAdam can be implemented efficiently on GPUs: on both million-scale (BERT) and billion-scale (LLaMA) models, MicroAdam provides practical convergence competitive to that of the uncompressed Adam baseline, with lower memory usage and similar running time. Our code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/MicroAdam.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers maintain information about gradients as training proceeds, creating memory costs beyond storing the model itself. MicroAdam modifies Adam to reduce that optimizer overhead while retaining convergence guarantees. Its central strategy is to compress gradient information before incorporating it into the optimizer’s stored state.

Compression introduces error, so the method uses error feedback to account for information lost during compression. Its distinctive feature is that the correction information is also compressed. This matters because maintaining a large, uncompressed correction would consume memory and undermine the practical benefit of compressing the optimizer state. The design addresses both the main state and the bookkeeping needed to control approximation error.

The paper proves convergence guarantees competitive with AMSGrad and presents an efficient GPU implementation. Experiments on million-scale BERT and billion-scale LLaMA models show practical convergence competitive with uncompressed Adam, alongside lower memory use and similar running time. The reported benefit is therefore reduced optimizer memory without an observed training-time penalty or loss of competitive convergence in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: MicroAdam compresses gradients and error corrections to reduce optimizer memory while maintaining theoretical guarantees and competitive practical convergence.

title: MicroAdam: Accurate Adaptive Optimization with Low Space Overhead and Provable Convergence

abstract: Implicit models such as Deep Equilibrium Models (DEQs) have emerged as promising alternative approaches for building deep neural networks. Their certified robustness has gained increasing research attention due to security concerns. Existing certified defenses for DEQs employing interval bound propagation and Lipschitz-bounds not only offer conservative certification bounds but also are restricted to specific forms of DEQs. In this paper, we provide the first randomized smoothing certified defense for DEQs to solve these limitations. Our study reveals that simply applying randomized smoothing to certify DEQs provides certified robustness generalized to large-scale datasets but incurs extremely expensive computation costs. To reduce computational redundancy, we propose a novel Serialized Randomized Smoothing (SRS) approach that leverages historical information. Additionally, we derive a new certified radius estimation for SRS to theoretically ensure the correctness of our algorithm. Extensive experiments and ablation studies on image recognition demonstrate that our algorithm can significantly accelerate the certification of DEQs by up to 7x almost without sacrificing the certified accuracy. The implementation will be publicly available upon the acceptance of this work. Our code is available at https://github.com/WeizhiGao/Serialized-Randomized-Smoothing.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to certify robustness for Deep Equilibrium Models, a class of implicit neural networks. A robustness certificate establishes a region of input changes within which a prediction is protected. Existing approaches based on interval propagation or Lipschitz bounds give conservative certificates and apply only to particular forms of these models.

The authors first investigate randomized smoothing as a more broadly applicable certification approach. They find that it extends to large-scale datasets, but straightforward application is computationally expensive. Their Serialized Randomized Smoothing method reuses historical information to reduce redundant computation. Because this changes the certification procedure, they also derive a new estimate of the certified radius to establish its theoretical correctness.

Image-recognition experiments and ablation studies report certification speedups of up to seven times, with almost no loss in certified accuracy. The result matters because certification itself can be a substantial computational burden. The contribution therefore combines a more efficient procedure with a matching correctness argument, while the reported speed and accuracy tradeoff remains an empirical finding.
summary.tldr: Serialized Randomized Smoothing reuses prior computation to certify Deep Equilibrium Models up to seven times faster with almost unchanged certified accuracy.

title: Certified Robustness for Deep Equilibrium Models via Serialized Random Smoothing

abstract: We study the interplay between local differential privacy (LDP) and robustness to Huber corruption and possibly heavy-tailed rewards in the context of multi-armed bandits (MABs). We consider two different practical settings: LDP-then-Corruption (LTC) where each user's locally private response might be further corrupted during the data collection process, and Corruption-then-LDP (CTL) where each user's raw data may be corrupted such that the LDP mechanism will only be applied to the corrupted data. To start with, we present the first tight characterization of the mean estimation error in high probability under both LTC and CTL settings. Leveraging this new result, we then present an almost tight characterization (up to log factor) of the minimax regret in online MABs and sub-optimality in offline MABs under both LTC and CTL settings, respectively. Our theoretical results in both settings are also corroborated by a set of systematic simulations. One key message in this paper is that LTC is a more difficult setting that leads to a worse performance guarantee compared to the CTL setting (in the minimax sense). Our sharp understanding of LTC and CTL also naturally allows us to give the first tight performance bounds for the most practical setting where corruption could happen both before and after the LDP mechanism. As an important by-product, we also give the first correct and tight regret bound for locally private and heavy-tailed online MABs, i.e., without Huber corruption, by identifying a fundamental flaw in the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Multi-armed bandit methods learn which actions yield better rewards, but their observations may require privacy protection and may also be corrupted. This paper studies those problems together, allowing rewards to be heavy-tailed. It distinguishes corruption after a locally private response is produced from corruption of raw data before privacy protection is applied.

The authors first establish tight high-probability bounds for estimating a mean in both settings. They then derive nearly tight bounds, up to logarithmic factors, for online regret and offline decision suboptimality. These characterize worst-case achievable performance, and systematic simulations corroborate the theoretical results.

A central finding is that corruption after privacy protection is harder in the minimax sense than corruption beforehand. The analysis also yields tight bounds when corruption can occur on both sides of the privacy mechanism. As a further result, the paper identifies a flaw in earlier work and supplies a correct tight regret bound for locally private online bandits with heavy-tailed rewards and no Huber corruption.
summary.tldr: Tight performance bounds show that bandit learning is harder when data corruption follows local privacy protection than when it precedes it.

title: Locally Private and Robust Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: Recent years have witnessed a clear trend towards language models with an ever-increasing number of parameters, as well as the growing training overhead and memory usage. Distributed training, particularly through Sharded Data Parallelism (ShardedDP) which partitions optimizer states among workers, has emerged as a crucial technique to mitigate training time and memory usage. Yet, a major challenge in the scalability of ShardedDP is the intensive communication of weights and gradients. While compression techniques can alleviate this issue, they often result in worse accuracy. Driven by this limitation, we propose SDP4Bit (Toward 4Bit Communication Quantization in Sharded Data Parallelism for LLM Training), which effectively reduces the communication of weights and gradients to nearly 4 bits via two novel techniques: quantization on weight differences, and two-level gradient smooth quantization. Furthermore, SDP4Bit presents an algorithm-system co-design with runtime optimization to minimize the computation overhead of compression. Additional to the theoretical guarantees of convergence, we empirically evaluate the accuracy of SDP4Bit on the pre-training of GPT models with up to 6.7 billion parameters, and the results demonstrate a negligible impact on training loss. Furthermore, speed experiments show that SDP4Bit achieves up to 4.08× speedup in end-to-end throughput on a scale of 128 GPUs.

In sharded data parallelism, this communication can limit scalability even though optimizer states are partitioned. SDP4Bit targets that bottleneck by compressing the communicated information while seeking to preserve training quality.

These results demonstrate substantial gains in the evaluated configurations while keeping the reported training-loss impact small.
summary.tldr: SDP4Bit compresses distributed training communication to nearly four bits, with negligible measured training-loss impact and up to 4.08-fold throughput gains.

title: SDP4Bit: Toward 4-bit Communication Quantization in Sharded Data Parallelism for LLM Training

abstract: While Distributed Machine Learning (DML) has been widely used to achieve decent performance, it is still challenging to take full advantage of data and devices distributed at multiple vantage points to adapt and learn, especially it is non-trivial to address dynamic and divergence challenges based on the linear aggregation framework as follows: (1) heterogeneous learning data at different devices (i.e., non-IID data) resulting in model divergence and (2) in the case of time-varying communication links, the limited ability for devices to reconcile model divergence. In this paper, we contribute a non-linear class aggregation framework HyperPrism that leverages distributed mirror descent with averaging done in the mirror descent dual space and adapts the degree of Weighted Power Mean (WPM) used in each round. Moreover, HyperPrism could adaptively choose different mapping for different layers of the local model with a dedicated hypernetwork per device, achieving automatic optimization of DML in high divergence settings. We perform rigorous analysis and experimental evaluations to demonstrate the effectiveness of adaptive, mirror-mapping DML. In particular, we extend the generalizability of existing related works and position them as special cases within HyperPrism. Our experimental results show that HyperPrism can improve the convergence speed up to 98.63% and scale well to more devices compared with the state-of-the-art, all with little additional computation overhead compared to traditional linear aggregation.

paragraphs: Distributed learning must combine models trained on different devices, even when their data distributions differ. Those differences can push local models apart, while changing communication links restrict opportunities to reconcile them. HyperPrism addresses these coupled problems by replacing a fixed linear aggregation framework with adaptive nonlinear aggregation.

The framework uses distributed mirror descent, performing averaging in its transformed dual space. It adjusts the degree of a weighted power mean in each round, changing how model contributions are combined. A dedicated hypernetwork on each device can also select different mappings for different model layers, allowing aggregation behavior to adapt more finely to model divergence.

The paper provides theoretical analysis and experiments, positioning related existing approaches as special cases of the broader framework. Reported results include convergence-speed improvements of up to 98.63%, good scaling to more devices, and little additional computation compared with traditional linear aggregation. These findings support adapting the combination rule itself when heterogeneous data and unreliable communication make ordinary model averaging less effective.
summary.tldr: HyperPrism adaptively combines distributed models in a transformed space to improve convergence with heterogeneous data and changing communication links.

title: HyperPrism: An Adaptive Non-linear Aggregation Framework for Distributed Machine Learning over Non-IID Data and Time-varying Communication Links

abstract: The CLIP network excels in various tasks, but struggles with text-visual images i.e., images that contain both text and visual objects; it risks confusing textual and visual representations. To address this issue, we propose MirrorCLIP, a zero-shot framework, which disentangles the image features of CLIP by exploiting the difference in the mirror effect between visual objects and text in the images. Specifically, MirrorCLIP takes both original and flipped images as inputs, comparing their features dimension-wise in the latent space to generate disentangling masks. With disentangling masks, we further design filters to separate textual and visual factors more precisely, and then get disentangled representations. Qualitative experiments using stable diffusion models and class activation mapping (CAM) validate the effectiveness of our disentanglement. Moreover, our proposed MirrorCLIP reduces confusion when encountering text-visual images and achieves a substantial improvement on typographic defense, further demonstrating its superior ability of disentanglement. Our code is available at https://github.com/tcwangbuaa/MirrorCLIP

paragraphs: MirrorCLIP addresses a source of confusion in CLIP: images can contain both visible objects and written text, and their representations can become mixed. The paper proposes a zero-shot framework that separates these factors by exploiting the different effects that mirroring has on text and visual objects.

The framework processes an original image and its flipped version, then compares their feature values dimension by dimension in CLIP's latent space. Those comparisons produce masks intended to disentangle the two kinds of information. Additional filters use the masks to separate textual and visual factors more precisely, yielding representations that distinguish the content channels.

The authors assess the separation qualitatively through stable diffusion models and class activation mapping. They also report reduced confusion on images containing text and objects, together with a substantial improvement in typographic defense. These findings support the usefulness of reflection as a signal for disentanglement: the method uses changes between two views of the same image to identify information that CLIP otherwise risks conflating.
summary.tldr: MirrorCLIP compares original and flipped images to separate textual and visual features and reduce CLIP's confusion.

title: CLIP in Mirror: Disentangling text from visual images through reflection

abstract: Due to the increasing popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI), more and more backdoor attacks are designed to mislead Deep Neural Network (DNN) predictions by manipulating training samples or processes. Although backdoor attacks have been investigated in various scenarios, they still suffer from the problems of both low fidelity of poisoned samples and non-negligible transfer in latent space, which make them easily identified by existing backdoor detection algorithms. To overcome this weakness, this paper proposes a novel frequency-based backdoor attack method named WaveAttack, which obtains high-frequency image features through Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) to generate highly stealthy backdoor triggers. By introducing an asymmetric frequency obfuscation method, our approach adds an adaptive residual to the training and inference stages to improve the impact of triggers, thus further enhancing the effectiveness of WaveAttack. Comprehensive experimental results show that, WaveAttack can not only achieve higher effectiveness than state-of-the-art backdoor attack methods, but also outperform them in the fidelity of images (i.e., by up to 28.27\% improvement in PSNR, 1.61\% improvement in SSIM, and 70.59\% reduction in IS). Our code is available at https://github.com/BililiCode/WaveAttack.

paragraphs: WaveAttack studies backdoor attacks that manipulate training samples or training processes to mislead a neural network. The paper identifies two weaknesses in earlier approaches: poisoned images can look noticeably altered, and their internal representations can shift enough to aid detection. Its objective is to improve attack effectiveness while preserving the visual fidelity of manipulated images.

The method uses the Discrete Wavelet Transform to obtain high-frequency image features for constructing subtle triggers. It also introduces asymmetric frequency obfuscation, with an adaptive residual used during training and inference to strengthen the triggers’ impact. These components connect the frequency-based representation with the attack’s behavior across the two stages.

The authors report greater effectiveness than state-of-the-art backdoor methods, along with improved image fidelity. Reported improvements reach 28.27% for PSNR and 1.61% for SSIM, with a reduction of up to 70.59% in IS. The findings show that, in the evaluated comparisons, a more effective attack can also leave images closer to their originals. This makes visual fidelity an important part of the paper’s assessment of backdoor stealth.
summary.tldr: WaveAttack uses frequency-based triggers and adaptive residuals to improve backdoor effectiveness while preserving image fidelity.

title: WaveAttack: Asymmetric Frequency Obfuscation-based Backdoor Attacks Against Deep Neural Networks

abstract: As part of the effort to understand how the brain learns, ongoing research seeks to combine biological knowledge with current artificial intelligence (AI) modeling in an attempt to find an efficient biologically plausible learning scheme. Current models often use a cortical-like combination of bottom-up (BU) and top-down (TD) processing, where the TD part carries feedback signals for learning. However, in the visual cortex, the TD pathway plays a second major role in visual attention, by guiding the visual process toward locations and tasks of interest. A biological model should therefore integrate both learning and visual guidance. We introduce a model that uses a cortical-like combination of BU and TD processing that naturally integrates the two major functions of the TD stream. This integration is achieved through an appropriate connectivity pattern between the BU and TD streams, a novel processing cycle that uses the TD stream twice, and a 'Counter-Hebb' learning mechanism that operates across both streams. We show that the 'Counter-Hebb' mechanism can provide an exact backpropagation synaptic modification. Additionally, our model can effectively guide the visual stream to perform a task of interest, achieving competitive performance on standard multi-task learning benchmarks compared to AI models. The successful combination of learning and visual guidance could provide a new view on combining BU and TD processing in human vision and suggests possible directions for both biologically plausible models and artificial instructed models, such as vision-language models (VLMs).

Additionally, our model can effectively guide the visual stream to perform a task of interest, achieving competitive performance on standard multi-task learning benchmarks compared to AI models. The successful combination of learning and visual guidance could provide a new view on combining BU and TD processing in human vision and suggests possible directions for both biologically plausible models and artificial instructed models, such as vision-language models (VLMs).

paragraphs: This paper develops a visual learning model in which top-down processing serves two purposes: carrying feedback for learning and directing vision toward a requested task or location. Existing biologically motivated models often emphasize the first role. The authors argue that integrating both roles is important for a model intended to reflect how visual processing is organized in the cortex.

Their architecture combines bottom-up and top-down streams through a particular connectivity pattern and a processing cycle that uses the top-down stream twice. A learning mechanism called Counter-Hebb operates across both streams. The paper shows that this mechanism can produce synaptic modifications exactly matching backpropagation, connecting the proposed learning scheme to an established way of training artificial networks.

The model also guides visual processing toward tasks of interest and achieves competitive results against AI models on standard multitask benchmarks. Together, these findings demonstrate that the architecture can support both learning feedback and task guidance. The authors present this combination as a possible direction for biologically plausible vision models and artificial instructed systems, including vision-language models.
summary.tldr: A biologically inspired vision model unifies top-down task guidance with a learning mechanism that can reproduce backpropagation updates.

title: Biologically Inspired Learning Model for Instructed Vision

abstract: Training an agent to achieve particular goals or perform desired behaviors is often accomplished through reinforcement learning, especially in the absence of expert demonstrations. However, supporting novel goals or behaviors through reinforcement learning requires the ad-hoc design of appropriate reward functions, which quickly becomes intractable. To address this challenge, we propose Text-Aware Diffusion for Policy Learning (TADPoLe), which uses a pretrained, frozen text-conditioned diffusion model to compute dense zero-shot reward signals for text-aligned policy learning. We hypothesize that large-scale pretrained generative models encode rich priors that can supervise a policy to behave not only in a text-aligned manner, but also in alignment with a notion of naturalness summarized from internet-scale training data. In our experiments, we demonstrate that TADPoLe is able to learn policies for novel goal-achievement and continuous locomotion behaviors specified by natural language, in both Humanoid and Dog environments. The behaviors are learned zero-shot without ground-truth rewards or expert demonstrations, and are qualitatively more natural according to human evaluation. We further show that TADPoLe performs competitively when applied to robotic manipulation tasks in the Meta-World environment, without having access to any in-domain demonstrations.

title: Text-Aware Diffusion for Policy Learning

abstract: Dataset Distillation (DD) is designed to generate condensed representations of extensive image datasets, enhancing training efficiency. Despite recent advances, there remains considerable potential for improvement, particularly in addressing the notable redundancy within the color space of distilled images. In this paper, we propose a two-fold optimization strategy to minimize color redundancy at the individual image and overall dataset levels, respectively. At the image level, we employ a palette network, a specialized neural network, to dynamically allocate colors from a reduced color space to each pixel. The palette network identifies essential areas in synthetic images for model training, and consequently assigns more unique colors to them. At the dataset level, we develop a color-guided initialization strategy to minimize redundancy among images. Representative images with the least replicated color patterns are selected based on the information gain. A comprehensive performance study involving various datasets and evaluation scenarios is conducted, demonstrating the superior performance of our proposed color-aware DD compared to existing DD methods.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation creates condensed representations of large image collections so that models can train more efficiently. This paper focuses on redundancy in the colors of distilled images. Its premise is that a compact training collection can use its color information more effectively by reducing repetition both within individual images and across the collection.

For individual images, the authors introduce a palette network that assigns pixels colors from a reduced color space. The assignments are adaptive: regions identified as important for model training receive more distinct colors. At the dataset level, a separate initialization strategy selects representative images whose color patterns repeat less, using information gain to guide that selection.

The two components address different sources of wasted capacity. One distributes color detail within synthetic examples, while the other reduces overlap among the examples used to initialize distillation. Evaluations across multiple datasets and scenarios report better performance than existing distillation methods. The findings support treating color allocation and color diversity as explicit parts of the distillation process.
summary.tldr: Color-aware dataset distillation reduces redundant colors within images and repeated color patterns across images to improve condensed training data.

title: Color-Oriented Redundancy Reduction in Dataset Distillation

abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiT) have attracted significant attention in research. However, they suffer from a slow convergence rate. In this paper, we aim to accelerate DiT training without any architectural modification. We identify the following issues in the training process: firstly, certain training strategies do not consistently perform well across different data. Secondly, the effectiveness of supervision at specific timesteps is limited. In response, we propose the following contributions: (1) We introduce a new perspective for interpreting the failure of the strategies. Specifically, we slightly extend the definition of Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and suggest observing the Probability Density Function (PDF) of SNR to understand the essence of the data robustness of the strategy. (2) We conduct numerous experiments and report over one hundred experimental results to empirically summarize a unified accelerating strategy from the perspective of PDF. (3) We develop a new supervision method that further accelerates the training process of DiT. Based on them, we propose FasterDiT, an exceedingly simple and practicable design strategy. With few lines of code modifications, it achieves 2.30 FID on ImageNet at 256x256 resolution with 1000 iterations, which is comparable to DiT (2.27 FID) but 7 times faster in training.

paragraphs: FasterDiT targets slow convergence in diffusion transformers while keeping the model architecture unchanged. The authors identify two training problems: strategies that work well on some data do not consistently transfer to other data, and supervision at certain diffusion timesteps provides limited benefit. Their approach changes the training strategy and supervision.

To understand variation across data, the paper slightly extends the definition of signal-to-noise ratio and examines its probability density. This shifts attention toward how signal-to-noise conditions are distributed during training. Drawing on more than one hundred experimental results, the authors empirically derive a unified acceleration strategy and add a new supervision method for further speed gains.

The resulting FasterDiT strategy requires only a few lines of code changes. The abstract reports an FID of 2.30 on ImageNet at 256×256 resolution with 1000 iterations, compared with 2.27 for DiT, alongside sevenfold faster training. This is a reported comparison of similar generation quality at substantially lower training cost, supporting the value of revising optimization and supervision without changing the architecture.
summary.tldr: FasterDiT revises diffusion-transformer training and supervision, reporting sevenfold faster training with comparable ImageNet generation quality.

title: FasterDiT: Towards Faster Diffusion Transformers Training without Architecture Modification

abstract: In this paper, we propose OpenSatMap, a fine-grained, high-resolution satellite dataset for large-scale map construction. Map construction is one of the foundations of the transportation industry, such as navigation and autonomous driving. Extracting road structures from satellite images is an efficient way to construct large-scale maps. However, existing satellite datasets provide only coarse semantic-level labels with a relatively low resolution (up to level 19), impeding the advancement of this field. In contrast, the proposed OpenSatMap (1) has fine-grained instance-level annotations; (2) consists of high-resolution images (level 20); (3) is currently the largest one of its kind; (4) collects data with high diversity. Moreover, OpenSatMap covers and aligns with the popular nuScenes dataset and Argoverse 2 dataset to potentially advance autonomous driving technologies. By publishing and maintaining the dataset, we provide a high-quality benchmark for satellite-based map construction and downstream tasks like autonomous driving.

paragraphs: OpenSatMap is a satellite-image dataset intended to support large-scale map construction. Extracting road structures from satellite imagery offers an efficient route to building maps for transportation applications. The paper identifies a data bottleneck: existing datasets have relatively low-resolution images and coarse labels that limit the detail researchers can learn to recover.

The dataset supplies instance-level annotations and level-20 imagery, compared with the level-19 maximum described for existing datasets. Instance annotations distinguish individual instances rather than providing only broad semantic categories. The authors also emphasize data diversity and describe OpenSatMap as the largest dataset of its kind at the time of the work.

OpenSatMap geographically covers and aligns with nuScenes and Argoverse 2, creating a potential connection to autonomous-driving research. Its contribution is a benchmark resource for learning and evaluating detailed satellite-based mapping. The alignment may support downstream driving applications, while the abstract presents that benefit as a possibility rather than a demonstrated improvement in autonomous-driving performance.
summary.tldr: OpenSatMap supplies high-resolution satellite imagery and instance-level annotations for detailed mapping, with alignment to autonomous-driving datasets.

title: OpenSatMap: A Fine-grained High-resolution Satellite Dataset for Large-scale Map Construction

abstract: Recent methodologies in LLM self-training mostly rely on LLM generating responses and filtering those with correct output answers as training data. This approach often yields a low-quality fine-tuning training set (e.g., incorrect plans or intermediate reasoning). In this paper, we develop a reinforced self-training approach, called ReST-MCTS*, based on integrating process reward guidance with tree search MCTS* for collecting higher-quality reasoning traces as well as per-step value to train policy and reward models. ReST-MCTS* circumvents the per-step manual annotation typically used to train process rewards by tree-search-based reinforcement learning: Given oracle final correct answers, ReST-MCTS* is able to infer the correct process rewards by estimating the probability this step can help lead to the correct answer. These inferred rewards serve dual purposes: they act as value targets for further refining the process reward model and also facilitate the selection of high-quality traces for policy model self-training. We first show that the tree-search policy in ReST-MCTS* achieves higher accuracy compared with prior LLM reasoning baselines such as Best-of-N and Tree-of-Thought, within the same search budget. We then show that by using traces searched by this tree-search policy as training data, we can continuously enhance the three language models for multiple iterations, and outperform other self-training algorithms such as ReST$^\text{EM}$ and Self-Rewarding LM.

paragraphs: ReST-MCTS* addresses a weakness in language-model self-training: a response can end with the correct answer while containing faulty plans or intermediate reasoning. Filtering generated responses by final-answer correctness can therefore produce poor training traces. The paper combines process-level reward guidance with tree search to improve the reasoning data collected.

Given oracle correct final answers, the method estimates how likely an intermediate step is to help reach the correct answer. These estimates supply step-level rewards without manual annotation of each step. They serve two purposes: training the process reward model and selecting higher-quality reasoning traces for training the policy model.

The reported tree-search policy achieves higher accuracy than Best-of-N and Tree-of-Thought under the same search budget. Using its traces for self-training also improves three language models across multiple iterations and outperforms ReST EM and Self-Rewarding LM in the reported comparisons. The results support a feedback loop in which search improves training traces and inferred step values refine reward guidance. Access to oracle final answers is an explicit condition of that process.
summary.tldr: ReST-MCTS* uses answer-supervised tree search to infer step rewards and generate better reasoning traces for iterative self-training.

title: ReST-MCTS*: LLM Self-Training via Process Reward Guided Tree Search

abstract: The ability of Language Models (LMs) to understand natural language makes them a powerful tool for parsing human instructions into task plans for autonomous robots. Unlike traditional planning methods that rely on domain-specific knowledge and handcrafted rules, LMs generalize from diverse data and adapt to various tasks with minimal tuning, acting as a compressed knowledge base. However, LMs in their standard form face challenges with long-horizon tasks, particularly in partially observable multi-agent settings. We propose an LM-based Long-Horizon Planner for Multi-Agent Robotics (LLaMAR), a cognitive architecture for planning that achieves state-of-the-art results in long-horizon tasks within partially observable environments. LLaMAR employs a plan-act-correct-verify framework, allowing self-correction from action execution feedback without relying on oracles or simulators. Additionally, we present MAP-THOR, a comprehensive test suite encompassing household tasks of varying complexity within the AI2-THOR environment. Experiments show that LLaMAR achieves a 30\% higher success rate than other state-of-the-art LM-based multi-agent planners in MAP-THOR and Search \& Rescue tasks. Code can be found at [https://github.com/nsidn98/LLaMAR](https://github.com/nsidn98/LLaMAR)

paragraphs: Language models can translate human instructions into robot task plans, but long tasks become difficult when several robots must cooperate with incomplete knowledge of their environment. A plan must remain useful across many actions even as execution reveals new information. LLaMAR addresses this challenge with a language-model-based planning architecture for partially observable multi-agent settings.

Its framework cycles through planning, acting, correcting, and verifying. Feedback from executed actions supports self-correction, allowing the planner to revise its behavior as the task unfolds. The correction mechanism does not rely on oracles or simulators. This places action feedback at the center of maintaining a long-horizon plan under incomplete observation.

The authors also introduce MAP-THOR, a test suite containing household tasks of varying complexity within AI2-THOR. Experiments on MAP-THOR and Search & Rescue tasks report a 30% higher success rate than other state-of-the-art language-model-based multi-agent planners. These results support the value of explicitly organizing planning around execution feedback and verification for the evaluated long-horizon tasks.
summary.tldr: LLaMAR uses a plan-act-correct-verify cycle to improve long-horizon multi-agent planning through feedback from executed actions.

title: Long-Horizon Planning for Multi-Agent Robots in Partially Observable Environments

abstract: Semi-supervised continual learning (SSCL) has attracted significant attention for addressing catastrophic forgetting in semi-supervised data. Knowledge distillation, which leverages data representation and pair-wise similarity, has shown significant potential in preserving information in SSCL. However, traditional distillation strategies often fail in unlabeled data with inaccurate or noisy information, limiting their efficiency in feature spaces undergoing substantial changes during continual learning. To address these limitations, we propose Persistence Homology Distillation (PsHD) to preserve intrinsic structural information that is insensitive to noise in semi-supervised continual learning. First, we capture the structural features using persistence homology by homological evolution across different scales in vision data, where the multi-scale characteristic established its stability under noise interference. Next, we propose a persistence homology distillation loss in SSCL and design an acceleration algorithm to reduce the computational cost of persistence homology in our module. Furthermore, we demonstrate the superior stability of PsHD compared to sample representation and pair-wise similarity distillation methods theoretically and experimentally. Finally, experimental results on three widely used datasets validate that the new PsHD outperforms state-of-the-art with 3.9% improvements on average, and also achieves 1.5% improvements while reducing 60% memory buffer size, highlighting the potential of utilizing unlabeled data in SSCL. Our code is available: https://github.com/fanyan0411/PsHD.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised continual learning must preserve old knowledge while learning from both labeled and unlabeled data. Distillation can help, but preserving individual representations or pairwise similarities becomes difficult when unlabeled information is noisy and the feature space changes substantially. This paper proposes preserving structural information that is more stable under such noise.

Persistence Homology Distillation, or PsHD, captures how structural features evolve across different scales in visual data. Its multiscale construction provides stability against noise interference. The authors turn these features into a distillation loss and introduce an acceleration algorithm to reduce the cost of computing persistence homology. This makes the structural preservation objective more practical within continual training.

The paper supplies theoretical and experimental evidence of greater stability than representation-based and pairwise-similarity distillation. Across three datasets, it reports an average improvement of 3.9% over the state of the art. It also reports a 1.5% improvement while reducing memory-buffer size by 60%. These findings support the potential of multiscale structural information for retaining knowledge and making better use of unlabeled data.
summary.tldr: PsHD preserves noise-stable, multiscale structural information to improve semi-supervised continual learning, including results with a substantially smaller memory buffer.

title: Persistence Homology Distillation for Semi-supervised Continual Learning

abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals provide essential information about the heart's condition and are widely used for diagnosing cardiovascular diseases. The morphology of a single heartbeat over the available leads is a primary biosignal for monitoring cardiac conditions. However, analyzing heartbeat morphology can be challenging due to noise and artifacts, missing leads, and a lack of annotated data.Generative models, such as denoising diffusion generative models (DDMs), have proven successful in generating complex data. We introduce $\texttt{BeatDiff}$, a light-weight DDM tailored for the morphology of multiple leads heartbeats.We then show that many important ECG downstream tasks can be formulated as conditional generation methods in a Bayesian inverse problem framework using $\texttt{BeatDiff}$ as priors. We propose $\texttt{EM-BeatDiff}$, an Expectation-Maximization algorithm, to solve this conditional generation tasks without fine-tuning. We illustrate our results with several tasks, such as removal of ECG noise and artifacts (baseline wander, electrode motion), reconstruction of a 12-lead ECG from a single lead (useful for ECG reconstruction of smartwatch experiments), and unsupervised explainable anomaly detection. Numerical experiments show that the combination of $\texttt{BeatDiff}$ and $\texttt{EM-BeatDiff}$ outperforms SOTA methods for the problems considered in this work.

paragraphs: The shape of a heartbeat across ECG leads carries information about cardiac condition, but noise, artifacts, and missing leads can make it difficult to analyze. This paper introduces BeatDiff, a lightweight diffusion model designed to represent heartbeat morphology across multiple leads. Its learned representation becomes a foundation for several reconstruction and analysis tasks.

The authors formulate those tasks as conditional generation within a Bayesian inverse-problem framework. BeatDiff supplies the prior over heartbeat shapes, while the available measurements provide the information to condition on. An expectation-maximization algorithm, EM-BeatDiff, solves these conditional generation problems without fine-tuning the diffusion model for each task.

The demonstrated applications include removing baseline wander and electrode-motion artifacts, reconstructing a 12-lead ECG from a single lead, and unsupervised explainable anomaly detection. Single-lead reconstruction is presented as useful for smartwatch-related ECG reconstruction experiments. Numerical evaluations show the combined methods outperforming state-of-the-art approaches on the problems studied. The shared framework matters because one model of heartbeat morphology supports several tasks involving incomplete, noisy, or otherwise indirect observations.
summary.tldr: BeatDiff and EM-BeatDiff use a shared diffusion prior to reconstruct and analyze ECG heartbeats without task-specific fine-tuning.

title: Leveraging an ECG Beat Diffusion Model for Morphological Reconstruction from Indirect Signals

abstract: Poor quality sleep can be characterized by the occurrence of events ranging from body movement to breathing impairment. Widely available earbuds equipped with sensors (also known as earables) can be combined with a sleep event detection algorithm to offer a convenient alternative to laborious clinical tests for individuals suffering from sleep disorders. Although various solutions utilizing such devices have been proposed to detect sleep events, they ignore the fact that individuals often share sleeping spaces with roommates or couples. To address this issue, we introduce DreamCatcher, the first publicly available dataset for wearer-aware sleep event algorithm development on earables. DreamCatcher encompasses eight distinct sleep events, including synchronous dual-channel audio and motion data collected from 12 pairs (24 participants) totaling 210 hours (420 hour.person) with fine-grained label. We tested multiple benchmark models on three tasks related to sleep event detection, demonstrating the usability and unique challenge of DreamCatcher. We hope that the proposed DreamCatcher can inspire other researchers to further explore efficient wearer-aware human vocal activity sensing on earables. DreamCatcher is publicly available at https://github.com/thuhci/DreamCatcher.

paragraphs: DreamCatcher addresses an everyday complication in earbud-based sleep monitoring: the wearer may share a room or bed with another person. Detecting a sleep-related event is then only part of the problem. A useful system must also account for whose activity it is sensing. The paper introduces a public dataset specifically for developing wearer-aware algorithms.

The dataset covers eight sleep events and combines synchronized dual-channel audio with motion measurements. It contains recordings from 12 pairs of participants, or 24 people, totaling 210 hours of recording and 420 person-hours. Fine-grained labels provide a basis for training and evaluating methods that connect sensor signals with sleep events.

The authors test multiple benchmark models on three sleep-event detection tasks. These experiments demonstrate the dataset's usability and the distinctive challenge created by shared sleeping environments. The contribution is a research resource for studying attribution as well as detection, with the broader aim of encouraging efficient wearer-aware sensing of human vocal activity through sensor-equipped earbuds.
summary.tldr: DreamCatcher provides paired audio and motion recordings for developing sleep-event detectors that account for who is wearing the earbuds.

title: DreamCatcher: A Wearer-aware Multi-modal Sleep Event Dataset Based on Earables in Non-restrictive Environments

abstract: The Schrödinger Bridge (SB) problem offers a powerful framework for combining optimal transport and diffusion models. A promising recent approach to solve the SB problem is the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) procedure, which alternates between Markovian and reciprocal projections of continuous-time stochastic processes. However, the model built by the IMF procedure has a long inference time due to using many steps of numerical solvers for stochastic differential equations. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Discrete-time IMF (D-IMF) procedure in which learning of stochastic processes is replaced by learning just a few transition probabilities in discrete time. Its great advantage is that in practice it can be naturally implemented using the Denoising Diffusion GAN (DD-GAN), an already well-established adversarial generative modeling technique. We show that our D-IMF procedure can provide the same quality of unpaired domain translation as the IMF, using only several generation steps instead of hundreds.
originalAbstract: The Schrödinger Bridge (SB) problem offers a powerful framework for combining optimal transport and diffusion models. A promising recent approach to solve the SB problem is the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) procedure, which alternates between Markovian and reciprocal projections of continuous-time stochastic processes. However, the model built by the IMF procedure has a long inference time due to using many steps of numerical solvers for stochastic differential equations. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Discrete-time IMF (D-IMF) procedure in which learning of stochastic processes is replaced by learning just a few transition probabilities in discrete time. Its great advantage is that in practice it can be naturally implemented using the Denoising Diffusion GAN (DD-GAN), an already well-established adversarial generative modeling technique. We show that our D-IMF procedure can provide the same quality of unpaired domain translation as the IMF, using only several generation steps instead of hundreds.

paragraphs: The Schrödinger Bridge problem connects optimal transport with diffusion modeling. One approach to solving it, Iterative Markovian Fitting, repeatedly alternates between two projections of a continuous-time random process. Although this provides a useful modeling framework, generating an output can require hundreds of numerical steps for stochastic differential equations, making inference slow.

The authors introduce Discrete-time Iterative Markovian Fitting to change what the model learns. Instead of learning a continuous-time process that must later be simulated through many small steps, it learns a few transition probabilities at discrete times. The procedure can be implemented naturally with Denoising Diffusion GAN, connecting the proposed formulation to an established adversarial generative modeling technique.

For unpaired domain translation, the authors show that the discrete procedure can match the quality of the original approach while using only several generation steps. The contribution therefore joins a reformulation of the fitting procedure with a practical implementation route. Its stated result is a substantial reduction in generation steps without losing translation quality in the demonstrated comparison.
summary.tldr: Discrete-time bridge fitting can match continuous-time IMF’s unpaired translation quality using several generation steps instead of hundreds.

title: Adversarial Schrödinger Bridge Matching

abstract: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) have gained popularity with multiple works showing promising results across various applications. However, to the best of our knowledge, existing works do not explicitly model the distribution of training camera poses, or consequently the triangulation quality, a key factor affecting reconstruction quality dating back to classical vision literature. We close this gap with ProvNeRF, an approach that models the provenance for each point -- i.e., the locations where it is likely visible -- of NeRFs as a stochastic field. We achieve this by extending implicit maximum likelihood estimation (IMLE) to functional space with an optimizable objective. We show that modeling per-point provenance during the NeRF optimization enriches the model with information on triangulation leading to improvements in novel view synthesis and uncertainty estimation under the challenging sparse, unconstrained view setting against competitive baselines. The code will be available at https://github.com/georgeNakayama/ProvNeRF.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields reconstruct scenes from images, but reconstruction quality depends partly on the viewpoints that observe each scene point. The arrangement of those viewpoints affects triangulation quality. ProvNeRF explicitly models this information, addressing the absence of a representation for training-camera pose distributions in existing work identified by the authors.

For each point, provenance means the locations from which that point is likely visible. ProvNeRF represents this provenance as a stochastic field, allowing it to describe a distribution rather than a single viewing location. To learn that field, the authors extend implicit maximum likelihood estimation into functional space and provide an objective that can be optimized alongside the NeRF.

Learning provenance gives the reconstruction information about its triangulation support. In the challenging setting of sparse, unconstrained views, the authors report improvements in both novel-view synthesis and uncertainty estimation against competitive baselines. The result links the quality of the available camera evidence to the learned scene representation, with empirical benefits for rendering new viewpoints and estimating uncertainty.
summary.tldr: ProvNeRF learns where each scene point is likely visible, improving novel-view synthesis and uncertainty estimation with sparse, unconstrained camera views.

title: ProvNeRF: Modeling per Point Provenance in NeRFs as a Stochastic Field

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have impactful applications in art, design, and entertainment, yet these technologies also pose significant risks by enabling the creation and dissemination of misinformation. Although recent advancements have produced AI-generated image detectors that claim robustness against various augmentations, their true effectiveness remains uncertain. Do these detectors reliably identify images with different levels of augmentation? Are they biased toward specific scenes or data distributions? To investigate, we introduce **Semi-Truths**, featuring $27,600$ real images, $223,400$ masks, and $1, 329, 155$ AI-augmented images that feature targeted and localized perturbations produced using diverse augmentation techniques, diffusion models, and data distributions. Each augmented image is accompanied by metadata for standardized and targeted evaluation of detector robustness. Our findings suggest that state-of-the-art detectors exhibit varying sensitivities to the types and degrees of perturbations, data distributions, and augmentation methods used, offering new insights into their performance and limitations. The code for the augmentation and evaluation pipeline is available at https://github.com/J-Kruk/SemiTruths.

paragraphs: An image can combine real content with localized AI-generated edits, making detector evaluation more complicated than distinguishing wholly real from wholly generated pictures. Semi-Truths is designed to test how detectors respond to different kinds and amounts of AI augmentation, as well as differences in scenes and data distributions.

The dataset includes 27,600 real images, 223,400 masks, and 1,329,155 AI-augmented images. Its targeted edits are produced with varied augmentation techniques, diffusion models, and source distributions. Each augmented image includes metadata that supports standardized evaluation and more focused tests of particular editing conditions.

The authors find that state-of-the-art detectors respond differently to perturbation type, perturbation degree, data distribution, and augmentation method. This means detector behavior can depend on how an image was modified and where it came from. The dataset makes those dependencies more directly examinable, providing a way to assess robustness across localized edits instead of relying only on a broad aggregate assessment of detection performance.
summary.tldr: Semi-Truths provides over 1.3 million locally AI-edited images to reveal how detector performance varies with edits, methods, and data distributions.

title: Semi-Truths: A Large-Scale Dataset of AI-Augmented Images for Evaluating Robustness of AI-Generated Image detectors

abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are a new approach to efficiently adjust language model behaviour at inference time by intervening on intermediate model activations. They have shown promise in terms of improving both capabilities and model alignment. However, the reliability and generalisation properties of this approach are unknown. In this work, we rigorously investigate these properties, and show that steering vectors have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution. In-distribution, steerability is highly variable across different inputs. Depending on the concept, spurious biases can substantially contribute to how effective steering is for each input, presenting a challenge for the widespread use of steering vectors. Out-of-distribution, while steering vectors often generalise well, for several concepts they are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt, resulting in them failing to generalise well. Overall, our findings show that while steering can work well in the right circumstances, there remain many technical difficulties of applying steering vectors to guide models' behaviour at scale.

paragraphs: Steering vectors adjust a language model’s behavior during inference by intervening on its internal activations. Their appeal is that they offer an efficient way to influence capabilities or alignment. This paper investigates whether those interventions behave reliably across inputs and whether their effects carry over to prompts outside the distribution in which they were developed.

Even within the original distribution, the authors find that steerability varies substantially from one input to another. For some concepts, incidental biases make a substantial contribution to apparent steering effectiveness. This means that success on a collection of inputs does not establish that an intervention will guide behavior equally well on other inputs from the same distribution.

Outside that distribution, the picture is mixed: steering vectors often transfer well, but several concepts are sensitive to reasonable prompt changes. Those changes can cause generalization to fail. The findings support a conditional view of steering: it can work well under suitable circumstances, while input variability and prompt sensitivity remain obstacles to dependable use at scale.
summary.tldr: Steering vectors can guide language models effectively, but their effects vary across inputs and can break under reasonable prompt changes.

title: Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability of Steering Vectors

abstract: We study a general clustering setting in which we have $n$ elements to be clustered, and we aim to perform as few queries as possible to an oracle that returns a noisy sample of the weighted similarity between two elements. Our setting encompasses many application domains in which the similarity function is costly to compute and inherently noisy. We introduce two novel formulations of online learning problems rooted in the paradigm of Pure Exploration in Combinatorial Multi-Armed Bandits (PE-CMAB): fixed confidence and fixed budget settings. For both settings, we design algorithms that combine a sampling strategy with a classic approximation algorithm for correlation clustering and study their theoretical guarantees. Our results are the first examples of polynomial-time algorithms that work for the case of PE-CMAB in which the underlying offline optimization problem is NP-hard.

We introduce two novel formulations of online learning problems rooted in the paradigm of Pure Exploration in Combinatorial Multi-Armed Bandits (PE-CMAB): fixed confidence and fixed budget settings.
