Our results are the first examples of polynomial-time algorithms that work for the case of PE-CMAB in which the underlying offline optimization problem is NP-hard.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering when discovering how similar two elements are requires a costly, noisy query. The goal is to group the elements while asking as few questions as possible. Because each answer is only a noisy sample of weighted similarity, the algorithm must manage uncertainty as well as decide which relationships deserve further measurement.

The authors formulate two versions of the problem using pure exploration in combinatorial multi-armed bandits. One works with a fixed confidence requirement; the other works with a fixed query budget. For each setting, they combine a strategy for sampling pairwise similarities with a classic approximation algorithm for correlation clustering, and analyze the resulting guarantees.

The contribution also concerns computational feasibility. The underlying offline optimization problem is NP-hard, yet the proposed procedures run in polynomial time. The authors identify these as the first such results for this class of pure-exploration problems with an NP-hard offline component. Using approximation makes it possible to connect query allocation with tractable clustering without claiming an efficient exact solution to the hard optimization problem.
summary.tldr: The paper combines adaptive similarity sampling with approximate correlation clustering to obtain polynomial-time guarantees under confidence or query-budget constraints.

title: Query-Efficient Correlation Clustering with Noisy Oracle

abstract: As generative large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT gain widespread adoption in various domains, their potential to propagate and amplify social biases, particularly in high-stakes areas such as the labor market, has become a pressing concern. AI algorithms are not only widely used in the selection of job applicants, individual job seekers may also make use of generative LLMs to help develop their job application materials. Against this backdrop, this research builds on a novel experimental design to examine social biases within ChatGPT-generated job applications in response to real job advertisements. By simulating the process of job application creation, we examine the language patterns and biases that emerge when the model is prompted with diverse job postings. Notably, we present a novel bias evaluation framework based on Masked Language Models to quantitatively assess social bias based on validated inventories of social cues/words, enabling a systematic analysis of the language used. Our findings show that the increasing adoption of generative AI, not only by employers but also increasingly by individual job seekers, can reinforce and exacerbate gender and social inequalities in the labor market through the use of biased and gendered language.

This paper examines social bias in ChatGPT-generated job applications. Its experimental design simulates application writing in response to real job advertisements, allowing the researchers to study language elicited by diverse postings.

The authors introduce a quantitative evaluation framework based on masked language models and validated inventories of social cues and words. This provides a systematic way to assess bias in the generated text. The focus is on language patterns appearing in application materials, connecting the evaluation directly to a plausible use of generative AI by job seekers.

The findings indicate that biased and gendered language in these materials can reinforce or exacerbate gender and social inequalities. This identifies a potential pathway by which wider AI adoption could reproduce labor-market disparities. The contribution combines a realistic prompting setup with a structured measurement approach, showing why applicant-side use deserves attention alongside employer-side automation.
summary.tldr: The study uses masked language models to assess social bias in ChatGPT-written job applications and identifies language that can reinforce labor-market inequalities.

title: Probing Social Bias in Labor Market Text Generation by ChatGPT: A Masked Language Model Approach

abstract: Engineering design optimization seeks to automatically determine the shapes, topologies, or parameters of components that maximize performance under given conditions. This process often depends on physics-based simulations, which are difficult to install, computationally expensive, and require domain-specific expertise. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce EngiBench, the first open‐source library and datasets spanning diverse domains for data‐driven engineering design. EngiBench provides a unified API and a curated set of benchmarks---covering aeronautics, heat conduction, photonics, and more---that enable fair, reproducible comparisons of optimization and machine learning algorithms, such as generative or surrogate models. We also release EngiOpt, a companion library offering a collection of such algorithms compatible with the EngiBench interface. Both libraries are modular, letting users plug in novel algorithms or problems, automate end-to-end experiment workflows, and leverage built-in utilities for visualization, dataset generation, feasibility checks, and performance analysis. We demonstrate their versatility through experiments comparing state-of-the-art techniques across multiple engineering design problems, an undertaking that was previously prohibitively time-consuming to perform. Finally, we show that these problems pose significant challenges for standard machine learning methods due to highly sensitive and constrained design manifolds.

paragraphs: Engineering design optimization searches for component shapes, structures, or parameters that perform well under specified conditions. Comparing methods is difficult because the required physics simulations can be expensive, hard to install, and dependent on specialist knowledge. EngiBench addresses this practical barrier with an open-source library and datasets covering multiple engineering domains.

The framework provides one interface for benchmarks in areas including aeronautics, heat conduction, and photonics. A companion library, EngiOpt, supplies compatible optimization and machine-learning algorithms. Both libraries allow new problems and algorithms to be added, and include utilities for generating datasets, checking feasibility, visualizing results, and analyzing performance within automated experimental workflows.

The authors demonstrate comparisons of leading techniques across several design problems, a process they describe as previously prohibitively time-consuming. They also find that standard machine-learning methods struggle with design spaces that are highly sensitive and tightly constrained. EngiBench therefore contributes both shared experimental infrastructure and a set of demanding problems for studying whether data-driven methods can handle engineering requirements.
summary.tldr: EngiBench and EngiOpt provide shared benchmarks, algorithms, and workflows for comparing data-driven engineering design methods across domains.

title: EngiBench: A Framework for Data-Driven Engineering Design Research

abstract: Video diffusion transformers have achieved remarkable progress in high-quality video generation, but remain computationally expensive due to the quadratic complexity of attention over high-dimensional video sequences. Recent acceleration methods enhance the efficiency by exploiting the local sparsity of attention scores; yet they often struggle with accelerating the long-range computation. To address this problem, we propose VORTA, an acceleration framework with two novel components: 1) a sparse attention mechanism that efficiently captures long-range dependencies, and 2) a routing strategy that adaptively replaces full 3D attention with specialized sparse attention variants. VORTA achieves an end-to-end speedup $1.76\times$ without loss of quality on VBench. Furthermore, it can seamlessly integrate with various other acceleration methods, such as model caching and step distillation, reaching up to speedup $14.41\times$ with negligible performance degradation. VORTA demonstrates its efficiency and enhances the practicality of video diffusion transformers in real-world settings. Codes and weights are available at https://github.com/wenhao728/VORTA.

paragraphs: VORTA accelerates video diffusion transformers by reducing the expense of attention over video sequences. Full attention becomes costly as the number of video elements grows. Existing methods exploit local sparsity, but the paper identifies long-range computation as a remaining obstacle to efficient generation.

The framework introduces a sparse attention mechanism designed to capture long-range dependencies and a routing strategy that adaptively substitutes specialized sparse variants for full three-dimensional attention. These components address both which interactions should be computed and how the model chooses among more economical attention patterns.

The authors report an end-to-end speedup of 1.76 times without a quality loss on VBench. VORTA can also combine with acceleration methods such as model caching and step distillation, reaching up to 14.41 times speedup with negligible performance degradation. The larger number describes the combined setup. The findings show that attention routing can contribute useful acceleration on its own and complement other techniques, while preserving the stated quality levels in the evaluated configurations.
summary.tldr: VORTA routes video attention through sparse variants, achieving 1.76-fold speedup alone and larger gains when combined with other accelerators.

title: VORTA: Efficient Video Diffusion via Routing Sparse Attention

abstract: The discovery of the *lazy neuron phenomenon* (Li et al., 2022), where fewer than 10% of the feedforward networks (FFN) parameters in trained Transformers are activated per token, has spurred significant interests in *activation sparsity* for enhancing large model efficiency. While notable progress has been made in translating such sparsity to wall-time benefits across CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs, modern Transformers have moved away from the ReLU activation function crucial to this phenomenon. Existing efforts on re-introducing activation sparsity, e.g., by reverting to ReLU or applying top-k masking, often degrade model quality, increase parameter count, or complicate training. Sparse attention, the application of sparse activation to the attention mechanism, often face similar challenges. This paper introduces the Spark Transformer, a novel architecture that achieves high activation sparsity in both FFN and the attention mechanism while maintaining model quality, parameter count, and standard training procedures. Our method realizes sparsity via top-$k$ masking for explicit control over sparsity level. Crucially, we introduce *statistical top-k*, a hardware-accelerator-friendly, linear-time approximate algorithm that avoids costly sorting and mitigates significant training slowdown from standard top-k operators. Furthermore, Spark Transformer reallocates existing FFN parameters and attention key embeddings to form a low-cost predictor for identifying activated entries. This design not only mitigates quality loss from enforced sparsity, but also enhances wall-time benefit. Pretrained with the Gemma-2 recipe, Spark Transformer demonstrates competitive performance on standard benchmarks while exhibiting significant sparsity: only 8\% of FFN neurons are activated, and each token attends to a maximum of 256 tokens. This translates to a 2.5x reduction in FLOPs, leading to decoding wall-time speedups of up to 1.79x on CPU and 1.40xon GPU.

summary.tldr: Spark Transformer combines efficient top-k selection with activation prediction to make feedforward layers and attention sparse while retaining competitive model quality.

title: Spark Transformer: Reactivating Sparsity in Transformer FFN and Attention

abstract: Learning complex functions that involve multi-step reasoning poses a significant challenge for standard supervised learning from input-output examples. Chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision, which augments training data with intermediate reasoning steps to provide a richer learning signal, has driven recent advances in large language model reasoning. This paper develops a statistical theory of learning under CoT supervision. Central to the theory is the *CoT information*, which measures the additional discriminative power offered by the chain-of-thought for distinguishing hypotheses with different end-to-end behaviors. The main theoretical results demonstrate how CoT supervision can yield significantly faster learning rates compared to standard end-to-end supervision, with both upper bounds and information-theoretic lower bounds characterized by the CoT information.

paragraphs: The paper develops a statistical account of why training on intermediate reasoning steps can help a learner master functions that require several steps. Ordinary supervised examples reveal an input and its final answer. Chain-of-thought supervision adds intermediate information, giving the learner more evidence about which candidate explanations of the task fit the training data.

The key quantity, called CoT information, measures the extra ability of those intermediate steps to distinguish hypotheses with different overall input-to-output behavior. This focuses the analysis on how informative the reasoning supervision is for separating competing solutions. The theoretical benefit is therefore tied to the discrimination that the added steps provide.

The authors establish both upper bounds on learning requirements and information-theoretic lower bounds, expressed through CoT information. These results show how reasoning-step supervision can produce substantially faster learning rates than supervision using final answers alone. By characterizing both achievable rates and fundamental constraints through the same quantity, the work provides a framework for understanding when richer supervision can reduce the examples needed to learn.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces CoT information to characterize how intermediate reasoning supervision can reduce the number of examples needed for learning.

title: CoT Information: Improved Sample Complexity under Chain-of-Thought Supervision

abstract: As hypothesis generation becomes increasingly automated, a new bottleneck has emerged: hypothesis assessment. Modern systems can surface thousands of statistical relationships—correlations, trends, causal links—but offer little guidance on which ones are novel, non-trivial, or worthy of expert attention. In this work, we study the complementary problem to hypothesis generation: automatic hypothesis assessment. Specifically, we ask—given a large set of statistical relationships, can we automatically assess which ones are novel and worth further exploration? We focus on correlations as they are a common entry point in exploratory data analysis that often serve as the basis for forming deeper scientific or causal hypotheses. To support automatic assessment, we propose to leverage the vast knowledge encoded in LLMs' weights to derive a prior distribution over the correlation value of a variable pair. If an LLM's prior expects the correlation value observed, then such correlation is not surprising, and vice versa. We propose the Logit-based Calibrated Prior, an LLM-elicited correlation prior that transforms the model’s raw output logits into a calibrated, continuous predictive distribution over correlation values. We evaluate the prior on a benchmark of 2,096 real-world variable pairs and it achieves a sign accuracy of 78.8%, a mean absolute error of 0.26, and 95% credible interval coverage of 89.2% in predicting Pearson correlation coefficient. It also outperforms a fine-tuned RoBERTa classifier in binary correlation prediction and achieves higher precision@K in hypothesis ranking. We further show that the prior generalizes to correlations not seen during LLM pretraining, reflecting context-sensitive reasoning rather than memorization.

This paper focuses on assessing correlations by comparing observed values with what a language model would expect. A relationship that differs from the model’s expectations can be ranked as more surprising and potentially worth further exploration.

The proposed Logit-based Calibrated Prior converts a model’s raw output scores into a continuous probability distribution over possible correlation values. This provides an expectation with uncertainty, rather than only a positive-or-negative prediction. The distribution acts as a reference for assessing observations, connecting knowledge encoded in model weights to hypothesis prioritization.

On 2,096 real-world variable pairs, the method achieves 78.8% sign accuracy and a mean absolute error of 0.26. Its 95% credible intervals cover 89.2% of observed values. It also improves binary prediction over a fine-tuned RoBERTa classifier and achieves higher precision in top-ranked hypotheses. Generalization to correlations absent from pretraining supports context-sensitive reasoning as an explanation beyond memorization.
summary.tldr: A calibrated distribution derived from LLM logits helps rank observed correlations by how surprising they are relative to model expectations.

title: Exploiting LLMs for Automatic Hypothesis Assessment via a Logit-Based Calibrated Prior

abstract: The *law of supply and demand* asserts that in a perfectly competitive market, the price of a good adjusts to a *market clearing price*. In a market clearing price $p^\star$ the number of sellers willing to sell the good at $p^\star$ equals the number of sellers willing to buy the good at price $p^\star$. In this work, we provide a mathematical foundation on the law of supply and demand through the lens of online learning. Specifically, we demonstrate that if each seller employs a no-swap regret algorithm to set their individual selling price—aiming to maximize its individual revenue—the collective pricing dynamics converge to the market-clearing price $p^\star$ . Our findings offer a novel perspective on the law of supply and demand, framing it as the emergent outcome of an adaptive learning processes among sellers.

This paper asks how that collective outcome can arise from the behavior of individual sellers. It approaches the question through online learning, where decisions are revised over repeated interactions.

Each seller chooses its own selling price to maximize its individual revenue. The central assumption is that every seller uses a no-swap regret algorithm. This learning criterion concerns whether consistently replacing chosen actions with other actions would have improved past performance. It provides a precise condition on how sellers adapt their pricing decisions over time.

Under that condition, the authors show that the collective pricing dynamics converge to the market-clearing price. The result gives a mathematical connection between individual revenue-seeking learning and market-level balance. Its significance is the emergence of coordinated pricing behavior from separate adaptive decisions, with convergence tied specifically to the stated learning rule and competitive-market setting.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that sellers using no-swap regret pricing algorithms collectively converge to a market-clearing price in its competitive-market setting.

title: Explaining the Law of Supply and Demand via Online Learning

abstract: Accelerating model convergence in resource-constrained environments is essential for fast and efficient neural network training. This work presents learn2mix, a new training strategy that adaptively adjusts class proportions within batches, focusing on classes with higher error rates. Unlike classical training methods that use static class proportions, learn2mix continually adapts class proportions during training, leading to faster convergence. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets show that neural networks trained with learn2mix converge faster than those trained with existing approaches, achieving improved results for classification, regression, and reconstruction tasks under limited training resources and with imbalanced classes. Our empirical findings are supported by theoretical analysis.

Learn2mix makes those proportions adaptive, with the aim of reaching useful performance more quickly under constrained training resources.

The strategy gives greater attention to classes with higher error rates and continually revises the mixture as training progresses. The key change is therefore in how available data are integrated into batches. A class that remains difficult can receive more training attention, connecting the sampling process to the model’s current performance rather than a fixed allocation.

Benchmark experiments report faster convergence than existing approaches and improved results across classification, regression, and reconstruction tasks, including settings with imbalanced classes and limited resources. The authors also provide theoretical analysis supporting their empirical findings. These results suggest that the composition of training data over time is an important efficiency choice: adapting the mixture can improve how effectively a network uses a restricted training budget.
summary.tldr: Learn2mix adapts batch class proportions toward higher-error classes, improving convergence and results under limited training resources.

title: Learn2Mix: Training Neural Networks Using Adaptive Data Integration

abstract: In recent years, the expressive power of various neural architectures---including graph neural networks (GNNs), transformers, and recurrent neural networks---has been characterised using tools from logic and formal language theory. As the capabilities of basic architectures are becoming well understood, increasing attention is turning to models that combine multiple architectural paradigms. Among them particularly important, and challenging to analyse, are temporal extensions of GNNs, which integrate both spatial (graph-structure) and temporal (evolution over time) dimensions. In this paper, we initiate the study of logical characterisation of temporal GNNs by connecting them to two-dimensional product logics. We show that the expressive power of temporal GNNs depends on how graph and temporal components are combined. In particular, temporal GNNs that apply static GNNs recursively over time can capture all properties definable in the product logic of (past) propositional temporal logic PTL and the modal logic K. In contrast, architectures such as graph-and-time TGNNs and global TGNNs can only express restricted fragments of this logic, where the interaction between temporal and spatial operators is syntactically constrained. These provide us with the first results on the logical expressiveness of temporal GNNs.

paragraphs: Temporal graph neural networks combine reasoning about graph structure with reasoning about changes over time. This paper studies their expressive power through logic: which properties of an evolving graph can an architecture represent? It connects temporal GNNs to two-dimensional product logics that describe both the spatial and temporal aspects of the data.

The key finding is that expressive power depends on how the graph and time components are combined. summary.tldr: The paper uses product logics to show how the combination of graph and temporal processing determines temporal GNN expressiveness.

title: The Logical Expressiveness of Temporal GNNs via Two-Dimensional Product Logics

abstract: We study the value of stochastic predictions in online optimal control with random disturbances. Prior work provides performance guarantees based on prediction error but ignores the stochastic dependence between predictions and disturbances. We introduce a general framework modeling their joint distribution and define "prediction power" as the control cost improvement from the optimal use of predictions compared to ignoring the predictions. In the time-varying Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) setting, we derive a closed-form expression for prediction power and discuss its mismatch with prediction accuracy and connection with online policy optimization. To extend beyond LQR, we study general dynamics and costs. We establish a lower bound on prediction power under two sufficient conditions that generalize the properties of the LQR setting, characterizing the fundamental benefit of incorporating stochastic predictions. We apply this lower bound to non-quadratic costs and show that even weakly dependent predictions yield significant performance gains.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much stochastic predictions actually help an online controller facing random disturbances. Prediction error alone does not capture the dependence between a forecast and the disturbance it concerns. The authors therefore model their joint distribution and define prediction power as the reduction in control cost from using predictions optimally compared with ignoring them.

For a time-varying Linear Quadratic Regulator, they derive a closed-form expression for prediction power. This reveals how a prediction's usefulness for control can differ from its accuracy. The paper also discusses the connection with online policy optimization, linking the assessment of forecasts to the decisions made using them.

The analysis extends to more general dynamics and costs through a lower bound on prediction power. That bound holds under two sufficient conditions that generalize properties of the linear-quadratic setting. Applying it to non-quadratic costs shows that even weakly dependent predictions can produce substantial gains. The result directs attention to decision-relevant statistical structure, while keeping the broader guarantee conditional on those sufficient conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper measures predictions by their optimal control-cost benefit and shows why forecast accuracy alone can misrepresent that value.

title: Maximizing the Value of Predictions in Control: Accuracy Is Not Enough

abstract: Calibration is a fundamental concept that aims at ensuring the reliability of probabilistic predictions by aligning them with real-world outcomes. There is a surge of studies on new calibration measures that are easier to optimize compared to the classical $\ell_1$-Calibration while still having strong implications for downstream applications. One recent such example is the work by Fishelson et al. (2025) who show that it is possible to achieve $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{1/3})$ pseudo $\ell_{2}$-Calibration error via minimizing pseudo swap regret of the squared loss, which in fact implies the same bound for all bounded proper losses with a smooth univariate form. In this work, we significantly generalize their result in the following ways: (a) in addition to smooth univariate forms, our algorithm also simultaneously achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{1/3})$ swap regret for any proper loss with a twice continuously differentiable univariate form (such as Tsallis entropy); (b) our bounds hold not only for pseudo swap regret that measures losses using the forecaster's distributions on predictions, but also hold for the actual swap regret that measures losses using the forecaster's actual realized predictions. We achieve so by introducing a new stronger notion of calibration called (pseudo) KL-Calibration, which we show is equivalent to the (pseudo) swap regret with respect to log loss. We prove that there exists an algorithm that achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{1/3})$ KL-Calibration error and provide an explicit algorithm that achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{1/3})$ pseudo KL-Calibration error. Moreover, we show that the same algorithm achieves ${\mathcal{O}}(T^{1/3} (\log T) ^ {-\frac{1}{3}}\log (T/{\delta}))$ swap regret with probability at least $1-\delta$ for any proper loss with a smooth univariate form, which implies $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{1/3})$ $\ell_2$-Calibration error. A technical contribution of our work is a new randomized rounding procedure and a non-uniform discretization scheme to minimize the swap regret for log loss.

summary.tldr: KL-Calibration links log-loss swap regret to broader calibration and simultaneous regret guarantees across classes of proper losses.

title: Simultaneous Swap Regret Minimization via KL-Calibration

abstract: Conformal prediction provides a powerful framework for constructing prediction intervals with finite-sample guarantees, yet its robustness under distribution shifts remains a significant challenge. This paper addresses this limitation by modeling distribution shifts using Lévy-Prokhorov (LP) ambiguity sets, which capture both local and global perturbations. We provide a self-contained overview of LP ambiguity sets and their connections to popular metrics such as Wasserstein and Total Variation. We show that the link between conformal prediction and LP ambiguity sets is a natural one: by propagating the LP ambiguity set through the scoring function, we reduce complex high-dimensional distribution shifts to manageable one-dimensional distribution shifts, enabling exact quantification of worst-case quantiles and coverage. Building on this analysis, we construct robust conformal prediction intervals that remain valid under distribution shifts, explicitly linking LP parameters to interval width and confidence levels. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs prediction intervals with finite-sample coverage guarantees, but changes in the data distribution can undermine those guarantees. This paper models such changes through Lévy-Prokhorov ambiguity sets. These sets describe a family of possible shifted distributions that includes both local and global perturbations.

The key step is to carry the ambiguity set through the scoring function used by conformal prediction. Doing so turns a potentially complicated, high-dimensional shift into a one-dimensional problem involving scores. Within this representation, the authors can quantify worst-case quantiles and coverage exactly, providing a tractable foundation for choosing robust prediction intervals.

The resulting intervals retain validity for shifts described by the specified ambiguity sets. The analysis explicitly connects the shift parameters to interval width and confidence, making the cost of accommodating distribution change visible. Experiments on real-world datasets support the approach’s effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both a mathematical reduction and a method for constructing intervals whose protection is tied to a stated model of distribution shift.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs conformal intervals that remain valid under distribution shifts modeled by Lévy-Prokhorov ambiguity sets.

title: Conformal Prediction under Lévy-Prokhorov Distribution Shifts: Robustness to Local and Global Perturbations

abstract: Significant progress has been achieved using Vision Transformers (ViTs) in computer vision. However, challenges persist in modeling multi-scale spatial relationships, hindering effective integration of fine-grained local details and long-range global dependencies. To address this limitation, a Multi-Kernel Correlation-Attention Vision Transformer (MK-CAViT) grounded in the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi (HGR) theory was proposed, introducing three key innovations. A parallel multi-kernel architecture was utilized to extract multi-scale features through small, medium, and large kernels, overcoming the single-scale constraints of conventional ViTs. The cross-scale interactions were enhanced through the Fast-HGR attention mechanism, which models nonlinear dependencies and applies adaptive scaling to weigh connections and refine contextual reasoning. Additionally, a stable multi-scale fusion strategy was adopted, integrating dynamic normalization and staged learning to mitigate gradient variance, progressively fusing local and global contexts, and improving training stability. The experimental results on ImageNet, COCO, and ADE20K validated the superiority of MK-CAViT in classification, detection, and segmentation, surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in capturing complex spatial relationships while maintaining efficiency. These contributions can establish a theoretically grounded framework for visual representation learning and address the longstanding limitations of ViTs.

The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in capturing complex spatial relationships while maintaining efficiency. The findings support the combined use of multiple feature scales, nonlinear cross-scale attention, and controlled fusion as a way to improve visual representations across several kinds of tasks.
summary.tldr: MK-CAViT combines multiple spatial scales with nonlinear correlation attention and stable fusion to improve classification, detection, and segmentation.

title: Multi-Kernel Correlation-Attention Vision Transformer for Enhanced Contextual Understanding and Multi-Scale Integration

abstract: Scoring the Optical Character Recognition (OCR) capabilities of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) has witnessed growing interest. Existing benchmarks have highlighted the impressive performance of LMMs in text recognition; however, their abilities in certain challenging tasks, such as text localization, handwritten content extraction, and logical reasoning, remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce OCRBench v2, a large-scale bilingual text-centric benchmark with currently the most comprehensive set of tasks ($4\times$ more tasks than the previous multi-scene benchmark OCRBench), the widest coverage of scenarios ($31$ diverse scenarios), and thorough evaluation metrics, with $10,000$ human-verified question-answering pairs and a high proportion of difficult samples. Moreover, we construct a private test set with $1,500$ manually annotated images. The consistent evaluation trends observed across both public and private test sets validate the OCRBench v2's reliability. After carefully benchmarking state-of-the-art LMMs, we find that most LMMs score below $50$ ($100$ in total) and suffer from five-type limitations, including less frequently encountered text recognition, fine-grained perception, layout perception, complex element parsing, and logical reasoning. The benchmark and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/Yuliang-Liu/MultimodalOCR.

paragraphs: Reading text in an image involves more than recognizing words. A model may also need to locate text, extract handwriting, understand layout, and reason about what it reads. OCRBench v2 broadens evaluation toward these harder abilities, which the authors identify as underexplored despite strong results on existing text-recognition benchmarks.

The bilingual benchmark contains 10,000 human-verified question-answer pairs across 31 scenarios, with a high proportion of difficult examples. It covers four times as many tasks as the earlier OCRBench and supplies evaluation metrics for this broader scope. The authors also create a private test set containing 1,500 manually annotated images. Similar evaluation trends on the public and private sets support the benchmark's reliability.

Most evaluated multimodal models score below 50 out of 100. The analysis identifies weaknesses in uncommon text recognition, fine-grained perception, layout understanding, complex-element parsing, and logical reasoning. These results show that strong text recognition does not by itself establish competence across the wider range of visual-text tasks measured by the benchmark.
summary.tldr: OCRBench v2 expands visual-text evaluation and reveals substantial weaknesses in multimodal models' localization, perception, and reasoning.

title: OCRBench v2: An Improved Benchmark for Evaluating Large Multimodal Models on Visual Text Localization and Reasoning

abstract: As multimodal large models (MLLMs) continue to advance across challenging tasks, a key question emerges: \textbf{\textit{What essential capabilities are still missing? }}A critical aspect of human learning is continuous interaction with the environment -- not limited to language, but also involving multimodal understanding and generation.To move closer to human-level intelligence, models must similarly support \textbf{multi-turn}, \textbf{multimodal interaction}. In particular, they should comprehend interleaved multimodal contexts and respond coherently in ongoing exchanges.In this work, we present \textbf{an initial exploration} through the \textsc{InterMT} -- \textbf{the first preference dataset for \textit{multi-turn} multimodal interaction}, grounded in real human feedback. In this exploration, we particularly emphasize the importance of human oversight, introducing expert annotations to guide the process, motivated by the fact that current MLLMs lack such complex interactive capabilities. \textsc{InterMT} captures human preferences at both global and local levels into nine sub-dimensions, consists of 15.6k prompts, 52.6k multi-turn dialogue instances, and 32.4k human-labeled preference pairs. To compensate for the lack of capability for multi-modal understanding and generation, we introduce an agentic workflow that leverages tool-augmented MLLMs to construct multi-turn QA instances.To further this goal, we introduce \textsc{InterMT-Bench} to assess the ability ofMLLMs in assisting judges with multi-turn, multimodal tasks.We demonstrate the utility of \textsc{InterMT} through applications such as judge moderation and further reveal the \textit{multi-turn scaling law} of judge model.We hope the open-source of our data can help facilitate further research on aligning current MLLMs to the next step.

paragraphs: InterMT studies how to align models for ongoing conversations that mix modalities. Such interactions require a model to understand interleaved context and respond coherently across multiple turns. The work is presented as an initial exploration, with expert human oversight playing a central role because current models struggle with these complex interactions.

The dataset records preferences at both the overall conversation level and more local levels across nine sub-dimensions. It contains 15.6 thousand prompts, 52.6 thousand multi-turn dialogue instances, and 32.4 thousand human-labeled preference pairs. To construct the interactions despite model capability gaps, the authors use an agentic workflow combining multimodal models with tools.

The accompanying InterMT-Bench evaluates models' ability to assist judges on multi-turn multimodal tasks. Applications including judge moderation demonstrate the dataset's utility, and the authors report a multi-turn scaling law for the judge model. The contribution supplies human-grounded preference data and an evaluation setting for studying interaction quality across exchanges, beyond the quality of a single isolated response.
summary.tldr: InterMT provides human preference data and a benchmark for evaluating and aligning multi-turn multimodal interactions.

title: InterMT: Multi-Turn Interleaved Preference Alignment with Human Feedback

abstract: Synthetic data is crucial for advancing autonomous driving (AD) systems, yet current state-of-the-art video generation models, despite their visual realism, suffer from subtle geometric distortions that limit their utility for downstream perception tasks. We identify and quantify this critical issue, demonstrating a significant performance gap in 3D object detection when using synthetic versus real data. To address this, we introduce Reinforcement Learning with Geometric Feedback (RLGF), RLGF uniquely refines video diffusion models by incorporating rewards from specialized latent-space AD perception models. Its core components include an efficient Latent-Space Windowing Optimization technique for targeted feedback during diffusion, and a Hierarchical Geometric Reward (HGR) system providing multi-level rewards for point-line-plane alignment, and scene occupancy coherence. To quantify these distortions, we propose GeoScores. Applied to models like DiVE on nuScenes, RLGF substantially reduces geometric errors (e.g., VP error by 21\%, Depth error by 57\%) and dramatically improves 3D object detection mAP by 12.7\%, narrowing the gap to real-data performance. RLGF offers a plug-and-play solution for generating geometrically sound and reliable synthetic videos for AD development.

We identify and quantify this critical issue, demonstrating a significant performance gap in 3D object detection when using synthetic versus real data. To address this, we introduce Reinforcement Learning with Geometric Feedback (RLGF), RLGF uniquely refines video diffusion models by incorporating rewards from specialized latent-space AD perception models. Its core components include an efficient Latent-Space Windowing Optimization technique for targeted feedback during diffusion, and a Hierarchical Geometric Reward (HGR) system providing multi-level rewards for point-line-plane alignment, and scene occupancy coherence. To quantify these distortions, we propose GeoScores. Applied to models like DiVE on nuScenes, RLGF substantially reduces geometric errors (e.g., VP error by 21\%, Depth error by 57\%) and dramatically improves 3D object detection mAP by 12.7\%, narrowing the gap to real-data performance. RLGF offers a plug-and-play solution for generating geometrically sound and reliable synthetic videos for AD development.

This paper identifies and quantifies that problem through a gap in 3D object-detection performance between synthetic and real data. RLGF addresses it by refining video diffusion models with reinforcement-learning rewards tied to geometry.

The rewards come from specialized autonomous-driving perception models operating in latent space. A windowing optimization method provides targeted feedback during diffusion, while a hierarchical reward system assesses point, line, and plane alignment along with scene occupancy coherence. The authors also introduce GeoScores to measure geometric distortions. These components connect generation quality to spatial properties relevant to downstream perception.

In applications including DiVE on nuScenes, the paper reports a 21% reduction in VP error and a 57% reduction in depth error. It also reports a 12.7% improvement in 3D object-detection mAP, narrowing the real-data performance gap. The findings support geometric feedback as a way to improve both synthetic video structure and its usefulness for perception.
summary.tldr: RLGF uses perception-based geometric rewards to improve synthetic driving videos and narrow the reported downstream 3D detection gap.

title: RLGF: Reinforcement Learning with Geometric Feedback for Autonomous Driving Video Generation

abstract: Recent advances in radiance fields and novel view synthesis enable creation of realistic digital twins from photographs. However, current methods struggle with flat, texture-less surfaces, creating uneven and semi-transparent reconstructions, due to an ill-conditioned photometric reconstruction objective. Surface reconstruction methods solve this issue but sacrifice visual quality. We propose a novel hybrid 2D/3D representation that jointly optimizes constrained planar (2D) Gaussians for modeling flat surfaces and freeform (3D) Gaussians for the rest of the scene. Our end-to-end approach dynamically detects and refines planar regions, improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy. It achieves state-of-the-art depth estimation on ScanNet++ and ScanNetv2, and excels at mesh extraction without overfitting to a specific camera model, showing its effectiveness in producing high-quality reconstruction of indoor scenes.

Flat surfaces with little texture are particularly difficult because matching image colors provides weak guidance about their shape. Existing methods can therefore produce surfaces that look uneven or partly transparent. Approaches focused on surface reconstruction address this problem but can reduce visual quality.

This paper introduces a representation that gives different parts of a scene different geometric flexibility. Constrained, planar Gaussians represent flat regions, while freeform three-dimensional Gaussians represent the remaining content. The system jointly optimizes both kinds of elements and dynamically detects and refines planar regions. This lets flat surfaces receive explicit geometric structure while retaining a flexible representation elsewhere.

They also report strong mesh extraction without overfitting to a particular camera model. These findings support the hybrid representation as a way to improve indoor reconstruction across appearance, depth, and extracted surface geometry.
summary.tldr: Combining planar and freeform Gaussians improves indoor scene reconstruction, especially for flat surfaces with little texture.

title: 3D Gaussian Flats: Hybrid 2D/3D Photometric Scene Reconstruction

abstract: Pseudo label based semi-supervised learning (SSL) for single-label and multi-label classification tasks has been extensively studied; however, semi-supervised label distribution learning (SSLDL) remains a largely unexplored area. Existing SSL methods fail in SSLDL because the pseudo-labels they generate only ensure overall similarity to the ground truth but do not preserve the ranking relationships between true labels, as they rely solely on KL divergence as the loss function during training. These skewed pseudo-labels lead the model to learn incorrect semantic relationships, resulting in reduced performance accuracy. To address these issues, we propose a novel SSLDL method called \textit{RankMatch}. \textit{RankMatch} fully considers the ranking relationships between different labels during the training phase with labeled data to generate higher-quality pseudo-labels. Furthermore, our key observation is that a flexible utilization of pseudo-labels can enhance SSLDL performance. Specifically, focusing solely on the ranking relationships between labels while disregarding their margins helps prevent model overfitting. Theoretically, we prove that incorporating ranking correlations enhances SSLDL performance and establish generalization error bounds for \textit{RankMatch}. Finally, extensive real-world experiments validate its effectiveness.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning predicts how strongly several labels apply to an example. In the semi-supervised setting, predicted labels help train on unlabeled examples. The paper argues that matching an overall distribution through KL divergence alone can still produce pseudo-labels with incorrect label ordering, causing the model to learn misleading semantic relationships.

RankMatch explicitly considers relationships between label rankings when learning from labeled data, aiming to generate better pseudo-labels. It then uses those pseudo-labels flexibly: focusing on their ordering while disregarding the margins between label values helps prevent overfitting. This separates confidence in which labels rank higher from confidence in the exact numerical gaps between them.

The authors provide a theoretical result that incorporating ranking correlations improves semi-supervised label distribution learning, along with generalization error bounds for RankMatch. Real-world experiments also support its effectiveness. The central contribution is to treat relative label order as useful supervision in its own right, rather than relying entirely on agreement between numerical distributions when learning from model-generated targets.
summary.tldr: RankMatch improves semi-supervised label distribution learning by preserving label rankings and avoiding overreliance on pseudo-label value gaps.

title: RankMatch: A Novel Approach to Semi-Supervised Label Distribution Learning Leveraging Rank Correlation between Labels

abstract: Agents are minimally entities that are influenced by their past observations and act to influence future observations. This latter capacity is captured by empowerment, which has served as a vital framing concept across artificial intelligence and cognitive science. This former capacity, however, is equally foundational: In what ways, and to what extent, can an agent be influenced by what it observes? In this paper, we ground this concept in a universal agent-centric measure that we refer to as plasticity, and reveal a fundamental connection to empowerment. Following a set of desiderata on a suitable definition, we define plasticity using a new information-theoretic quantity we call the generalized directed information. We show that this new quantity strictly generalizes the directed information introduced by Massey (1990) while preserving all of its desirable properties. Under this definition, we find that plasticity is well thought of as the mirror of empowerment: The two concepts are defined using the same measure, with only the direction of influence reversed. Our main result establishes a tension between the plasticity and empowerment of an agent, suggesting that agent design needs to be mindful of both characteristics. We explore the implications of these findings, and suggest that plasticity, empowerment, and their relationship are essential to understanding agency.

paragraphs: An agent both responds to past observations and acts to influence future observations. Empowerment captures the latter capacity. This paper develops a corresponding measure for the former: plasticity, understood as how and to what extent observations can influence an agent. The goal is to place both directions of influence within one mathematical framework.

Starting from requirements for a suitable definition, the authors introduce generalized directed information. They show that this quantity strictly extends the existing notion of directed information while retaining its desirable properties. Plasticity and empowerment can then be expressed using the same measure, with the direction of influence reversed.

The main result establishes a tension between an agent's plasticity and empowerment. This suggests that agent design should consider responsiveness to observations alongside the capacity to shape future observations. The contribution is a formal account of their relationship, giving the two capacities a shared basis for analysis and making their interaction part of the study of agency.
summary.tldr: A new information-theoretic measure links an agent's responsiveness to observations with its ability to influence them.

title: Plasticity as the Mirror of Empowerment

abstract: We consider the problem of reliably selecting an optimal subset of fixed size from a given set of choice alternatives, based on noisy information about the quality of these alternatives. Problems of similar kind have been tackled by means of adaptive sampling schemes called racing algorithms. However, in contrast to existing approaches, we do not assume that each alternative is characterized by a real-valued random variable, and that samples are taken from the corresponding distributions. Instead, we only assume that alternatives can be compared in terms of pairwise preferences. We propose and formally analyze a general preference-based racing algorithm that we instantiate with three specific ranking procedures and corresponding sampling schemes. Experiments with real and synthetic data are presented to show the efficiency of our approach.

paragraphs: Selecting the best fixed-size subset of alternatives becomes difficult when information about their quality is noisy. Racing algorithms address such problems through adaptive sampling. This paper considers a setting in which the available evidence consists of pairwise preferences: observations compare two alternatives rather than supply a numerical quality measurement for each one.

That change in feedback is central to the approach. The method does not assume each alternative has its own real-valued random variable from which samples can be drawn. The authors instead propose and formally analyze a general preference-based racing algorithm, then instantiate it with three ranking procedures and their associated sampling schemes.

These instantiations connect the general algorithm to concrete ways of ranking alternatives and choosing comparisons. Experiments on real and synthetic data demonstrate the approach's efficiency. The work therefore provides a framework for reliable subset selection when comparative judgments are the natural evidence, extending adaptive racing to a setting that lacks the numerical sampling model used by existing approaches.
summary.tldr: A preference-based racing framework selects top-k alternatives using adaptive noisy pairwise comparisons instead of numerical quality samples.

title: Top-k Selection based on Adaptive Sampling of Noisy Preferences

abstract: Graphical models are widely used in inference problems. In practice, one may construct a single large-scale model to explain a phenomenon of interest, which may be utilized in a variety of settings. The latent variables of interest, which can differ in each setting, may only represent a small subset of all variables. The marginals of variables of interest may change after the addition of measurements at different time points. In such adaptive settings, naive algorithms, such as standard belief propagation (BP), may utilize many unnecessary computations by propagating messages over the entire graph. Here, we formulate an efficient inference procedure, termed adaptive BP (AdaBP), suitable for adaptive inference settings. We show that it gives exact results for trees in discrete and Gaussian Markov Random Fields (MRFs), and provide an extension to Gaussian loopy graphs. We also provide extensions on finding the most likely sequence of the entire latent graph. Lastly, we compare the proposed method to standard BP and to that of (Sumer et al., 2011), which tackles the same problem. We show in synthetic and real experiments that it outperforms standard BP by orders of magnitude and explore the settings that it is advantageous over (Sumer et al., 2011).

paragraphs: A large graphical model may be reused for many inference questions, even when each question concerns only a small subset of its hidden variables. New measurements can also change the probabilities of interest over time. Standard belief propagation may perform unnecessary work in these settings by sending messages across the entire graph whenever inference is needed.

The paper introduces adaptive belief propagation, or AdaBP, as an inference procedure designed for these changing queries and measurements. It gives exact results on tree-structured discrete and Gaussian Markov random fields. The authors also extend the approach to Gaussian graphs with loops and to finding the most likely configuration of the entire latent graph.

Synthetic and real experiments report performance improvements of orders of magnitude over standard belief propagation. The paper also investigates when AdaBP is advantageous over another method addressing the same adaptive problem. The exactness claim is specifically established for trees; the broader contribution is an inference approach tailored to repeated, changing uses of a large model.
summary.tldr: AdaBP accelerates inference as queries and measurements change, with exact results on discrete and Gaussian tree models.

title: Adaptive Belief Propagation

abstract: The organizer of a machine learning competition faces the problem of maintaining an accurate leaderboard that faithfully represents the quality of the best submission of each competing team. What makes this estimation problem particularly challenging is its sequential and adaptive nature. As participants are allowed to repeatedly evaluate their submissions on the leaderboard, they may begin to overfit to the holdout data that supports the leaderboard. Few theoretical results give actionable advice on how to design a reliable leaderboard. Existing approaches therefore often resort to poorly understood heuristics such as limiting the bit precision of answers and the rate of re-submission. In this work, we introduce a notion of leaderboard accuracy tailored to the format of a competition. We introduce a natural algorithm called the Ladder and demonstrate that it simultaneously supports strong theoretical guarantees in a fully adaptive model of estimation, withstands practical adversarial attacks, and achieves high utility on real submission files from a Kaggle competition. Notably, we are able to sidestep a powerful recent hardness result for adaptive risk estimation that rules out algorithms such as ours under a seemingly very similar notion of accuracy. On a practical note, we provide a completely parameter-free variant of our algorithm that can be deployed in a real competition with no tuning required whatsoever.

paragraphs: A competition leaderboard repeatedly evaluates submissions using held-out data. Because participants adapt later submissions to earlier scores, they can gradually overfit that data. This paper asks how a leaderboard can continue to represent the quality of each team's best submission accurately despite this feedback loop.

The authors define an accuracy criterion tailored to leaderboards and introduce the Ladder algorithm. They establish strong theoretical guarantees in a fully adaptive estimation setting. The choice of criterion is consequential: it allows them to avoid a hardness result that would prohibit such algorithms under a different, seemingly similar definition of adaptive estimation accuracy.

The evaluation shows resistance to practical adversarial attacks and high utility on actual submission files from a Kaggle competition. The paper also supplies a parameter-free variant intended for deployment without tuning. Together, these contributions provide a theoretically grounded way to maintain useful competition feedback, with practical evidence supporting its reliability under adaptive use.
summary.tldr: The Ladder maintains reliable competition feedback under adaptive submissions using a leaderboard-specific accuracy criterion.

title: The Ladder: A Reliable Leaderboard for Machine Learning Competitions

abstract: We seek decision rules for \it prediction-time cost reduction, where complete data is available for training, but during prediction-time, each feature can only be acquired for an additional cost. We propose a novel random forest algorithm to minimize prediction error for a user-specified \it average feature acquisition budget. While random forests yield strong generalization performance, they do not explicitly account for feature costs and furthermore require low correlation among trees, which amplifies costs. Our random forest grows trees with low acquisition cost and high strength based on greedy minimax cost-weighted-impurity splits. Theoretically, we establish near-optimal acquisition cost guarantees for our algorithm. Empirically, on a number of benchmark datasets we demonstrate competitive accuracy-cost curves against state-of-the-art prediction-time algorithms.

paragraphs: Some prediction systems must pay to obtain each feature, even though complete data are available during training. This paper develops a random forest for that setting, aiming to minimize prediction error under a user-chosen average feature acquisition budget. The budget concerns average cost, rather than a stated fixed cap for every prediction.

Ordinary random forests do not explicitly account for feature prices. Their reliance on low correlation among trees can also amplify acquisition costs. The proposed algorithm grows trees using greedy minimax splits that weight impurity by cost, seeking trees that are both strong predictors and inexpensive to use.

The authors establish near-optimal guarantees for feature acquisition cost. They also evaluate the method on benchmark datasets and report competitive accuracy-cost curves against state-of-the-art prediction-time algorithms. These curves assess prediction quality across spending levels, matching the practical objective of deciding how much feature information to purchase. The contribution makes acquisition cost an explicit part of forest construction.
summary.tldr: A cost-aware random forest balances prediction error against an average feature acquisition budget.

title: Feature-Budgeted Random Forest

abstract: Bayesian nonparametric mixture models based on the Dirichlet process (DP) have been widely used for solving problems like clustering, density estimation and topic modelling. These models make weak assumptions about the underlying process that generated the observed data. Thus, when more data are collected, the complexity of these models can change accordingly. These theoretical properties often lead to superior predictive performance when compared to traditional finite mixture models. However, despite the increasing amount of data available, the application of Bayesian nonparametric mixture models is so far limited to relatively small data sets. In this paper, we propose an efficient distributed inference algorithm for the DP and the HDP mixture model. The proposed method is based on a variant of the slice sampler for DPs. Since this sampler does not involve a pre-determined truncation, the stationary distribution of the sampling algorithm is unbiased. We provide both local thread-level and distributed machine-level parallel implementations and study the performance of this sampler through an extensive set of experiments on image and text data. When compared to existing inference algorithms, the proposed method exhibits state-of-the-art accuracy and strong scalability with up to 512 cores.

The paper addresses that gap with a distributed inference algorithm for both Dirichlet process and hierarchical Dirichlet process mixtures.

This property concerns the distribution targeted by the sampler; it does not mean that any finite collection of samples is automatically exact. The authors implement parallelism both among local threads and across separate machines.

Experiments on image and text data compare the method with existing inference algorithms. The reported results combine state-of-the-art accuracy with strong scalability up to 512 cores. The contribution is therefore both statistical and computational: the method retains the untruncated sampling target while making inference practical across substantially more computing resources.
summary.tldr: A distributed slice sampler scales DP and HDP mixture inference to 512 cores without predetermined truncation.

title: Distributed Inference for Dirichlet Process Mixture Models

abstract: Spectral methods for dimensionality reduction and clustering require solving an eigenproblem defined by a sparse affinity matrix. When this matrix is large, one seeks an approximate solution. The standard way to do this is the Nystrom method, which first solves a small eigenproblem considering only a subset of landmark points, and then applies an out-of-sample formula to extrapolate the solution to the entire dataset. We show that by constraining the original problem to satisfy the Nystrom formula, we obtain an approximation that is computationally simple and efficient, but achieves a lower approximation error using fewer landmarks and less runtime. We also study the role of normalization in the computational cost and quality of the resulting solution.

paragraphs: Spectral methods for clustering and dimensionality reduction require solving an eigenproblem derived from an affinity matrix. When the matrix is large, an approximate solution becomes attractive. The standard Nyström approach first solves a smaller problem using selected landmark points, then extends that solution to the rest of the dataset through an out-of-sample formula.

This paper changes how that formula enters the computation. Instead of using it only to extend a solution obtained from landmarks, the authors constrain the original problem to satisfy the Nyström formula. The approximation is thus derived from the original optimization problem under the restriction imposed by that representation.

The authors show that this variational approach is computationally simple and efficient, while achieving lower approximation error with fewer landmarks and less runtime. They also examine how normalization affects both computational cost and solution quality. The contribution demonstrates that the same general landmark-based representation can yield a better approximation when it is incorporated into the problem formulation, rather than used solely as an extrapolation step.
summary.tldr: A variational formulation of the Nyström approximation achieves lower error with fewer landmarks and less runtime.

title: The Variational Nystrom method for large-scale spectral problems

abstract: We provide the first oracle efficient sublinear regret algorithms for adversarial versions of the contextual bandit problem. In this problem, the learner repeatedly makes an action on the basis of a context and receives reward for the chosen action, with the goal of achieving reward competitive with a large class of policies. We analyze two settings: i) in the transductive setting the learner knows the set of contexts a priori, ii) in the small separator setting, there exists a small set of contexts such that any two policies behave differently on one of the contexts in the set. Our algorithms fall into the Follow-The-Perturbed-Leader family (Kalai and Vempala, 2005) and achieve regret O(T^3/4\sqrtK\log(N)) in the transductive setting and O(T^2/3 d^3/4 K\sqrt\log(N)) in the separator setting, where T is the number of rounds, K is the number of actions, N is the number of baseline policies, and d is the size of the separator. We actually solve the more general adversarial contextual semi-bandit linear optimization problem, whilst in the full information setting we address the even more general contextual combinatorial optimization. We provide several extensions and implications of our algorithms, such as switching regret and efficient learning with predictable sequences.

paragraphs: In contextual bandit learning, a learner observes a context, chooses an action, and receives feedback for that action. Its aim is to compete with a large collection of policies. This paper develops oracle-efficient algorithms with sublinear regret for adversarial versions of the problem, meaning their average reward shortfall relative to the comparison class diminishes over time.

The guarantees concern two structured settings. In the transductive setting, the learner knows the collection of contexts in advance. In the small-separator setting, a small collection of contexts distinguishes every pair of policies. The algorithms use the Follow-The-Perturbed-Leader approach, with regret growing as T to the three-quarters power or two-thirds power, respectively, alongside factors involving actions, policies, and separator size.

The methods also solve a more general contextual semi-bandit linear optimization problem. With full information, the scope extends to contextual combinatorial optimization. Further implications include switching regret and learning with predictable sequences. These extensions broaden the contribution while the stated structural settings remain central to the principal guarantees.
summary.tldr: Oracle-efficient algorithms achieve sublinear regret in two structured adversarial contextual-learning settings, with extensions to richer optimization and feedback problems.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Adversarial Contextual Learning

abstract: Given samples from a distribution, how many new elements should we expect to find if we keep on sampling this distribution? This is an important and actively studied problem, with many applications ranging from species estimation to genomics. We generalize this extrapolation and related unseen estimation problems to the multiple population setting, where population $j$ has an unknown distribution $D_j$ from which we observe $n_j$ samples. We derive an optimal estimator for the total number of elements we expect to find among new samples across the populations. Surprisingly, we prove that our estimator’s accuracy is independent of the number of populations. We also develop an efficient optimization algorithm to solve the more general problem of estimating multi-population frequency distributions. We validate our methods and theory through extensive experiments. Finally, on a real dataset of human genomes across multiple ancestries, we demonstrate how our approach for unseen estimation can enable cohort designs that can discover interesting mutations with greater efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many new elements additional sampling will reveal when observations come from several populations. Each population has its own unknown distribution and an existing sample. This extends unseen-element estimation beyond a single source, making the problem relevant to settings where future observations can be collected across different groups.

The authors derive an optimal estimator for the total number of elements expected in new samples across those populations. They prove that its accuracy is independent of the number of populations. This is a specific theoretical result about the estimator, showing that increasing the population count does not itself impose the accuracy dependence one might expect.

The work also develops an efficient optimization algorithm for the broader task of estimating frequency distributions across multiple populations. Extensive experiments evaluate the methods and theory. An application to human genomes from multiple ancestries demonstrates how unseen estimation can inform cohort design, helping select sampling plans that discover interesting mutations more efficiently.
summary.tldr: An optimal estimator predicts discoveries from additional sampling across populations, with accuracy proved independent of the population count.

title: Estimating the unseen from multiple populations

abstract: Efficient simulation of the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid flow is a long standing problem in applied mathematics, for which state-of-the-art methods require large compute resources. In this work, we propose a data-driven approach that leverages the approximation power of deep-learning with the precision of standard solvers to obtain fast and highly realistic simulations. Our method solves the incompressible Euler equations using the standard operator splitting method, in which a large sparse linear system with many free parameters must be solved. We use a Convolutional Network with a highly tailored architecture, trained using a novel unsupervised learning framework to solve the linear system. We present real-time 2D and 3D simulations that outperform recently proposed data-driven methods; the obtained results are realistic and show good generalization properties.

This paper combines a conventional simulation procedure with a learned component to accelerate that work. Although the motivation concerns the broader challenge of fluid simulation, the proposed method specifically solves the incompressible Euler equations.

The authors target this computational task with a convolutional network whose architecture is tailored to the problem. They train the network through an unsupervised learning framework, embedding learned approximation within the established solver procedure.

The authors present real-time simulations in both two and three dimensions and report improvements over recently proposed data-driven methods. They describe the resulting flows as realistic and report good generalization. These findings support the usefulness of learning a demanding component of a numerical simulation: the network contributes speed while the surrounding conventional procedure retains its role in organizing the fluid calculation.
summary.tldr: A tailored convolutional network accelerates a linear-system solve within a conventional fluid simulator, enabling realistic real-time 2D and 3D results.

title: Accelerating Eulerian Fluid Simulation With Convolutional Networks

abstract: We propose to tackle the problem of end-to-end learning for raw waveform signals by introducing learnable continuous time-frequency atoms. The derivation of these filters is achieved by defining a functional space with a given smoothness order and boundary conditions. From this space, we derive the parametric analytical filters. Their differentiability property allows gradient-based optimization. As such, one can utilize any Deep Neural Network (DNN) with these filters. This enables us to tackle in a front-end fashion a large scale bird detection task based on the freefield1010 dataset known to contain key challenges, such as the dimensionality of the inputs data ($>100,000$) and the presence of additional noises: multiple sources and soundscapes.

The stated challenges include raw inputs with more than 100,000 dimensions and additional noise from multiple sources and soundscapes. This application brings the filter construction into a demanding waveform-processing setting, demonstrating how an explicitly defined family of continuous filters can participate in neural-network training directly from raw signals.
summary.tldr: Differentiable spline-based time-frequency filters provide a trainable front end for neural networks processing raw waveforms.

title: Spline Filters For End-to-End Deep Learning

abstract: The ability to transfer skills across tasks has the potential to scale up reinforcement learning (RL) agents to environments currently out of reach. Recently, a framework based on two ideas, successor features (SFs) and generalised policy improvement (GPI), has been introduced as a principled way of transferring skills. In this paper we extend the SF&GPI framework in two ways. One of the basic assumptions underlying the original formulation of SF&GPI is that rewards for all tasks of interest can be computed as linear combinations of a fixed set of features. We relax this constraint and show that the theoretical guarantees supporting the framework can be extended to any set of tasks that only differ in the reward function. Our second contribution is to show that one can use the reward functions themselves as features for future tasks, without any loss of expressiveness, thus removing the need to specify a set of features beforehand. This makes it possible to combine SF&GPI with deep learning in a more stable way. We empirically verify this claim on a complex 3D environment where observations are images from a first-person perspective. We show that the transfer promoted by SF&GPI leads to very good policies on unseen tasks almost instantaneously. We also describe how to learn policies specialised to the new tasks in a way that allows them to be added to the agent’s set of skills, and thus be reused in the future.

summary.tldr: An extended successor-feature framework supports rapid skill transfer across reward-changing tasks without requiring a predefined feature set.

title: Transfer in Deep Reinforcement Learning Using Successor Features and Generalised Policy Improvement

abstract: We introduce a kernel approximation strategy that enables computation of the Gaussian process log marginal likelihood and all hyperparameter derivatives in O(p) time. Our GRIEF kernel consists of p eigenfunctions found using a Nystrom approximation from a dense Cartesian product grid of inducing points. By exploiting algebraic properties of Kronecker and Khatri-Rao tensor products, computational complexity of the training procedure can be practically independent of the number of inducing points. This allows us to use arbitrarily many inducing points to achieve a globally accurate kernel approximation, even in high-dimensional problems. The fast likelihood evaluation enables type-I or II Bayesian inference on large-scale datasets. We benchmark our algorithms on real-world problems with up to two-million training points and 10^33 inducing points.

The authors benchmark the methods on real-world problems with up to two million training points and 10^33 inducing points. The distinction between p eigenfunctions and the much larger inducing grid is central: the stated evaluation cost depends on the representation size p, while structured algebra handles the grid.
summary.tldr: GP-GRIEF uses grid structure and eigenfunction approximations to support fast Gaussian process likelihood calculations with enormous inducing grids.

title: Scalable Gaussian Processes with Grid-Structured Eigenfunctions (GP-GRIEF)

abstract: We present novel understandings of the Gamma-Poisson (GaP) model, a probabilistic matrix factorization model for count data. We show that GaP can be rewritten free of the score/activation matrix. This gives us new insights about the estimation of the topic/dictionary matrix by maximum marginal likelihood estimation. In particular, this explains the robustness of this estimator to over-specified values of the factorization rank, especially its ability to automatically prune irrelevant dictionary columns, as empirically observed in previous work. The marginalization of the activation matrix leads in turn to a new Monte Carlo Expectation-Maximization algorithm with favorable properties.
