paragraphs: The Gamma-Poisson model represents count data through probabilistic matrix factorization. Its components include a topic or dictionary matrix and a score or activation matrix. This paper develops a reformulation that removes the activation matrix from the model expression through marginalization, allowing the dictionary to be studied through a marginal likelihood.

That reformulation provides insight into maximum marginal likelihood estimation of the dictionary. In particular, it explains why this estimator can remain robust when the chosen factorization rank is larger than needed. The authors connect this robustness to its ability to automatically prune irrelevant dictionary columns, a behavior previously observed empirically.

Marginalizing the activation matrix also leads to a new Monte Carlo Expectation-Maximization algorithm with favorable properties. The contribution therefore combines an explanation of existing empirical behavior with a new estimation procedure. It shows how changing the mathematical representation of the model can clarify why unnecessary components disappear while also supporting a different approach to fitting the remaining dictionary.
summary.tldr: Marginalizing Gamma-Poisson activations explains dictionary pruning under excessive rank and yields a new Monte Carlo EM algorithm.

title: Closed-form Marginal Likelihood in Gamma-Poisson Matrix Factorization

abstract: Most commonly used distributed machine learning systems are either synchronous or centralized asynchronous. Synchronous algorithms like AllReduce-SGD perform poorly in a heterogeneous environment, while asynchronous algorithms using a parameter server suffer from 1) communication bottleneck at parameter servers when workers are many, and 2) significantly worse convergence when the traffic to parameter server is congested. Can we design an algorithm that is robust in a heterogeneous environment, while being communication efficient and maintaining the best-possible convergence rate? In this paper, we propose an asynchronous decentralized stochastic gradient decent algorithm (AD-PSGD) satisfying all above expectations. Our theoretical analysis shows AD-PSGD converges at the optimal $O(1/\sqrt{K})$ rate as SGD and has linear speedup w.r.t. number of workers. Empirically, AD-PSGD outperforms the best of decentralized parallel SGD (D-PSGD), asynchronous parallel SGD (A-PSGD), and standard data parallel SGD (AllReduce-SGD), often by orders of magnitude in a heterogeneous environment. When training ResNet-50 on ImageNet with up to 128 GPUs, AD-PSGD converges (w.r.t epochs) similarly to the AllReduce-SGD, but each epoch can be up to 4-8x faster than its synchronous counterparts in a network-sharing HPC environment. To the best of our knowledge, AD-PSGD is the first asynchronous algorithm that achieves a similar epoch-wise convergence rate as AllReduce-SGD, at an over 100-GPU scale.

This paper proposes asynchronous decentralized stochastic gradient descent, AD-PSGD, to combine tolerance for heterogeneous workers with efficient communication.

The theoretical analysis establishes the optimal O(1/√K) convergence rate associated with SGD and linear speedup with the number of workers. In the tested network-sharing high-performance computing environment, epochs can be up to four to eight times faster than with synchronous alternatives. The distinction matters: the reported advantage combines similar learning progress per epoch with substantially less elapsed time for that progress.
summary.tldr: AD-PSGD combines asynchronous decentralized training with convergence guarantees and substantial reported speedups in heterogeneous computing environments.

title: Asynchronous Decentralized Parallel Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: We tackle the problem of one-shot segmentation: finding and segmenting a previously unseen object in a cluttered scene based on a single instruction example. We propose a novel dataset, which we call cluttered Omniglot . Using a baseline architecture combining a Siamese embedding for detection with a U-net for segmentation we show that increasing levels of clutter make the task progressively harder. Using oracle models with access to various amounts of ground-truth information, we evaluate different aspects of the problem and show that in this kind of visual search task, detection and segmentation are two intertwined problems, the solution to each of which helps solving the other. We therefore introduce MaskNet , an improved model that attends to multiple candidate locations, generates segmentation proposals to mask out background clutter and selects among the segmented objects. Our findings suggest that such image recognition models based on an iterative refinement of object detection and foreground segmentation may provide a way to deal with highly cluttered scenes.

paragraphs: One-shot segmentation requires finding a previously unseen object and identifying its pixels from a single example. This paper studies the task in cluttered scenes and introduces cluttered Omniglot as a dataset. A baseline combines a Siamese embedding for detection with a U-net for segmentation, showing that more clutter makes the task harder.

The authors use oracle models with different amounts of ground-truth information to examine how the task’s parts interact. Their findings show that locating an object and separating it from its background are intertwined: better detection helps segmentation, and better segmentation helps detection. This motivates a model that gives the two processes opportunities to support each other.

The resulting MaskNet examines multiple candidate locations, proposes segmentations that mask away background clutter, and chooses among the segmented objects. The findings suggest that iteratively refining detection and foreground segmentation may help recognition in highly cluttered scenes. The contribution combines a dataset, an investigation of the task’s structure, and a model designed around that interaction.
summary.tldr: MaskNet addresses one-shot segmentation in clutter by using candidate segmentations to help locate and select the requested object.

title: One-Shot Segmentation in Clutter

abstract: Sparse Subspace Clustering (SSC) is a popular unsupervised machine learning method for clustering data lying close to an unknown union of low-dimensional linear subspaces; a problem with numerous applications in pattern recognition and computer vision. Even though the behavior of SSC for complete data is by now well-understood, little is known about its theoretical properties when applied to data with missing entries. In this paper we give theoretical guarantees for SSC with incomplete data, and provide theoretical evidence that projecting the zero-filled data onto the observation pattern of the point being expressed can lead to substantial improvement in performance; a phenomenon already known experimentally. The main insight of our analysis is that even though this projection induces additional missing entries, this is counterbalanced by the fact that the projected and zero-filled data are in effect incomplete points associated with the union of the corresponding projected subspaces, with respect to which the point being expressed is complete. The significance of this phenomenon potentially extends to the entire class of self-expressive methods.

paragraphs: Sparse Subspace Clustering groups observations that lie near several unknown low-dimensional linear subspaces. This paper studies what happens when some coordinates of those observations are missing. It develops theoretical guarantees for incomplete data and examines a projection strategy whose practical benefits had already been observed experimentally.

The strategy first fills missing entries with zeros, then projects the data onto the coordinates observed for the point being represented. This removes further entries from other points, which might appear harmful. The analysis explains why it can help: after projection, the reference point is complete relative to the projected subspaces, even though the other points remain incomplete.

This change in the geometry counterbalances the extra missing information and provides theoretical evidence for potentially substantial performance improvements. The result helps explain why matching the representation to a point’s observation pattern can matter more than simply preserving every available coordinate. The authors suggest that the same phenomenon may extend to the broader family of self-expressive methods.
summary.tldr: The paper explains why projecting incomplete data onto a point’s observed coordinates can improve sparse subspace clustering.

title: Theoretical Analysis of Sparse Subspace Clustering with Missing Entries

abstract: Recent works have cast some light on the mystery of why deep nets fit any data and generalize despite being very overparametrized. This paper analyzes training and generalization for a simple 2-layer ReLU net with random initialization, and provides the following improvements over recent works: (i) Using a tighter characterization of training speed than recent papers, an explanation for why training a neural net with random labels leads to slower training, as originally observed in [Zhang et al. ICLR’17]. (ii) Generalization bound independent of network size, using a data-dependent complexity measure. Our measure distinguishes clearly between random labels and true labels on MNIST and CIFAR, as shown by experiments. Moreover, recent papers require sample complexity to increase (slowly) with the size, while our sample complexity is completely independent of the network size. (iii) Learnability of a broad class of smooth functions by 2-layer ReLU nets trained via gradient descent. The key idea is to track dynamics of training and generalization via properties of a related kernel.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how an overparameterized two-layer ReLU network trains and generalizes when initialized randomly. It addresses a puzzle behind large networks: they can fit arbitrary labels, yet can also learn patterns that transfer to unseen data. The analysis follows training and generalization through properties of a related kernel.

A tighter description of training speed explains why fitting random labels takes longer than fitting meaningful labels. The authors also derive a generalization bound based on a data-dependent complexity measure, rather than network size. In experiments on MNIST and CIFAR, that measure clearly separates random labels from true labels, making it sensitive to the structure of the learning problem.

The resulting sample-complexity guarantee is completely independent of network size, improving on analyses in which the required number of samples grows with model size. The paper additionally establishes that gradient descent on two-layer ReLU networks can learn a broad class of smooth functions. These results connect optimization speed, label structure, and generalization within the stated two-layer setting.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based analysis explains slower training on random labels and gives network-size-independent generalization guarantees for overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks.

title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Optimization and Generalization for Overparameterized Two-Layer Neural Networks

abstract: We design coresets for Ordered k-Median, a generalization of classical clustering problems such as k-Median and k-Center. Its objective function is defined via the Ordered Weighted Averaging (OWA) paradigm of Yager (1988), where data points are weighted according to a predefined weight vector, but in order of their contribution to the objective (distance from the centers). A powerful data-reduction technique, called a coreset, is to summarize a point set $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ into a small (weighted) point set $X’$, such that for every set of $k$ potential centers, the objective value of the coreset $X’$ approximates that of $X$ within factor $1\pm \epsilon$. When there are multiple objectives (weights), the above standard coreset might have limited usefulness, whereas in a simultaneous coreset, the above approximation holds for all weights (in addition to all centers). Our main result is a construction of a simultaneous coreset of size $O_{\epsilon, d}(k^2 \log^2 |X|)$ for Ordered k-Median. We validate our algorithm on a real geographical data set, and we find our coreset leads to a massive speedup of clustering computations, while maintaining high accuracy for a range of weights.

paragraphs: Ordered k-Median is a clustering problem in which points receive weights according to their rank in distance from the chosen centers. Different weight choices express different clustering objectives, including classical k-Median and k-Center. This paper develops small summaries of a dataset that preserve these objectives well enough to accelerate clustering computations.

Such a summary, called a coreset, is a weighted collection of points whose objective value approximates that of the full data for every possible set of k centers. The authors strengthen this requirement: their simultaneous coreset works for every weight choice as well. That matters when users want to explore multiple clustering priorities without constructing a separate summary for each.

The main construction has size proportional to k squared times the squared logarithm of the dataset size, with additional dependence on dimension and approximation accuracy. Its guarantee preserves objective values within a factor of one plus or minus the chosen error tolerance. On a real geographical dataset, the authors report a large computational speedup while maintaining high accuracy across a range of weights.
summary.tldr: A simultaneous coreset compresses clustering data while approximating Ordered k-Median costs for every choice of centers and weights.

title: Coresets for Ordered Weighted Clustering

abstract: This work studies the second-order convergence for both standard alternating minimization and proximal alternating minimization. We show that under mild assumptions on the (nonconvex) objective function, both algorithms avoid strict saddles almost surely from random initialization. Together with known first-order convergence results, this implies both algorithms converge to a second-order stationary point. This solves an open problem for the second-order convergence of alternating minimization algorithms that have been widely used in practice to solve large-scale nonconvex problems due to their simple implementation, fast convergence, and superb empirical performance.
originalAbstract: This work studies the second-order convergence for both standard alternating minimization and proximal alternating minimization. We show that under mild assumptions on the (nonconvex) objective function, both algorithms avoid strict saddles almost surely from random initialization. Together with known first-order convergence results, this implies both algorithms converge to a second-order stationary point. This solves an open problem for the second-order convergence of alternating minimization algorithms that have been widely used in practice to solve large-scale nonconvex problems due to their simple implementation, fast convergence, and superb empirical performance.

paragraphs: Alternating minimization tackles an optimization problem by updating different groups of variables in turn. Its simple implementation and strong practical performance have made it useful for large nonconvex problems. This paper asks what kind of stationary solution the method reaches, going beyond the first-order convergence results already available.

The authors analyze both standard alternating minimization and its proximal variant. Under assumptions on the nonconvex objective described as mild, they show that random initialization leads both algorithms to avoid strict saddle points almost surely. Such points are stationary but have a direction of negative curvature, so first-order stationarity alone does not exclude them.

Combining this saddle-avoidance result with known first-order convergence results yields convergence to a second-order stationary point. This gives a stronger characterization of the algorithms’ destinations and resolves an open question about their behavior. The conclusion remains conditional on the stated assumptions and random initialization; second-order stationarity is also a different claim from finding a globally best solution.
summary.tldr: Under mild objective assumptions and random initialization, standard and proximal alternating minimization avoid strict saddles and converge to second-order stationary points.

title: Alternating Minimizations Converge to Second-Order Optimal Solutions

abstract: Popular machine learning estimators involve regularization parameters that can be challenging to tune, and standard strategies rely on grid search for this task. In this paper, we revisit the techniques of approximating the regularization path up to predefined tolerance $\epsilon$ in a unified framework and show that its complexity is $O(1/\sqrt[d]{\epsilon})$ for uniformly convex loss of order $d \geq 2$ and $O(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ for Generalized Self-Concordant functions. This framework encompasses least-squares but also logistic regression, a case that as far as we know was not handled as precisely in previous works. We leverage our technique to provide refined bounds on the validation error as well as a practical algorithm for hyperparameter tuning. The latter has global convergence guarantee when targeting a prescribed accuracy on the validation set. Last but not least, our approach helps relieving the practitioner from the (often neglected) task of selecting a stopping criterion when optimizing over the training set: our method automatically calibrates this criterion based on the targeted accuracy on the validation set.
originalAbstract: Popular machine learning estimators involve regularization parameters that can be challenging to tune, and standard strategies rely on grid search for this task. In this paper, we revisit the techniques of approximating the regularization path up to predefined tolerance $\epsilon$ in a unified framework and show that its complexity is $O(1/\sqrt[d]{\epsilon})$ for uniformly convex loss of order $d \geq 2$ and $O(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ for Generalized Self-Concordant functions. This framework encompasses least-squares but also logistic regression, a case that as far as we know was not handled as precisely in previous works. We leverage our technique to provide refined bounds on the validation error as well as a practical algorithm for hyperparameter tuning. The latter has global convergence guarantee when targeting a prescribed accuracy on the validation set. Last but not least, our approach helps relieving the practitioner from the (often neglected) task of selecting a stopping criterion when optimizing over the training set: our method automatically calibrates this criterion based on the targeted accuracy on the validation set.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to tune regularization parameters while controlling the accuracy of the search. It develops a unified framework for approximating the regularization path, the collection of solutions obtained as regularization varies, within a prescribed tolerance. This makes the desired approximation accuracy an explicit part of the tuning procedure.

The authors establish complexity of O(epsilon^(-1/d)) for uniformly convex losses of order d at least two, and O(epsilon^(-1/2)) for generalized self-concordant functions. The framework includes least-squares and logistic regression. These results connect the amount of work needed to the requested tolerance and the mathematical properties of the loss function.

The technique also yields refined validation-error bounds and a practical hyperparameter-tuning algorithm with a global convergence guarantee for a prescribed validation-set accuracy. It automatically calibrates the stopping criterion for training optimization from that target. This connects two decisions that practitioners otherwise have to make separately: how accurately to solve each training problem and how accurately to tune the regularization parameter.
summary.tldr: A tolerance-controlled regularization search provides complexity guarantees and automatically sets training stopping criteria from validation accuracy targets.

title: Safe Grid Search with Optimal Complexity

abstract: We give the first superpolynomial lower bounds for learning one-layer neural networks with respect to the Gaussian distribution for a broad class of algorithms. In the regression setting, we prove that gradient descent run on any classifier with respect to square loss will fail to achieve small test error in polynomial time. Prior work held only for gradient descent run with small batch sizes and sufficiently smooth classifiers. For classification, we give a stronger result, namely that any statistical query (SQ) algorithm will fail to achieve small test error in polynomial time. Our lower bounds hold for commonly used activations such as ReLU and sigmoid. The core of our result relies on a novel construction of a simple family of neural networks that are exactly orthogonal with respect to all spherically symmetric distributions.

paragraphs: Even a one-layer neural network can present a difficult learning problem. This paper establishes superpolynomial lower bounds for learning such networks under Gaussian input distributions. The results concern broad algorithm classes and commonly used activations, including ReLU and sigmoid, showing that shallow architecture alone does not ensure efficient learnability.

For regression with squared loss, the authors prove a polynomial-time barrier to achieving small test error with gradient descent, even when it is run on any classifier. This extends earlier results that required small batches and sufficiently smooth classifiers. For classification, the lower bound covers any statistical query algorithm, giving a broader algorithmic obstruction in that setting.

The proof uses a newly constructed family of simple neural networks that are exactly orthogonal under every spherically symmetric distribution. That construction provides the core of the hardness argument. The conclusions establish difficult learning instances under the stated distribution and algorithmic conditions; they do not say that every one-layer network is difficult to learn in practice.
summary.tldr: The paper proves superpolynomial learning lower bounds for one-layer networks under Gaussian inputs, covering gradient descent and statistical query methods.

title: Superpolynomial Lower Bounds for Learning One-Layer Neural Networks using Gradient Descent

abstract: We propose a novel interactive learning framework which we refer to as Interactive Attention Learning (IAL), in which the human supervisors interactively manipulate the allocated attentions, to correct the model’s behaviour by updating the attention-generating network. However, such a model is prone to overfitting due to scarcity of human annotations, and requires costly retraining. Moreover, it is almost infeasible for the human annotators to examine attentions on tons of instances and features. We tackle these challenges by proposing a sample-efficient attention mechanism and a cost-effective reranking algorithm for instances and features. First, we propose Neural Attention Processes (NAP), which is an attention generator that can update its behaviour by incorporating new attention-level supervisions without any retraining. Secondly, we propose an algorithm which prioritizes the instances and the features by their negative impacts, such that the model can yield large improvements with minimal human feedback. We validate IAL on various time-series datasets from multiple domains (healthcare, real-estate, and computer vision) on which it significantly outperforms baselines with conventional attention mechanisms, or without cost-effective reranking, with substantially less retraining and human-model interaction cost.

paragraphs: Interactive Attention Learning lets a human correct model behavior by changing where the model allocates attention. This creates a practical challenge: attention feedback is scarce, retraining can be expensive, and people cannot inspect every feature of every example. The paper develops a framework that addresses both model adaptation and the cost of deciding what humans should review.

Its first component, Neural Attention Processes, generates attention and incorporates new attention-level supervision without retraining. Its second component ranks examples and features according to their negative impacts. This prioritization directs feedback toward corrections intended to produce large improvements with relatively little human effort, rather than requiring exhaustive inspection.

Experiments use time-series datasets from healthcare, real estate, and computer vision. The framework significantly outperforms the evaluated alternatives using conventional attention or omitting the cost-effective ranking procedure, while substantially reducing retraining and interaction costs. The findings support treating efficient human correction as a joint problem: the model must absorb feedback cheaply, and the interaction process must identify useful opportunities for correction.
summary.tldr: Neural Attention Processes absorb human attention corrections without retraining, while impact-based prioritization reduces the feedback needed in the reported experiments.

title: Cost-Effective Interactive Attention Learning with Neural Attention Processes

abstract: There has been a growing realization of the potential of Bayesian machine learning as a platform that can provide both flexible modeling, accurate predictions as well as coherent uncertainty statements. In particular, Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) have emerged as one of today’s most effective general approaches to predictive modeling under minimal assumptions. Statistical theoretical developments for machine learning have been mostly concerned with approximability or rates of estimation when recovering infinite dimensional objects (curves or densities). Despite the impressive array of available theoretical results, the literature has been largely silent about uncertainty quantification. In this work, we continue the theoretical investigation of BART initiated recently by Rockova and van der Pas (2017). We focus on statistical inference questions. In particular, we study the Bernstein-von Mises (BvM) phenomenon (i.e. asymptotic normality) for smooth linear functionals of the regression surface within the framework of non-parametric regression with fixed covariates. Our semi-parametric BvM results show that, beyond rate-optimal estimation, BART can be also used for valid statistical inference.

paragraphs: Bayesian Additive Regression Trees, or BART, provide a flexible approach to prediction. This paper examines a different question: whether BART also supports statistically valid uncertainty statements. Accurate estimation of a regression function and reliable inference about quantities derived from that function are related goals, but establishing one does not by itself establish the other.

The analysis considers nonparametric regression with fixed covariates and focuses on smooth linear functionals of the regression surface. These are particular summaries of the underlying function. The authors establish semi-parametric Bernstein-von Mises results, studying the asymptotic normality that makes inference about those summaries possible.

The findings show that BART can support valid statistical inference beyond achieving optimal estimation rates in the setting studied. Their importance lies in supplying theoretical justification for uncertainty quantification, an area the abstract identifies as less developed than approximation and estimation theory. The result concerns asymptotic behavior for the specified functionals and regression framework, giving a precise scope to the inference claim.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes asymptotic inference guarantees for smooth linear summaries of BART regression functions with fixed covariates.

title: On Semi-parametric Inference for BART

abstract: The performance of optimizers, particularly in deep learning, depends considerably on their chosen hyperparameter configuration. The efficacy of optimizers is often studied under near-optimal problem-specific hyperparameters, and finding these settings may be prohibitively costly for practitioners. In this work, we argue that a fair assessment of optimizers’ performance must take the computational cost of hyperparameter tuning into account, i.e., how easy it is to find good hyperparameter configurations using an automatic hyperparameter search. Evaluating a variety of optimizers on an extensive set of standard datasets and architectures, our results indicate that Adam is the most practical solution, particularly in low-budget scenarios.

Evaluating a variety of optimizers on an extensive set of standard datasets and architectures, our results indicate that Adam is the most practical solution, particularly in low-budget scenarios.

paragraphs: An optimizer's performance depends strongly on its hyperparameter settings. This paper argues that comparing optimizers only after finding nearly ideal settings can give practitioners an incomplete picture. Those settings may require a costly search, so the performance eventually achieved does not by itself capture how practical an optimizer is to use.

The authors propose accounting for the computational expense of automatic hyperparameter tuning when assessing optimizers. The relevant question includes how readily a search procedure finds good configurations. This places the cost of discovering effective settings alongside the quality of the resulting training run, making the comparison more closely reflect a practitioner working within a limited computational budget.

They evaluate a range of optimizers across an extensive collection of standard datasets and architectures. Their results indicate that Adam is the most practical option in those comparisons, especially when budgets are small. This is an empirical conclusion about optimizer performance when tuning cost is included. The broader methodological contribution is a criterion for benchmarking: strong results under carefully chosen settings should be assessed together with the effort needed to obtain those settings.
summary.tldr: Optimizer comparisons should include hyperparameter search costs, with the paper's experiments favoring Adam especially under small budgets.

title: Optimizer Benchmarking Needs to Account for Hyperparameter Tuning

abstract: Deep energy-based models (EBMs) are very flexible in distribution parametrization but computationally challenging because of the intractable partition function. They are typically trained via maximum likelihood, using contrastive divergence to approximate the gradient of the KL divergence between data and model distribution. While KL divergence has many desirable properties, other f-divergences have shown advantages in training implicit density generative models such as generative adversarial networks. In this paper, we propose a general variational framework termed f-EBM to train EBMs using any desired f-divergence. We introduce a corresponding optimization algorithm and prove its local convergence property with non-linear dynamical systems theory. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of f-EBM over contrastive divergence, as well as the benefits of training EBMs using f-divergences other than KL.

paragraphs: Deep energy-based models offer flexible ways to represent probability distributions, but training is difficult because their partition function is intractable. Standard training typically uses maximum likelihood, with contrastive divergence approximating the gradient associated with KL divergence. This paper asks how to train these models using other members of the broader f-divergence family.

The proposed f-EBM framework uses a variational formulation that supports any desired f-divergence. The authors introduce a corresponding optimization algorithm and analyze it using nonlinear dynamical systems theory. They prove a local convergence property, establishing behavior near a solution rather than a global convergence guarantee from arbitrary starting points.

Experiments show that f-EBM outperforms contrastive divergence and that choosing divergences other than KL can benefit energy-based model training. The contribution separates the model’s flexible distribution representation from a fixed choice of training divergence. It provides both an optimization framework for making that choice and empirical evidence that the choice can affect the quality of training.
summary.tldr: f-EBM trains energy-based models with any chosen f-divergence, with a local convergence result and empirical gains over contrastive divergence.

title: Training Deep Energy-Based Models with f-Divergence Minimization

abstract: Understanding classifier decision under novel environments is central to the community, and a common practice is evaluating it on labeled test sets. However, in real-world testing, image annotations are difficult and expensive to obtain, especially when the test environment is changing. A natural question then arises: given a trained classifier, can we evaluate its accuracy on varying unlabeled test sets? In this work, we train semantic classification and rotation prediction in a multi-task way. On a series of datasets, we report an interesting finding, i.e., the semantic classification accuracy exhibits a strong linear relationship with the accuracy of the rotation prediction task (Pearson’s Correlation r > 0.88). This finding allows us to utilize linear regression to estimate classifier performance from the accuracy of rotation prediction which can be obtained on the test set through the freely generated rotation labels.

paragraphs: Measuring a classifier’s accuracy normally requires labeled test examples. When testing environments change, repeatedly obtaining image annotations can become expensive and difficult. This paper investigates an indirect measurement: whether performance on an automatically labeled rotation-prediction task can indicate performance on the semantic classification task of interest.

The authors train semantic classification and rotation prediction together in a multi-task setup. Across a series of datasets, they find a strong linear relationship between the accuracies of the two tasks, reporting Pearson correlation above 0.88. Rotation labels are available because the applied image rotations can be generated and recorded without semantic annotation.

This observed relationship allows linear regression to estimate semantic classification accuracy from rotation accuracy on an otherwise unlabeled test set. The result offers an empirical route to monitoring performance as testing conditions vary. Its basis is the measured relationship in the studied multi-task setting, so the finding establishes a useful performance signal there rather than a universal rule connecting rotation prediction and classification accuracy.
summary.tldr: Rotation-prediction accuracy strongly correlates with classification accuracy in the studied multi-task models, enabling estimates on semantically unlabeled test sets.

title: What Does Rotation Prediction Tell Us about Classifier Accuracy under Varying Testing Environments?

abstract: Variational autoencoder (VAE) estimates the posterior parameters (mean and variance) of latent variables corresponding to each input data. While it is used for many tasks, the transparency of the model is still an underlying issue. This paper provides a quantitative understanding of VAE property through the differential geometric and information-theoretic interpretations of VAE. According to the Rate-distortion theory, the optimal transform coding is achieved by using an orthonormal transform with PCA basis where the transform space is isometric to the input. Considering the analogy of transform coding to VAE, we clarify theoretically and experimentally that VAE can be mapped to an implicit isometric embedding with a scale factor derived from the posterior parameter. As a result, we can estimate the data probabilities in the input space from the prior, loss metrics, and corresponding posterior parameters, and further, the quantitative importance of each latent variable can be evaluated like the eigenvalue of PCA.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder assigns latent-variable means and variances to each input, but the quantitative meaning of these values can be difficult to interpret. This paper studies that meaning through differential geometry and information theory. It connects the VAE's representation to a scaled embedding that preserves geometry, offering a way to interpret its latent space more quantitatively.

The argument draws an analogy with transform coding and rate-distortion theory, where an orthonormal transform using a principal-component basis provides an isometric transform space. The authors show theoretically and experimentally that a VAE can be mapped to an implicit isometric embedding. Its scale factor comes from the posterior parameters, linking the geometry to quantities the model already estimates.

This interpretation allows input-space data probabilities to be estimated using the prior, loss metrics, and corresponding posterior parameters. It also enables a quantitative assessment of each latent variable's importance, analogous to the role of an eigenvalue in principal component analysis. The contribution therefore turns a geometric interpretation into tools for understanding probability and importance within the learned representation.
summary.tldr: A geometric and information-theoretic interpretation of VAEs enables estimates of input probabilities and quantitative latent-variable importance.

title: Quantitative Understanding of VAE as a Non-linearly Scaled Isometric Embedding

abstract: Personalized federated learning is tasked with training machine learning models for multiple clients, each with its own data distribution. The goal is to train personalized models collaboratively while accounting for data disparities across clients and reducing communication costs. We propose a novel approach to this problem using hypernetworks, termed pFedHN for personalized Federated HyperNetworks. In this approach, a central hypernetwork model is trained to generate a set of models, one model for each client. This architecture provides effective parameter sharing across clients while maintaining the capacity to generate unique and diverse personal models. Furthermore, since hypernetwork parameters are never transmitted, this approach decouples the communication cost from the trainable model size. We test pFedHN empirically in several personalized federated learning challenges and find that it outperforms previous methods. Finally, since hypernetworks share information across clients, we show that pFedHN can generalize better to new clients whose distributions differ from any client observed during training.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning aims to train models collaboratively while allowing different clients to have different data distributions. Sharing information is useful, but each client may need a distinct model. This paper proposes pFedHN, which uses a central hypernetwork to generate an individual model for each participating client.

A hypernetwork produces the parameters of other networks. Here, one shared generator provides a route for information to pass across clients while retaining the ability to create diverse personalized models. Because the hypernetwork’s own parameters are never transmitted, its trainable size is decoupled from communication cost. This makes the architecture’s shared learning capacity distinct from the parameters that must be communicated.

Across several personalized federated learning challenges, pFedHN outperforms the previous methods evaluated by the authors. They also show better generalization to new clients whose distributions differ from those observed during training. These empirical findings suggest that sharing a model-generating mechanism can support both personalization for existing clients and adaptation to previously unseen client distributions.
summary.tldr: pFedHN shares a central hypernetwork that generates personalized client models and improves performance on the evaluated federated learning challenges.

title: Personalized Federated Learning using Hypernetworks

abstract: In many applications, we encounter data on Riemannian manifolds such as torus and rotation groups. Standard statistical procedures for multivariate data are not applicable to such data. In this study, we develop goodness-of-fit testing and interpretable model criticism methods for general distributions on Riemannian manifolds, including those with an intractable normalization constant. The proposed methods are based on extensions of kernel Stein discrepancy, which are derived from Stein operators on Riemannian manifolds. We discuss the connections between the proposed tests with existing ones and provide a theoretical analysis of their asymptotic Bahadur efficiency. Simulation results and real data applications show the validity and usefulness of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Some data lie on geometric spaces such as a torus or a group of rotations. The paper addresses statistical testing on these Riemannian manifolds, where ordinary multivariate procedures do not directly apply. Its goal is to assess whether a proposed probability distribution fits the observed data and to support interpretable criticism of that model.

The authors extend kernel Stein discrepancy using Stein operators defined on Riemannian manifolds. These extensions provide a geometry-aware basis for goodness-of-fit tests. The methods cover general distributions on these spaces, including distributions whose normalization constants are intractable, broadening the models that can be assessed within the framework.

The paper relates its tests to existing approaches and analyzes their asymptotic Bahadur efficiency, a theoretical measure of testing efficiency as sample sizes grow. Simulations and real-data applications support the methods’ validity and usefulness. Together, these contributions connect statistical model checking with the geometry of the data, while combining formal efficiency analysis with evidence from practical applications.
summary.tldr: Geometry-aware Stein tests assess and interpret distributional fit on Riemannian manifolds, including models with intractable normalization constants.

title: Interpretable Stein Goodness-of-fit Tests on Riemannian Manifold

abstract: We study online learning problems in which a decision maker wants to maximize their expected reward without violating a finite set of $m$ resource constraints. By casting the learning process over a suitably defined space of strategy mixtures, we recover strong duality on a Lagrangian relaxation of the underlying optimization problem, even for general settings with non-convex reward and resource-consumption functions. Then, we provide the first best-of-both-worlds type framework for this setting, with no-regret guarantees both under stochastic and adversarial inputs. Our framework yields the same regret guarantees of prior work in the stochastic case. On the other hand, when budgets grow at least linearly in the time horizon, it allows us to provide a constant competitive ratio in the adversarial case, which improves over the $O(m \log T)$ competitive ratio of Immorlica et al. [FOCS’19]. Moreover, our framework allows the decision maker to handle non-convex reward and cost functions. We provide two game-theoretic applications of our framework to give further evidence of its flexibility.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated decision-making with limited resources. A learner wants high expected reward while respecting several resource budgets. The challenge includes both stochastic inputs and adversarially chosen inputs, as well as reward and resource-consumption functions that need not be convex.

The authors formulate learning over mixtures of strategies. In that space, they recover strong duality for a Lagrangian relaxation, allowing the reward objective and resource constraints to be handled through an equivalent optimization relationship. This provides the foundation for a framework with no-regret guarantees in both stochastic and adversarial settings.

For adversarial inputs, it achieves a constant competitive ratio when budgets grow at least linearly with the time horizon, improving on a prior ratio that depends on the number of constraints and the logarithm of the horizon. Two game-theoretic applications illustrate flexibility. The budget-growth condition matters specifically to the stated adversarial competitive guarantee, while the formulation also accommodates non-convex rewards and costs.
summary.tldr: A strategy-mixture framework handles resource-constrained online learning in stochastic and adversarial settings, with stronger adversarial guarantees under sufficient budget growth.

title: Online Learning with Knapsacks: the Best of Both Worlds

abstract: Causal contributions measure the strengths of different causes to a target quantity. Understanding causal contributions is important in empirical sciences and data-driven disciplines since it allows to answer practical queries like “what are the contributions of each cause to the effect?” In this paper, we develop a principled method for quantifying causal contributions. First, we provide desiderata of properties axioms that causal contribution measures should satisfy and propose the do-Shapley values (inspired by do-interventions [Pearl, 2000]) as a unique method satisfying these properties. Next, we develop a criterion under which the do-Shapley values can be efficiently inferred from non-experimental data. Finally, we provide do-Shapley estimators exhibiting consistency, computational feasibility, and statistical robustness. Simulation results corroborate with the theory.

paragraphs: Quantifying causal contributions means assigning strengths to the different causes of a target outcome. This paper approaches that assignment by first asking what properties a reasonable contribution measure should satisfy. Starting with explicit axioms makes the meaning of the resulting allocation part of the mathematical specification.

The authors introduce do-Shapley values, a contribution measure inspired by causal interventions. They show that it is the unique measure satisfying their proposed properties. This uniqueness is relative to the selected axioms: the result connects those requirements to a particular way of attributing causal influence, giving the measure a principled foundation.

The paper then develops a criterion under which these values can be inferred efficiently from non-experimental data. It also provides estimators with consistency, computational feasibility, and statistical robustness, with simulations supporting the theoretical results. Together, these steps connect the definition of a causal contribution to conditions for recovering it from observations and to practical estimation procedures. The observational inference claim depends on the stated criterion being met.
summary.tldr: Do-Shapley values uniquely satisfy the paper’s causal-contribution axioms and admit robust estimation from observational data under a specified criterion.

title: On Measuring Causal Contributions via do-interventions

abstract: We study the problem of learning from positive and unlabeled (PU) data in the federated setting, where each client only labels a little part of their dataset due to the limitation of resources and time. Different from the settings in traditional PU learning where the negative class consists of a single class, the negative samples which cannot be identified by a client in the federated setting may come from multiple classes which are unknown to the client. Therefore, existing PU learning methods can be hardly applied in this situation. To address this problem, we propose a novel framework, namely Federated learning with Positive and Unlabeled data (FedPU), to minimize the expected risk of multiple negative classes by leveraging the labeled data in other clients. We theoretically analyze the generalization bound of the proposed FedPU. Empirical experiments show that the FedPU can achieve much better performance than conventional supervised and semi-supervised federated learning methods.

To address this problem, we propose a novel framework, namely Federated learning with Positive and Unlabeled data (FedPU), to minimize the expected risk of multiple negative classes by leveraging the labeled data in other clients. We theoretically analyze the generalization bound of the proposed FedPU. Empirical experiments show that the FedPU can achieve much better performance than conventional supervised and semi-supervised federated learning methods.

paragraphs: In the federated setting studied here, each client labels only a small part of its data because annotation requires time and resources. A client's unlabeled examples may include several classes it does not recognize. This complicates positive-and-unlabeled learning, whose traditional setting in the abstract treats the negative category as a single class.

FedPU uses labeled information available at other clients to address those multiple unknown negative classes. Its objective is to minimize their expected risk, allowing information distributed across clients to help resolve what an individual client cannot identify from its own labels. The design directly addresses the mismatch between local labeling knowledge and the broader collection of classes.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of FedPU's generalization bound and evaluate it empirically. In the reported experiments, it performs substantially better than conventional supervised and semi-supervised federated methods. The result suggests that explicitly modeling this positive-and-unlabeled structure can be more effective than applying those conventional approaches to sparsely labeled federated data.
summary.tldr: FedPU uses labeled information across clients to learn from positive and unlabeled data containing multiple locally unknown negative classes.

title: Federated Learning with Positive and Unlabeled Data

abstract: We study the problem of networked online convex optimization, where each agent individually decides on an action at every time step and agents cooperatively seek to minimize the total global cost over a finite horizon. The global cost is made up of three types of local costs: convex node costs, temporal interaction costs, and spatial interaction costs. In deciding their individual action at each time, an agent has access to predictions of local cost functions for the next $k$ time steps in an $r$-hop neighborhood. Our work proposes a novel online algorithm, Localized Predictive Control (LPC), which generalizes predictive control to multi-agent systems. We show that LPC achieves a competitive ratio of $1 + \tilde{O}(\rho_T^k) + \tilde{O}(\rho_S^r)$ in an adversarial setting, where $\rho_T$ and $\rho_S$ are constants in $(0, 1)$ that increase with the relative strength of temporal and spatial interaction costs, respectively. This is the first competitive ratio bound on decentralized predictive control for networked online convex optimization. Further, we show that the dependence on $k$ and $r$ in our results is near optimal by lower bounding the competitive ratio of any decentralized online algorithm.

Costs arise at individual nodes, from interactions across time, and from interactions across the network. Each agent can access predictions extending k steps ahead, but only within a neighborhood reaching r network hops away.

The proposed Localized Predictive Control algorithm adapts predictive control to this decentralized setting. Its competitive-ratio guarantee is one plus terms that decay exponentially with prediction length and neighborhood radius, up to the factors hidden by the stated notation. The decay constants lie between zero and one, and increase as the corresponding temporal or spatial interactions become stronger.

The bound quantifies how additional foresight and access to a wider neighborhood improve the guarantee, even in an adversarial setting. Stronger interactions make those improvements decay more slowly with k or r. The authors also establish lower bounds for any decentralized online algorithm, showing that their dependence on these two information resources is near optimal.
summary.tldr: Localized Predictive Control achieves near-optimal dependence on prediction horizon and neighborhood radius in decentralized online convex optimization.

title: Decentralized Online Convex Optimization in Networked Systems

abstract: Recent progress in center-based clustering algorithms combats poor local minima by implicit annealing through a family of generalized means. These methods are variations of Lloyd’s celebrated k-means algorithm, and are most appropriate for spherical clusters such as those arising from Gaussian data. In this paper, we bridge these new algorithmic advances to classical work on hard clustering under Bregman divergences, which enjoy a bijection to exponential family distributions and are thus well-suited for clustering objects arising from a breadth of data generating mechanisms. The elegant properties of Bregman divergences allow us to maintain closed form updates in a simple and transparent algorithm, and moreover lead to new theoretical arguments for establishing finite sample bounds that relax the bounded support assumption made in the existing state of the art. Additionally, we consider thorough empirical analyses on simulated experiments and a case study on rainfall data, finding that the proposed method outperforms existing peer methods in a variety of non-Gaussian data settings.

Recent variations of k-means address this through implicit annealing using generalized means, but their geometry is most suitable for roughly spherical clusters. This paper extends those algorithmic ideas to data whose generating mechanisms need a different notion of distance from a cluster center.

The method combines generalized-mean clustering with Bregman divergences. These divergences correspond to exponential-family distributions, providing a way to align clustering with a broader range of data types. Their mathematical structure also preserves closed-form updates, so the extension retains a simple computational form despite accommodating more varied distributions.

The authors establish finite-sample bounds that relax the bounded-support assumption used in prior work. Simulated experiments and a rainfall case study show improvements over peer methods in several non-Gaussian settings. The contribution therefore joins three concerns: avoiding poor local minima, choosing a suitable geometry for the data, and retaining an algorithm whose updates and theoretical behavior can be analyzed directly.
summary.tldr: Bregman power k-means extends annealing-based clustering to broader data distributions while retaining closed-form updates and finite-sample guarantees.

title: Bregman Power k-Means for Clustering Exponential Family Data

abstract: Studying neural network loss landscapes provides insights into the nature of the underlying optimization problems. Unfortunately, loss landscapes are notoriously difficult to visualize in a human-comprehensible fashion. One common way to address this problem is to plot linear slices of the landscape, for example from the initial state of the network to the final state after optimization. On the basis of this analysis, prior work has drawn broader conclusions about the difficulty of the optimization problem. In this paper, we put inferences of this kind to the test, systematically evaluating how linear interpolation and final performance vary when altering the data, choice of initialization, and other optimizer and architecture design choices. Further, we use linear interpolation to study the role played by individual layers and substructures of the network. We find that certain layers are more sensitive to the choice of initialization, but that the shape of the linear path is not indicative of the changes in test accuracy of the model. Our results cast doubt on the broader intuition that the presence or absence of barriers when interpolating necessarily relates to the success of optimization.

paragraphs: Neural-network loss landscapes are difficult to visualize, so researchers often inspect a straight path between two parameter settings, such as initialization and the trained model. A smooth path or a barrier can seem informative about optimization difficulty. This paper tests whether those visual patterns justify broader conclusions about training success.

The authors systematically change the data, initialization, optimizer choices, and architecture, then examine both linear-interpolation behavior and final performance. They also apply interpolation to individual layers and network substructures. This lets them investigate whether the visual behavior of the whole network reflects more specific sensitivities within its components.

They find that some layers are particularly sensitive to initialization, but the shape of the linear path does not indicate the corresponding changes in test accuracy. The results cast doubt on treating the presence or absence of interpolation barriers as a necessary indicator of optimization success. Linear slices can reveal behavior along the chosen path, while the study challenges broader performance inferences drawn from that picture.
summary.tldr: Linear loss-landscape slices reveal initialization sensitivities but do not reliably indicate changes in test accuracy in the reported study.

title: What Can Linear Interpolation of Neural Network Loss Landscapes Tell Us?

abstract: Message passing neural networks have shown a lot of success on graph-structured data. However, there are many instances where message passing can lead to over-smoothing or fail when neighboring nodes belong to different classes. In this work, we introduce a simple yet general framework for improving learning in message passing neural networks. Our approach essentially upsamples edges in the original graph by adding "slow nodes" at each edge that can mediate communication between a source and a target node. Our method only modifies the input graph, making it plug-and-play and easy to use with existing models. To understand the benefits of slowing down message passing, we provide theoretical and empirical analyses. We report results on several supervised and self-supervised benchmarks, and show improvements across the board, notably in heterophilic conditions where adjacent nodes are more likely to have different labels. Finally, we show how our approach can be used to generate augmentations for self-supervised learning, where slow nodes are randomly introduced into different edges in the graph to generate multi-scale views with variable path lengths.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks commonly learn by passing information between neighboring nodes. This can blur useful distinctions through over-smoothing, and it can fail when connected nodes belong to different classes. Half-Hop changes the graph itself to slow this exchange, giving existing message-passing models a different communication structure without requiring a redesign of the model.

The method inserts additional slow nodes along edges. These nodes mediate communication between the original source and target, extending the route that information must travel. Because the intervention modifies the input graph, it can be used with existing models. The paper supports the approach with both theoretical analysis and empirical investigation of slower message passing.

Reported improvements span supervised and self-supervised benchmarks, with particularly notable results when adjacent nodes are likely to have different labels. The same mechanism also creates training augmentations: randomly inserting slow nodes on different edges produces graph views with different path lengths and scales. Thus, one graph modification serves both as a learning aid and as a way to generate varied views for self-supervision.
summary.tldr: Half-Hop inserts intermediary nodes into graph edges to slow message passing and improve learning, especially when neighbors have different labels.

title: Half-Hop: A graph upsampling approach for slowing down message passing

abstract: A hallmark of biological neural networks, which distinguishes them from their artificial counterparts, is the high degree of sparsity in their activations. This discrepancy raises three questions our work helps to answer: (i) Why are biological networks so sparse? (ii) What are the benefits of this sparsity? (iii) How can these benefits be utilized by deep learning models? Our answers to all of these questions center around training networks to handle random noise. Surprisingly, we discover that noisy training introduces three implicit loss terms that result in sparsely firing neurons specializing to high variance features of the dataset. When trained to reconstruct noisy-CIFAR10, neurons learn biological receptive fields. More broadly, noisy training presents a new approach to potentially increase model interpretability with additional benefits to robustness and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Biological neural networks often activate only a small fraction of their neurons, whereas artificial networks typically have less sparse activity. This paper investigates whether learning to handle random noise can help explain that difference and offer a useful route to sparsity in artificial models.

The authors find that noisy training introduces three implicit terms into the learning objective. These terms produce neurons that fire sparsely and specialise in features with high variance in the data. The connection matters because sparsity emerges through the demands of handling noise, linking the training task to both how often neurons activate and which features they represent.

In experiments reconstructing noisy CIFAR10 data, the neurons learn receptive fields described as biological. This supplies empirical support for the proposed connection between noisy learning and biologically relevant representations. More broadly, the authors present noisy training as a possible way to improve interpretability, with additional benefits for robustness and computational efficiency. The work offers a mechanism that helps address questions about biological sparsity without establishing a complete explanation of biological networks.
summary.tldr: Training networks to handle noise introduces implicit loss terms that produce sparse, specialised neurons and potentially more interpretable representations.

title: Emergence of Sparse Representations from Noise

abstract: The policy gradient theorem gives a convenient form of the policy gradient in terms of three factors: an action value, a gradient of the action likelihood, and a state distribution involving discounting called the discounted stationary distribution . But commonly used on-policy methods based on the policy gradient theorem ignores the discount factor in the state distribution, which is technically incorrect and may even cause degenerate learning behavior in some environments. An existing solution corrects this discrepancy by using $\gamma^t$ as a factor in the gradient estimate. However, this solution is not widely adopted and does not work well in tasks where the later states are similar to earlier states. We introduce a novel distribution correction to account for the discounted stationary distribution that can be plugged into many existing gradient estimators. Our correction circumvents the performance degradation associated with the $\gamma^t$ correction with a lower variance. Importantly, compared to the uncorrected estimators, our algorithm provides improved state emphasis to evade suboptimal policies in certain environments and consistently matches or exceeds the original performance on several OpenAI gym and DeepMind suite benchmarks.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods use experience to adjust how an agent chooses actions. The theorem behind these methods includes discounting in the distribution that determines how strongly different states contribute to an update. Common implementations omit this part, creating a mismatch that can produce degenerate learning behavior in some environments.

One existing correction multiplies contributions at time t by the discount factor raised to t. However, that correction performs poorly in tasks where later states resemble earlier ones. The paper introduces a different correction to the state distribution that can be inserted into many existing gradient estimators. It accounts for the intended discounted distribution while avoiding the performance degradation associated with the time-based correction and having lower variance.

The practical consequence is a change in which states receive emphasis during learning. In certain environments, this helps the algorithm avoid suboptimal policies that uncorrected estimators can reach. Across several OpenAI Gym and DeepMind suite benchmarks, the corrected approach consistently matches or improves the original performance, supporting its usefulness beyond resolving the mathematical discrepancy.
summary.tldr: A correction to policy gradients' state weighting addresses discount-factor mismatch and matches or improves performance on several benchmarks.

title: Correcting discount-factor mismatch in on-policy policy gradient methods

abstract: We present IRNeXt, a simple yet effective convolutional network architecture for image restoration. Recently, Transformer models have dominated the field of image restoration due to the powerful ability of modeling long-range pixels interactions. In this paper, we excavate the potential of the convolutional neural network (CNN) and show that our CNN-based model can receive comparable or better performance than Transformer models with low computation overhead on several image restoration tasks. By re-examining the characteristics possessed by advanced image restoration algorithms, we discover several key factors leading to the performance improvement of restoration models. This motivates us to develop a novel network for image restoration based on cheap convolution operators. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that IRNeXt delivers state-of-the-art performance among numerous datasets on a range of image restoration tasks with low computational complexity, including image dehazing, single-image defocus/motion deblurring, image deraining, and image desnowing. https://github.com/c-yn/IRNeXt.

paragraphs: IRNeXt is a convolutional neural network designed to restore degraded images. The paper examines the potential of convolutional architectures in a field where Transformers have become prominent because they can model interactions between distant pixels. Its central question is whether a carefully designed convolutional network can deliver strong restoration quality while keeping computational demands low.

The authors revisit characteristics of advanced restoration methods and identify factors associated with improved performance. They use those findings to design a network built around inexpensive convolution operations. The approach makes architecture design the route to better restoration: it seeks to capture useful properties of successful methods while retaining the computational advantages of cheap operators.

Experiments cover dehazing, single-image defocus and motion deblurring, deraining, and desnowing across numerous datasets. The authors report state-of-the-art performance with low computational complexity, including results comparable to or better than Transformer models on several restoration tasks. These findings demonstrate the competitive potential of the proposed CNN design across multiple kinds of image degradation.
summary.tldr: IRNeXt uses inexpensive convolution operations to achieve strong image restoration results with low computational overhead.

title: IRNeXt: Rethinking Convolutional Network Design for Image Restoration

abstract: Forward Gradients - the idea of using directional derivatives in forward differentiation mode - have recently been shown to be utilizable for neural network training while avoiding problems generally associated with backpropagation gradient computation, such as locking and memorization requirements. The cost is the requirement to guess the step direction, which is hard in high dimensions. While current solutions rely on weighted averages over isotropic guess vector distributions, we propose to strongly bias our gradient guesses in directions that are much more promising, such as feedback obtained from small, local auxiliary networks. For a standard computer vision neural network, we conduct a rigorous study systematically covering a variety of combinations of gradient targets and gradient guesses, including those previously presented in the literature. We find that using gradients obtained from a local loss as a candidate direction drastically improves on random noise in Forward Gradient methods.

paragraphs: Forward-gradient training uses directional derivatives computed through forward differentiation. It offers a route around locking and memory requirements associated with backpropagation, but introduces a difficult choice: which direction should the method test? In a high-dimensional parameter space, an uninformed guess may provide a poor candidate for a useful training update.

The paper investigates replacing isotropic random guesses with deliberately biased directions. Small local auxiliary networks provide feedback that can point toward more promising updates. The authors systematically study combinations of gradient targets and candidate directions in a standard computer vision network, including combinations used in earlier work. This separates the choice of what gradient to target from the choice of how to guess its direction.

The central finding is that gradients from a local loss make much better candidate directions than random noise for forward-gradient methods. That result identifies direction selection as an important practical component of this training approach. It supports using locally available learning signals to improve forward-gradient training, without establishing that the method universally matches backpropagation.
summary.tldr: Using local-loss gradients as candidate directions substantially improves forward-gradient training over random directional guesses.

title: Can Forward Gradient Match Backpropagation?

abstract: Recently proposed Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for vertex clustering are trained with an unsupervised minimum cut objective, approximated by a Spectral Clustering (SC) relaxation. However, the SC relaxation is loose and, while it offers a closed-form solution, it also yields overly smooth cluster assignments that poorly separate the vertices. In this paper, we propose a GNN model that computes cluster assignments by optimizing a tighter relaxation of the minimum cut based on graph total variation (GTV). The cluster assignments can be used directly to perform vertex clustering or to implement graph pooling in a graph classification framework. Our model consists of two core components: i) a message-passing layer that minimizes the $\ell_1$ distance in the features of adjacent vertices, which is key to achieving sharp transitions between clusters; ii) an unsupervised loss function that minimizes the GTV of the cluster assignments while ensuring balanced partitions. Experimental results show that our model outperforms other GNNs for vertex clustering and graph classification.

paragraphs: Graph clustering aims to separate vertices into meaningful groups. Some graph neural networks learn these groups using a relaxed minimum-cut objective based on spectral clustering. This paper argues that the relaxation is loose and can produce excessively smooth assignments, weakening the separation between clusters.

The authors instead use a tighter relaxation based on graph total variation. Their model combines a message passing layer that minimizes the absolute, or L1, differences between neighboring vertex features with an unsupervised loss on cluster assignments. The loss minimizes graph total variation while encouraging balanced partitions. This formulation is designed to support sharper transitions between clusters.

The learned assignments can directly define vertex clusters or serve as graph pooling within a graph classification system. Experiments show better performance than the other GNNs evaluated on both vertex clustering and graph classification. The results connect the choice of optimization objective to the usefulness of the learned groups: sharper, balanced assignments can support both local grouping and downstream prediction about an entire graph.
summary.tldr: A graph total variation objective produces sharper cluster assignments and improves the reported clustering and graph classification results.

title: Total Variation Graph Neural Networks

abstract: In this paper, we examine the effectiveness of pre-training for visuo-motor control tasks. We revisit a simple Learning-from-Scratch (LfS) baseline that incorporates data augmentation and a shallow ConvNet, and find that this baseline is surprisingly competitive with recent approaches (PVR, MVP, R3M) that leverage frozen visual representations trained on large-scale vision datasets – across a variety of algorithms, task domains, and metrics in simulation and on a real robot. Our results demonstrate that these methods are hindered by a significant domain gap between the pre-training datasets and current benchmarks for visuo-motor control, which is alleviated by finetuning. Based on our findings, we provide recommendations for future research in pre-training for control and hope that our simple yet strong baseline will aid in accurately benchmarking progress in this area. Code: https://github.com/gemcollector/learning-from-scratch.

paragraphs: This paper reexamines whether visual pretraining delivers clear advantages for control tasks that use images to guide actions. The authors revisit a simple learning-from-scratch approach using a shallow convolutional network and data augmentation. They compare it with PVR, MVP, and R3M approaches that use frozen visual representations pretrained on large vision datasets.

The simple baseline is surprisingly competitive across multiple learning algorithms, task domains, and evaluation measures, both in simulation and on a real robot. This makes the baseline consequential for evaluating progress: comparisons need to account for what a straightforward task-trained visual model can already achieve.

The authors attribute a substantial obstacle for the pretrained methods to the domain gap between their pretraining data and the visual control benchmarks. Fine-tuning alleviates that mismatch. The findings therefore concern how pretrained representations transfer and whether they remain frozen, rather than establishing that pretraining is generally unhelpful. The paper uses this evidence to offer recommendations for future pretraining research and stronger benchmarking.
summary.tldr: A shallow vision model trained from scratch competes strongly with frozen pretrained representations, whose domain mismatch is alleviated by fine-tuning.

title: On Pre-Training for Visuo-Motor Control: Revisiting a Learning-from-Scratch Baseline

abstract: MDPs with low-rank transitions—that is, the transition matrix can be factored into the product of two matrices, left and right—is a highly representative structure that enables tractable learning. The left matrix enables expressive function approximation for value-based learning and has been studied extensively. In this work, we instead investigate sample-efficient learning with density features, i.e., the right matrix, which induce powerful models for state-occupancy distributions. This setting not only sheds light on leveraging unsupervised learning in RL, but also enables plug-in solutions for settings like convex RL. In the offline setting, we propose an algorithm for off-policy estimation of occupancies that can handle non-exploratory data. Using this as a subroutine, we further devise an online algorithm that constructs exploratory data distributions in a level-by-level manner. As a central technical challenge, the additive error of occupancy estimation is incompatible with the multiplicative definition of data coverage. In the absence of strong assumptions like reachability, this incompatibility easily leads to exponential error blow-up, which we overcome via novel technical tools. Our results also readily extend to the representation learning setting, when the density features are unknown and must be learned from an exponentially large candidate set.
