paragraphs: Editing a human-object interaction requires changing a relationship while preserving the relevant person and object. The paper argues that existing benchmarks blur this task with static attribute editing, and that global image metrics miss interaction validity and pair preservation. HOI-Edit addresses this gap with three progressively demanding cognitive levels.

Its HOI-Eval metric uses a vision-language model to reason and answer questions about images with grounded human-object pairs. The authors also evaluate image-to-video models for editing, finding their temporal generation capabilities well suited to changing interactions. Generated videos expose how an attempted edit unfolds, providing a replay that helps diagnose the process behind a failure.

SCPE builds on this diagnosability by iteratively refining prompts that constrain video generation toward the target interaction. Frames extracted from the resulting videos become the final edited images. On HOI-Edit, the framework achieves interaction performance competitive with state-of-the-art image editors such as Nano Banana. The work connects targeted evaluation with a process-based route to self-correcting image edits.
summary.tldr: HOI-Edit evaluates human-object interaction edits, while SCPE uses iteratively corrected video generation to produce competitive edited images.

title: Taming I2V models for Image HOI Editing: A Cognitive Benchmark and Agentic Self-Correcting Framework

abstract: In many multi-agent systems, agents interact repeatedly and are expected to settle into stable, rational behavior over time. Yet in practice, behavior often drifts, and detecting such deviations in real time remains an open challenge. We introduce a sequential testing framework that monitors whether observed play is consistent with a benchmark of strategic behavior, without assuming a fixed sample size. Our approach builds on the e-value framework for safe anytime-valid inference: by "betting" against the benchmark, we construct a test supermartingale that accumulates evidence whenever observed payoffs systematically violate the expected conditions. For repeated normal-form games, we take equilibrium as the benchmark, yielding a statistically sound, interpretable measure of departure from equilibrium that can be monitored online; our framework unifies the treatment of Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria, offering finite-time guarantees and a detailed analysis of detection times. We also leverage Benjamini-Hochberg-type procedures to increase detection power in large games while rigorously controlling the false discovery rate. Finally, we extend our method to stochastic games, verifying online whether observed trajectories adhere to a specified target policy, such as a computed equilibrium, broadening the framework’s applicability to dynamic, state-dependent settings.

paragraphs: Repeated interactions between agents are often expected to follow a stable strategic pattern, but actual behavior can drift. Together, these results turn strategic consistency into an online statistical question, including settings where behavior depends on the current state.
summary.tldr: An anytime-valid statistical framework detects departures from equilibrium or a target policy as multi-agent interactions unfold.

title: Anytime Detection of Strategic Deviations in Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: Deep neural networks learn feature representations via complex geometric transformations of the input data manifold. Despite the models’ empirical success across domains, our understanding of neural feature representations is still incomplete. In this work we investigate neural feature geometry through the lens of discrete geometry. Since the input data manifold is typically unobserved, we approximate it using geometric graphs that encode local similarity structure. We provide theoretical results on the evolution of these graphs during training, showing that nonlinear activations play a crucial role in shaping feature geometry in feedforward neural networks. Moreover, we discover that the geometric transformations resemble a discrete Ricci flow on these graphs, suggesting that neural feature geometry evolves analogous to Ricci flow. This connection is supported by experiments on over 20,000 feedforward neural networks trained on binary classification tasks across both synthetic and real-world datasets. We observe that the emergence of class separability corresponds to the emergence of community structure in the associated graph representations, which is known to relate to discrete Ricci flow dynamics. Building on these insights, we introduce a novel framework for locally evaluating geometric transformations through comparison with discrete Ricci flow dynamics. Our experimental results further suggest connections between the evolution of feature geometry, and training time and network depth.

summary.tldr: Graph-based analysis suggests that feature geometry in trained feedforward networks evolves in ways resembling discrete Ricci flow.

title: Neural Feature Geometry Evolves as Discrete Ricci Flow

abstract: Label noise is pervasive in real-world datasets and significantly compromises model generalization, fueling extensive research into Learning with Noisy Labels (LNL). Most LNL methods focus on robust discriminative learning, while recent generative classifiers such as label diffusion models (LDMs) show superior robustness by modeling class posteriors. However, current LDMs predominantly rely on standard $\epsilon$-prediction, where Gaussian pnoise lacks explicit class semantics, limiting both optimization and inference under label noise environments. To address this issue, we propose just y-prediction (JYP), a novel training paradigm that enables LDMs to directly characterize the label manifold and leverage explicit class-semantic guidance. Theoretically, we prove that JYP converges to an optimal solution equivalent to that of $\epsilon$-prediction within the label diffusion framework, while facilitating accelerated convergence and enabling one-step inference. Leveraging JYP as a foundation, we further incorporate historical cumulative inconsistency to adaptively tailor optimization strategies for clean, noisy, and hard samples. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms competitors across diverse synthetic noisy datasets and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple real-world benchmarks.

paragraphs: Just Y-Prediction addresses learning from datasets whose labels contain errors. Label diffusion models approach classification by modeling class posteriors, but commonly train by predicting Gaussian noise. The paper argues that this prediction target lacks explicit class meaning, limiting optimization and inference when training labels are unreliable.

The proposed JYP paradigm instead predicts labels directly, allowing the model to characterize the label manifold with explicit semantic guidance. The authors prove that, within their label diffusion framework, JYP converges to an optimal solution equivalent to that of noise prediction. They also report accelerated convergence and support for one-step inference, connecting the change in prediction target to practical efficiency.

Building on JYP, the method uses accumulated historical inconsistency to adapt optimization for clean, noisy, and hard examples. This lets training respond differently to samples with different reliability and difficulty. Experiments report consistent improvements over competitors on synthetic noisy datasets and state-of-the-art results on multiple real-world benchmarks. Together, the results support direct label prediction as a foundation for both efficient diffusion classification and more adaptive treatment of unreliable supervision.
summary.tldr: JYP trains label diffusion models to predict labels directly, enabling one-step inference and adaptive learning from clean, noisy, and hard samples.

title: Just Y-Prediction: Enabling Historical Cumulative Inconsistency in Label Diffusion for Learning with Noisy Labels

abstract: Large language model (LLM) watermarking has shown promise in detecting AI-generated content and mitigating misuse, with prior work claiming robustness against paraphrasing and text editing. In this paper, we argue that existing evaluations are not sufficiently adversarial, obscuring critical vulnerabilities and overstating the security. To address this, we introduce the adaptive robustness radius, a formal metric that quantifies the worst-case resilience of watermarks against adaptive adversaries. By lifting the paraphrase space into a KL-divergence ball, we approximate this radius and theoretically demonstrate that optimizing the attack context and model parameters can significantly reduce the approximated radius, making watermarks highly vulnerable to paraphrase attacks. Leveraging this insight, we propose RLCracker, a reinforcement learning (RL)–based adaptive attack that erases watermarks while preserving semantic fidelity. RLCracker requires only limited watermarked examples and zero access to the detector. Despite weak supervision, it empowers a 3B model to achieve 98.5% removal success with minimal semantic shift on 1,500-token Unigram-marked texts after training on only 100 short samples. This performance dramatically exceeds 6.75% by GPT-4o and generalizes across five model sizes over ten watermarking schemes. Our code is available in this repository.

paragraphs: Watermarks can help identify AI-generated text, but robustness against ordinary editing does not necessarily establish robustness against an adaptive adversary. This paper argues that existing evaluations can overstate security by using insufficiently adversarial tests. It introduces an adaptive robustness radius to formalize worst-case resilience under attacks that adjust to the watermarking problem.

Evaluations span five model sizes and ten watermarking schemes. The findings demonstrate vulnerabilities under adaptive testing, with the headline rate tied to the specified experiment.
summary.tldr: RLCracker shows that adaptive reinforcement-learning paraphrasing can undermine text watermarks with limited examples and no detector access.

title: RLCracker: Evaluating the Worst-Case Vulnerability of LLM Watermarks with Adaptive RL Attacks

abstract: In-Context Learning has shown great potential for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human values, helping reduce harmful outputs and accommodate diverse preferences without costly post-training, known as In-Context Alignment (ICA). However, LLMs’ comprehension of input prompts remains agnostic, limiting ICA’s ability to address value tensions—human values are inherently pluralistic, often imposing conflicting demands, e.g., stimulation vs. tradition. Current ICA methods therefore face the Instruction Bottleneck challenge, where LLMs struggle to reconcile multiple intended values within a single prompt, leading to incomplete or biased alignment. To address this, we propose PICACO, a novel pluralistic ICA method. Without fine-tuning, PICACO optimizes a meta-instruction that incorporates multiple values to better elicit LLMs’ understanding of them and improve alignment. This is achieved by maximizing the total correlation between specified values and LLM responses, which theoretically reinforces value conformity and reduces distractive noise, resulting in more effective instructions. Extensive experiments on five value sets show that PICACO works well with both black-box and open-source LLMs, outperforms several recent strong baselines, and achieves a better balance across up to 8 distinct values.

paragraphs: Prompt-based value alignment becomes difficult when several requested values pull in different directions. A model may follow only part of the instruction or favor some values over others. PICACO addresses this instruction bottleneck by optimizing a meta-instruction that helps a language model respond to multiple intended values together.

The approach works without fine-tuning. It maximizes total correlation between the specified values and model responses, using that objective to improve the instruction itself. The paper’s theoretical account connects this optimization to stronger value conformity and reduced distracting noise. The intended effect is to make the prompt communicate the joint value requirements more effectively.

Experiments cover five value sets and include both black-box and open-source language models. PICACO outperforms several recent strong baselines and achieves a better balance across as many as eight distinct values. These results support instruction optimization as a way to improve pluralistic alignment in the tested settings, where success depends on responding to several potentially conflicting requirements rather than satisfying a single preference.
summary.tldr: PICACO optimizes prompts without fine-tuning to help language models balance multiple, potentially conflicting human values.

title: PICACO: Pluralistic In-Context Value Alignment via Total Correlation Optimization

abstract: Function-guided protein design is a crucial task with significant applications in drug discovery and enzyme engineering. However, the field lacks a unified and comprehensive evaluation framework. Current models are assessed using inconsistent and limited subsets of metrics, which prevents fair comparison and a clear understanding of the relationships between different evaluation criteria. To address this gap, we introduce PDFBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for function-guided de novo protein design. Our benchmark systematically evaluates eight state-of-the-art models on 16 metrics across two key settings: description-guided design, for which we repurpose the Mol-Instructions dataset, originally lacking quantitative benchmarking, and keyword-guided design, for which we introduce a new test set, SwissTest, created with a strict datetime cutoff to ensure data integrity. By benchmarking across a wide array of metrics and analyzing their correlations, PDFBench enables more reliable model comparisons and provides key insights to guide future research.

paragraphs: Function-guided protein design aims to create proteins from descriptions of what they should do, with applications in drug discovery and enzyme engineering. Comparing models is difficult when studies choose different, limited sets of evaluation criteria. PDFBench addresses this by providing a shared benchmark that evaluates eight models using 16 metrics across two forms of functional guidance.

For keyword-guided design, they introduce SwissTest, a new test set constructed with a strict datetime cutoff to support data integrity. These two settings allow the benchmark to examine models under distinct ways of specifying a desired function.

The benchmark also analyzes correlations among evaluation metrics, helping researchers understand how different criteria relate rather than treating every score as independent. Its main contribution is the evaluation framework: a more consistent basis for model comparisons and for interpreting what different measures reveal. This addresses both fairness across models and the broader problem of understanding performance across multiple aspects of protein design.
summary.tldr: PDFBench standardizes function-guided protein-design evaluation across eight models, 16 metrics, and description- and keyword-guided tasks.

title: PDFBench: A Benchmark for De Novo Protein Design from Function

abstract: Causal discovery in time series is increasingly performed using nonlinear machine-learning models, yet the resulting causal relationships are almost always summarized by scalar edge scores. We argue that this practice obscures the true object learned by nonlinear autoregressive models: a state-dependent function whose effect varies across regimes, magnitudes, and contexts. We formalize function-valued causal influence for additive, contribution-decomposable architectures and show that scalar causal scores constitute a severe information bottleneck, conflating between-state variation with within-state residual noise. Using Neural Additive Vector Autoregression as a representative architecture, we introduce a practical framework based on Individual Conditional Expectation for estimating causal response functions directly from trained models. Through controlled synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that edges with indistinguishable scalar scores can exhibit qualitatively different functional behaviors, including monotonic, thresholded, saturating, and sign-changing effects. An applied case study on democratic development further shows that function-valued analysis reveals regime-specific and asymmetric causal structure systematically missed by score-centric approaches.

paragraphs: A nonlinear time-series model can learn relationships whose direction and strength change with the current state. Summarizing each relationship with one number can hide those changes. This paper argues that the more informative object is a response function describing how influence varies across magnitudes, regimes, and contexts, rather than a single score attached to an edge.

The authors formalize this perspective for additive architectures whose contributions can be separated. Using Neural Additive Vector Autoregression, they develop a practical method based on Individual Conditional Expectation to extract response functions from trained models. Their analysis shows how scalar summaries can mix variation between states with residual noise within a state, losing distinctions the nonlinear model has learned.

Controlled synthetic experiments show that indistinguishable edge scores can conceal monotonic, thresholded, saturating, or sign-changing effects. A democratic-development case study also reveals regime-specific and asymmetric relationships missed by score-centered analysis. The contribution is a way to inspect the functional structure of learned causal influence within the stated architectural setting.
summary.tldr: Function-valued analysis reveals state-dependent causal relationships that single-number edge scores can obscure in nonlinear time-series models.

title: Function-Valued Causal Influence in Nonlinear Time Series

abstract: A variety of widely used optimization methods like SignSGD and Muon can be interpreted as instances of steepest descent under different norm-induced geometries. In this work, we study the implicit bias of mini-batch stochastic steepest descent in multi-class classification, characterizing how batch size, momentum, and variance reduction shape the limiting max-margin behavior and convergence rates under general entry-wise and Schatten-$p$ norms. We show that, without momentum, worst-case convergence and successful classification can only be guaranteed with full-batch gradient. In contrast, momentum enables small-batch convergence to an approximate max-margin solution through a batch-momentum trade-off, though it slows convergence. This approach provides fully explicit, dimension-free rates that improve upon prior results. Moreover, we prove that variance reduction can recover the exact full-batch implicit bias for any batch size, albeit at a slower convergence rate. Finally, we further investigate the batch-size-one steepest descent without momentum, and reveal its convergence to a fundamentally different bias via a concrete data example, which reveals a key limitation of purely stochastic updates. Overall, our unified analysis clarifies when stochastic optimization aligns with full-batch behavior, and paves the way for perform deeper explorations of the training behavior of stochastic gradient steepest descent algorithms.

paragraphs: Optimization methods can favor particular solutions even without explicitly requesting them, a phenomenon called implicit bias. This paper studies that preference for mini-batch stochastic steepest descent in multiclass classification. It covers geometries induced by entry-wise and Schatten-p norms, connecting the analysis to methods such as SignSGD and Muon.

Without momentum, worst-case convergence and successful classification can only be guaranteed with full-batch gradients in the studied setting. This demonstrates a possible divergence from full-batch behavior, rather than universal failure of stochastic learning. Together, the results explain which mechanisms can align stochastic solution preferences with their full-batch counterparts.
summary.tldr: The analysis shows how momentum and variance reduction can recover approximate or exact full-batch solution preferences in stochastic steepest descent.

title: The Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent with Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient

abstract: Reinforcement learning for program repair is hindered by sparse execution feedback and coarse sequence-level rewards that obscure which edits actually fix bugs. We present BoostAPR, a three-stage framework: (1) supervised fine-tuning on execution-verified demonstrations with reasoning traces, (2) training dual reward models—a sequence-level assessor and a line-level credit allocator—from execution outcomes, and (3) PPO optimization where the line-level model redistributes rewards to critical edit regions. This line-level credit assignment operates at an intermediate granularity naturally suited to code changes. Trained on SWE-Gym and evaluated on four benchmarks, BoostAPR achieves 40.7% on SWE-bench Verified (+22.9pp over the base model), 24.8% on Defects4J (Python$\rightarrow$Java transfer), 84.5% on HumanEval-Java, and 95.0% on QuixBugs, showing competitive open-source performance with strong cross-language generalization.

This line-level credit assignment operates at an intermediate granularity naturally suited to code changes. paragraphs: Training a model to repair programs requires feedback about whether its edits work. Execution results provide that grounding, but they can be sparse. A reward assigned to an entire repair also leaves unclear which changed lines contributed to fixing the bug. BoostAPR addresses this credit-assignment problem by combining overall assessment with more localized feedback.

Training proceeds in three stages. First, the model learns from execution-verified repair demonstrations containing reasoning traces. Next, two reward models learn from execution outcomes: one assesses complete sequences, and the other allocates credit at the line level. Finally, PPO reinforcement learning uses the line-level model to redistribute rewards toward critical edit regions. Lines provide an intermediate unit of feedback suited to code modifications.

Trained on SWE-Gym, BoostAPR reports 40.7% on SWE-bench Verified, a 22.9-percentage-point improvement over its base model. It also reaches 24.8% on Defects4J with Python-to-Java transfer, 84.5% on HumanEval-Java, and 95.0% on QuixBugs. These results support the framework’s competitive open-source performance and its ability to generalize across languages in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: BoostAPR uses execution-grounded rewards at both sequence and line levels to improve automated program repair.

title: BOOSTAPR: Boosting Automated Program Repair via Execution-Grounded Reinforcement Learning with Dual Reward Models

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucination in LLMs by incorporating external knowledge, but relies on chunk-based retrieval that lacks structural semantics. GraphRAG methods improve RAG by modeling knowledge as entity-relation graphs, but still face challenges in high construction cost, fixed one-time retrieval, and reliance on long-context reasoning and prompt design. To address these challenges, we propose Graph-R1, the first agentic GraphRAG framework via end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL). It introduces lightweight knowledge hypergraph construction, models retrieval as a multi-turn agent-environment interaction, and optimizes the agent process via an end-to-end reward mechanism. Experiments on standard RAG datasets show that Graph-R1 outperforms traditional GraphRAG and RL-enhanced RAG methods in reasoning accuracy, retrieval efficiency, and generation quality. Our software and data are publicly available.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies language models with external knowledge to reduce hallucination. Retrieving isolated text chunks can miss relationships among facts, so GraphRAG represents knowledge through connected entities and relations. The paper targets remaining difficulties: costly graph construction, retrieval performed only once, and heavy dependence on long-context reasoning and carefully designed prompts.

Graph-R1 combines lightweight knowledge hypergraph construction with an agent that retrieves information over multiple turns. Retrieval becomes an interaction between the agent and its environment, rather than a fixed preliminary step. An end-to-end reinforcement-learning reward mechanism optimizes the overall agent process, connecting its retrieval behavior to the quality of the task outcome.

On standard retrieval-augmented generation datasets, Graph-R1 exceeds traditional GraphRAG and reinforcement-learning-enhanced RAG methods in reasoning accuracy, retrieval efficiency, and generation quality. These results support learning a sequence of retrieval actions over structured knowledge. The approach brings construction, interactive information gathering, and answer production into one framework, addressing several sources of cost and rigidity in existing graph-based retrieval systems.
summary.tldr: Graph-R1 learns multi-turn retrieval over a lightweight knowledge hypergraph, improving accuracy, efficiency, and answer quality on tested RAG datasets.

title: Graph-R1: Towards Agentic GraphRAG Framework via End-to-end Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Model-based representations recently stand out as a promising framework that embeds latent dynamics information into the representations for downstream off-policy actor-critic learning. It implicitly combines the advantages of both model-free and model-based approaches while avoiding the training costs associated with model-based methods. Nevertheless, existing model-based representation methods can fail to capture sufficient information about relevant variables and can overfit to early experiences in the replay buffer. These incur biases in representation and actor-critic learning, leading to inferior performance. To address this, we propose Debiased model-based Representations for Q-learning, tagged DR.Q algorithm. DR.Q explicitly maximizes the mutual information between the representations of the current state-action pair and the next state besides minimizing their deviations, and samples transitions with faded prioritized experience replay. We evaluate DR.Q on numerous continuous control benchmarks with a single set of hyperparameters, and the results demonstrate that DR.Q can match or surpass recent strong baselines, sometimes outperforming them by a large margin. Our code is available at https://github.com/dmksjfl/DR.Q.
originalAbstract: Model-based representations recently stand out as a promising framework that embeds latent dynamics information into the representations for downstream off-policy actor-critic learning. It implicitly combines the advantages of both model-free and model-based approaches while avoiding the training costs associated with model-based methods. Nevertheless, existing model-based representation methods can fail to capture sufficient information about relevant variables and can overfit to early experiences in the replay buffer. These incur biases in representation and actor-critic learning, leading to inferior performance. To address this, we propose Debiased model-based Representations for Q-learning, tagged DR.Q algorithm. DR.Q explicitly maximizes the mutual information between the representations of the current state-action pair and the next state besides minimizing their deviations, and samples transitions with faded prioritized experience replay. We evaluate DR.Q on numerous continuous control benchmarks with a single set of hyperparameters, and the results demonstrate that DR.Q can match or surpass recent strong baselines, sometimes outperforming them by a large margin. Our code is available at https://github.com/dmksjfl/DR.Q.

paragraphs: Model-based representations incorporate information about environment dynamics into features used by an actor–critic learner. This offers a way to combine benefits of model-based and model-free reinforcement learning without the training costs associated with model-based methods. The paper identifies two weaknesses: representations can omit relevant information, and training can overfit to early experiences stored in the replay buffer.

DR.Q addresses both problems. Alongside reducing differences between representations of the current state–action pair and the next state, it explicitly maximizes their mutual information. That objective encourages the representations to retain information shared across the transition. The method also uses faded prioritized experience replay to change how stored transitions are sampled, addressing the influence of early experience.

The authors evaluate DR.Q on numerous continuous-control benchmarks using one set of hyperparameters. It matches or exceeds recent strong baselines, with large improvements in some cases. The findings support treating representation quality and replay sampling as complementary parts of sample-efficient control, rather than expecting a dynamics-informed representation alone to remove learning biases.
summary.tldr: DR.Q improves dynamics-informed representations and replay sampling, matching or surpassing strong continuous-control baselines with a single hyperparameter setting.

title: Debiased Model-based Representations for Sample-efficient Continuous Control

abstract: GPT-style language models are sensitive to single-token changes at generation points where the predicted probability distribution is spread across multiple tokens. Viewing this sensitivity as a geometric property, we derive an $\mathfrak{so}(n)$-valued 1-form that depends only on the geometry of the token embeddings. Despite this purely geometric origin, we show that its curvature is semantically meaningful: on chess reasoning tasks, the curvature couples to the world model of an off-the-shelf instruction-tuned model, with transformations clustering by board region and respecting piece importance. Our findings suggest that token space geometry directly reflects how models internally represent problems.

paragraphs: When a language model assigns substantial probability to several possible next tokens, choosing one can noticeably change what follows. This paper studies that sensitivity through geometry. It asks whether the arrangement of token embeddings—the representations associated with tokens—can help explain how sampling relates to the model’s internal representation of a problem.

The authors derive a mathematical object called an so(n)-valued 1-form using only token-embedding geometry. They then examine its curvature, a geometric quantity associated with that construction. The central question is whether this quantity carries meaningful information about the task, despite being derived without directly building task semantics into it.

On chess reasoning tasks, the curvature relates to the internal world model of an existing instruction-tuned model. The associated transformations group by board region and reflect the importance of different pieces. These findings suggest a connection between token geometry and internal problem representations. The evidence supports that interpretation in the studied chess setting rather than establishing a universal account of sampling sensitivity.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis of token embeddings links sampling sensitivity to meaningful internal structure on chess reasoning tasks.

title: A geometric relation of the error introduced by sampling a language model’s output distribution to its internal state

abstract: Make-on-demand combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs) like Enamine REAL have significantly enabled drug discovery efforts. However, their large size presents a challenge for virtual screening, where the goal is to identify the top compounds in a library according to a computational objective (e.g., optimizing docking score) subject to computational constraints under a limited computational budget. For current library sizes—numbering in the tens of billions of compounds—and scoring functions of interest, a routine virtual screening campaign may be limited to scoring fewer than 0.1% of the available compounds, leaving potentially many high scoring compounds undiscovered. Furthermore, as constraints (and sometimes objectives) change during the course of a virtual screening campaign, existing virtual screening algorithms typically offer little room for amortization. We propose the approximate-but-exhaustive search protocol for CSLs, or APEX. APEX utilizes a neural network surrogate that exploits the structure of CSLs in the prediction of objectives and constraints to make full enumeration on a consumer GPU possible in under a minute, allowing for exact retrieval of approximate top-k sets. To demonstrate APEX’s capabilities, we develop a benchmark CSL comprised of more than 10 million compounds, all of which have been annotated with their docking scores on five medically relevant targets along with physicohemical properties measured with RDKit such that, for any objective and set of constraints, the ground truth top-k compounds can be identified and compared against the retrievals from any virtual screening algorithm. We show APEX’s consistently strong performance both in retrieval accuracy and runtime compared to alternative methods.

paragraphs: Virtual screening searches large chemical libraries for compounds that score well while satisfying practical constraints. Libraries containing tens of billions of candidates make direct scoring expensive: a routine campaign may examine fewer than 0.1% of them. Changing requirements can also make previous search work difficult to reuse.

APEX addresses this problem with a neural surrogate that predicts objectives and constraints using the library’s combinatorial structure. Its inexpensive predictions make exhaustive enumeration possible on a consumer GPU in under a minute. The distinction is important: retrieval is exact according to the approximate predictions, rather than guaranteed exact according to the original scoring function.

The authors also construct a benchmark containing more than 10 million compounds, with docking scores for five targets and computed physicochemical properties. These annotations allow retrieved candidates to be checked against the true best candidates under benchmark objectives and constraints. APEX shows consistently strong retrieval accuracy and runtime against alternative methods, supporting exhaustive surrogate search as a practical screening strategy.
summary.tldr: APEX searches entire combinatorial chemical libraries using fast neural predictions, enabling exact retrieval under approximate scores.

title: APEX: Approximate-but-exhaustive search for ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries

abstract: Hallucination detection is critical for ensuring the reliability of large language models (LLMs) in context-based generation. Prior work has explored intrinsic signals available during generation, among which attention offers a direct view of grounding behavior. However, existing approaches typically rely on coarse summaries that fail to capture fine-grained instabilities in attention. Inspired by signal processing, we introduce a frequency-aware perspective on attention by analyzing its variation during generation. We model attention distributions as discrete signals and extract high-frequency components that reflect rapid local changes in attention. Our analysis reveals that hallucinated tokens are associated with high-frequency attention energy, reflecting fragmented and unstable grounding behavior. Based on this insight, we develop a lightweight hallucination detector using high-frequency attention features. Experiments on the RAGTruth and HalluRAG benchmarks show that our approach achieves performance gains over verification-based, internal-representation-based, and attention-based methods across models and tasks.

paragraphs: When a language model answers using supplied context, its attention patterns provide clues about how it uses that material. Earlier detectors summarize those patterns coarsely, which can hide rapid changes. This paper asks whether the variation within attention carries useful evidence of contextual hallucination, rather than looking only at broad measures of attention allocation.

The authors treat attention distributions as discrete signals and extract their high-frequency components. Here, high frequency refers to rapid local changes in attention. Their analysis associates hallucinated tokens with higher energy in these components, interpreting the pattern as fragmented and unstable grounding. They then turn those features into a lightweight detector that uses signals available during generation.

On RAGTruth and HalluRAG, the detector improves over methods based on verification, internal representations, and other attention features across the tested models and tasks. The finding supports attention instability as a useful detection signal. It establishes an association that helps classification, rather than claiming that every rapid attention change proves a hallucination or that attention alone explains why hallucinations occur.
summary.tldr: Rapid local changes in attention provide lightweight features for detecting contextual hallucinations, improving results on two benchmarks.

title: Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Models with Frequency-Aware Attention

abstract: When computing gradients, deep learning training algorithms typically treat the mini-batch as a fundamental unit — only returning batch-averaged gradients. Computing non-linear statistics of the mini-batch gradient distribution has traditionally been viewed as prohibitively expensive or requiring complex, custom implementations. We challenge this view by demonstrating that sequence-level architectures offer a natural testbed for prototyping algorithms based on per-example gradients. We show that staged programming languages like JAX enable generic manipulations of mini-batch gradient computations. We then build on Dangel et. al. (2019) to derive implementations of specific per-example or per-token operations with negligible computational or memory overhead. Finally, we leverage our findings to re-examine two nonlinear optimization operations. First, we analyze signSGD, showing that the optimal placement of the sign operation is critical to success and can be predicted via a simple signal-to-noise ratio argument. Second, we investigate per-example variations of the Adam preconditioner and find that, contrary to conventional wisdom, optimization is best served when the preconditioner is dominated by the mean squared of the gradient distribution rather than its variance. Overall our work shows that accessible per-example gradient information unlocks new avenues for algorithm analysis and design.

paragraphs: Training usually exposes a gradient averaged across a mini-batch, hiding differences among the examples that contributed to it. This paper investigates algorithms that use those individual gradients. It shows that sequence-level architectures and staged programming systems such as JAX provide a practical setting for manipulating per-example gradient computations.

The authors derive implementations of specific per-example and per-token operations with negligible computation or memory overhead. This makes nonlinear operations on gradient information more accessible. Such operations are sensitive to when averaging occurs, so retaining individual contributions can reveal choices that disappear when only the batch average is available.

The paper examines two optimizer components. For signSGD, it shows that where the sign operation is applied is critical, and explains the preferred placement using a signal-to-noise argument. For variants of Adam’s preconditioner, the findings favor dominance by the squared mean of the gradient distribution over its variance. Together, these analyses show how accessible per-example information can support both explanations of optimizer behavior and new algorithm designs.
summary.tldr: Efficient access to per-example gradients reveals consequential choices in signSGD and Adam-style optimizer design.

title: Per-example Gradients: a New Frontier for Understanding and Improving Optimizers

abstract: Link prediction (LP) is a fundamental problem in graph learning and can be broadly categorized into node-based and subgraph-based approaches. While subgraph-based LP methods often achieve superior predictive performance by exploiting localized structural information, they suffer from efficiency bottlenecks due to the high computational cost of per-query subgraph message-passing during both training and inference. To address this challenge, we propose MIMO-LP, a Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) framework that accelerates subgraph-based LP. Given a batch of query node pairs and their corresponding subgraphs extracted from a shared full graph, MIMO-LP superposes their message-passing processes into a shared latent space while ensuring minimal interference among them. This design enables MIMO-LP to multiplex multiple queries within a single forward pass during both training and inference, substantially reducing redundant message-passing computations in overlapping subgraph regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MIMO-LP achieves a 14x-44x speedup over existing one-to-one subgraph-based methods, while maintaining comparable predictive performance.

paragraphs: MIMO-LP accelerates link prediction methods that examine local subgraphs around candidate node pairs. These methods can predict links well because they exploit nearby graph structure. Their cost is repeatedly passing messages through a separate subgraph for each query during both training and inference, including repeated work wherever those subgraphs overlap.

The framework processes a batch of query pairs whose subgraphs come from the same full graph. It superposes their message-passing computations in a shared latent space while keeping interference between queries minimal. Multiple link predictions can therefore be produced in one forward pass, reducing redundant computation in the shared regions of their subgraphs.

This makes the local structural information more economical to use without requiring a separate message-passing execution for every candidate link. Experiments report speedups ranging from 14 to 44 times over existing one-to-one subgraph methods, with comparable predictive performance. The result is an efficiency improvement that applies to both learning and deployment while preserving the predictive value of subgraph-based reasoning.
summary.tldr: MIMO-LP shares message passing across multiple link queries, reporting 14–44-fold speedups with comparable predictive performance.

title: MIMO-LP: A Multi-Input Multi-Output Framework for Subgraph-based Link Prediction

abstract: Anomaly detection in tabular data poses significant challenges due to heterogeneous feature types—mixing numerical, categorical, and textual attributes, which complicate learning meaningful representations of normality. Recent work has applied large language models (LLMs) to this problem by serializing table rows as text sequences, yet these approaches rely on one-shot supervised fine-tuning that offers limited signal to tighten the model’s description of normality. We propose DiSPaT, a self-play fine-tuning framework that strengthens the model’s understanding of normal data. Building on the theoretical foundation of $f$-divergence minimization, we derive a tight approximation connecting our training objective to reducing the distributional gap between real normal data and model-generated samples. DiSPaT operates through an alternating optimization: at each iteration, the current policy generates synthetic samples that serve as pseudo-anomalies, while a critic discriminator learns to distinguish these from real normal samples; this signal drives policy updates that progressively align the model distribution with the true normal-data distribution. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DiSPaT consistently outperforms prior LLM-based methods, deep learning approaches, and classical unsupervised detectors for tabular anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Detecting unusual table rows is difficult when columns mix numbers, categories, and text. LLM-based approaches can turn rows into text, but a single supervised fine-tuning stage gives limited feedback for refining what normal data should look like. DiSPaT introduces an iterative self-play process intended to strengthen that description of normality.

At each iteration, the current model generates synthetic rows that act as pseudo-anomalies. A critic learns to distinguish those rows from real normal examples, and its feedback guides updates to the generator. The synthetic samples provide a changing comparison set as training proceeds, while the generator is pushed toward the distribution represented by the normal data.

The authors derive a tight approximation connecting this objective to f-divergence minimization, giving a theoretical basis for interpreting training as reducing a distributional gap. Across diverse benchmarks, DiSPaT consistently outperforms earlier LLM methods, deep learning approaches, and classical unsupervised detectors. These empirical results support iterative distribution alignment as a useful way to learn normality for tabular anomaly detection.
summary.tldr: DiSPaT uses alternating generation and discrimination to improve an LLM’s model of normal table rows and detect anomalies.

title: $f$-Divergence Self-Play for Tabular Anomaly Detection via Large Language Models

abstract: Foundation models often generate unreliable answers, while heuristic uncertainty estimators fail to fully distinguish correct from incorrect outputs, causing users to accept erroneous answers without any statistical guarantee. We address this problem through selection-conditioned risk control, aiming to ensure that an accepted prediction has an error probability no larger than a user-specified risk level. To this end, we propose LEC, a principled framework that reframes selective prediction as a decision problem governed by a linear expectation constraint over selection and error indicators. This formulation directly controls the ratio between the expected number of accepted errors and the expected number of accepted predictions, which corresponds to the marginal error probability conditioned on selection. Under exchangeability, we derive a finite-sample sufficient condition that relies only on a held-out calibration set, enabling the computation of a risk-constrained, retention-maximizing threshold. Furthermore, we extend LEC to two-model routing systems: if the primary model’s uncertainty exceeds its calibrated threshold, the input is delegated to a subsequent model, while maintaining system-level selection-conditioned error control. Experiments on both closed-ended and open-ended question answering (QA) and vision question answering (VQA) demonstrate that LEC maintains the prescribed risk level in accepted predictions and substantially improves sample retention compared to baselines.

paragraphs: A system that accepts only confident predictions needs to control errors among the answers it actually returns. An uncertainty score alone does not supply that guarantee. LEC formulates acceptance as a constrained decision problem, targeting the marginal probability of error conditional on a prediction being selected.

Its linear expectation constraint relates accepted errors to accepted predictions. Specifically, controlling the ratio of their expected counts controls the desired selection-conditioned risk. Under exchangeability, the authors derive a finite-sample sufficient condition based only on held-out calibration data. This enables selection of a threshold that maximizes retention while satisfying the risk constraint; the condition is sufficient, rather than asserted to be necessary.

LEC also extends to routing between two models: inputs above the primary model’s calibrated uncertainty threshold can move to a subsequent model while preserving system-level error control. Experiments on closed-ended and open-ended question answering, including visual questions, maintain the prescribed risk level and substantially improve retention over baselines. The benefit is more accepted predictions at a controlled marginal error level.
summary.tldr: LEC calibrates acceptance and routing thresholds to maximize retained predictions while controlling selection-conditioned error under exchangeability.

title: LEC: Linear Expectation Constraints for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Selective Prediction and Routing Systems

abstract: Spatial-temporal time series forecasting is challenging due to complex lead-lag dependencies, which are often ignored or inadequately modeled by existing methods. Thus, we propose LagLLM, the first LLM-empowered framework that explicitly models lead–lag dependencies by unifying data-driven dynamics modeling and knowledge-driven semantic reasoning. Specifically, LagLLM constructs a lead-lag graph by integrating learnable embeddings, spatial proximity, and prompt-guided reasoning from a frozen LLM, which can capture lead-lag dependencies informed by the underlying data structure and semantic knowledge. In addition, LagLLM introduces structural token sorting based on the graph, which can make a fine-tuned LLM explicitly perceive directional and delayed interactions. Experiments on eight real-world datasets show that LagLLM achieves the state-of-the-art performance with improved accuracy, robustness, and interpretability. The code is available at https://github.com/w2obin/LagLLM-2026.

paragraphs: Spatial-temporal forecasting must account for relationships in which changes in one series precede changes in another. LagLLM explicitly models these directional delays, combining patterns learned from data with semantic reasoning supplied by a language model. The aim is to represent more than proximity or simultaneous association between series.

The framework constructs a lead–lag graph from learnable embeddings, spatial proximity, and prompt-guided reasoning from a frozen language model. It then uses this graph to sort tokens structurally before a fine-tuned language model processes them. These are distinct roles: one model contributes knowledge to the relationship graph, while the forecasting model receives an ordering designed to expose delayed, directional interactions.

Experiments on eight real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance with improvements in accuracy, robustness, and interpretability. The findings support making lead–lag structure explicit in both the representation of relationships and the organization of model inputs. LagLLM's contribution is the connection between knowledge-informed graph construction and a forecasting model trained to use that structure.
summary.tldr: LagLLM combines data and language-model reasoning to build lead–lag graphs that organize inputs for spatial-temporal forecasting.

title: LagLLM: LLM-empowered lead–lag dependency learning for spatial-temporal time series forecasting

abstract: Alignment plays a fundamental role in many machine learning problems, such as multi-network analysis, multimodal learning, and point cloud registration. Recent works increasingly leverage optimal transport (OT) for distributional alignment, whose effectiveness largely depends on sparse supervision that is hard or costly to obtain in practice. Existing works, however, largely overlook how to actively acquire high-quality supervision to improve their alignment performance under OT frameworks. In this paper, we propose a principled active alignment framework for optimal transport alignment called AvAtar. We quantify the informativeness of a candidate by measuring its gradient-based impact on the global alignment result, computed as the gradient propagation from the global alignment result to all possible supervisions of the candidate through the entropy-regularized OT formulation. While differentiating through OT is challenging given its constrained nature, we leverage the adjoint-state method to reformulate the computation to a linear system solvable by the conjugate gradient method with linear complexity and guaranteed convergence. By encoding the global alignment result via effective utility functions, AvAtar is applicable to general alignment problems under the OT framework. Extensive experiments on three representative alignment tasks demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and generalizability of the proposed AvAtar.

paragraphs: Alignment connects corresponding elements across sources, such as networks, modalities, or point clouds. Optimal transport provides a framework for aligning distributions, but its effectiveness can depend on a small amount of expensive supervision. AvAtar addresses the question of which additional supervision would be most informative for the overall alignment.

It scores a candidate by tracing how its possible supervision would affect the global alignment result through an entropy-regularized optimal transport formulation. This gradient-based view connects a local request for information to its potential effect on the whole problem. Because differentiating through constrained optimal transport is difficult, the method uses an adjoint-state reformulation that produces a linear system.

That system is solved with conjugate gradients, with linear complexity and guaranteed convergence as stated in the abstract. Utility functions express the desired global alignment outcome, allowing the framework to accommodate different alignment problems. Experiments on three representative tasks support its effectiveness, scalability, and generalizability. The central contribution is making supervision acquisition an explicit part of optimal transport alignment.
summary.tldr: AvAtar selects informative alignment supervision by efficiently estimating its gradient-based effect on an optimal transport solution.

title: AvAtar: Learning to Align via Active Optimal Transport

abstract: Logical reasoning is a fundamental aspect of human intelligence and an essential capability for multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Despite the significant advancement in multimodal reasoning, existing benchmarks fail to comprehensively evaluate their reasoning abilities due to the lack of explicit categorization for logical reasoning types and an unclear understanding of reasoning. To address these issues, we introduce MME-Reasoning, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the reasoning ability of MLLMs, which covers all three types of reasoning (i.e., inductive, deductive, and abductive). We carefully curate the data to ensure that each question effectively evaluates reasoning ability rather than perceptual skills or knowledge breadth, and extend the evaluation protocols to cover the evaluation of diverse questions. Our evaluation reveals substantial limitations of SoTA MLLMs when subjected to holistic assessments of logical reasoning capabilities. Even the most advanced MLLMs show limited performance in comprehensive logical reasoning, with notable performance imbalances across reasoning types. In addition, we conducted an in-depth analysis of approaches such as “thinking mode” and Rule-based RL, which are commonly believed to enhance reasoning abilities. We hope the community can pay more attention to the comprehensive reasoning capabilities of MLLMs instead of only focusing on its subset.

paragraphs: MME-Reasoning evaluates logical reasoning in multimodal language models across three categories: induction, deduction, and abduction. These correspond to drawing general patterns, deriving conclusions from premises, and inferring explanations. The benchmark responds to evaluations that lack explicit reasoning categories, making it difficult to tell whether strong results reflect broad reasoning competence or strength in a narrower subset.

The authors curate questions to target reasoning rather than visual perception or breadth of factual knowledge. They also extend evaluation protocols to accommodate diverse questions. This design matters because successful multimodal answers can depend on several abilities at once; clearer question construction helps make reasoning itself the focus of the assessment.

The evaluation finds substantial limitations even among the strongest tested models, along with pronounced differences in performance across reasoning types. The paper also examines thinking modes and rule-based reinforcement learning, approaches commonly associated with reasoning improvements. Its central finding is that comprehensive assessment reveals uneven capability, motivating attention to the full range of logical reasoning rather than only selected forms.
summary.tldr: MME-Reasoning tests three forms of logical reasoning and reveals substantial, uneven weaknesses in leading multimodal models.

title: MME-Reasoning: A Broad-Spectrum Benchmark for Evaluating Logical Reasoning in MLLMs

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently suffer from visual perception errors and hallucinations that compromise answer accuracy in complex reasoning tasks. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) offers a promising solution by optimizing policies using answer correctness signals. Despite their effectiveness, prevailing RLVR methods face two critical limitations. First, much of the sampling budget is wasted on trajectories doomed to fail due to early visual description errors. Second, sparse rewards cannot distinguish whether failures stem from visual perception or reasoning stages. We introduce MIRL, a decoupled framework that addresses both limitations by leveraging mutual information (MI) between generated descriptions and visual inputs as a cheap pre-screening signal. This enables intelligent budget allocation toward high-potential trajectories via forking, while decoupled training provides independent MI-based rewards for visual perception optimization, resolving reward blindness. Experiments on six vision-language reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MIRL achieves 70.22% average accuracy and successfully surpasses the performance of sampling 16 complete trajectories using only 10 pre-samples with top-6 selection (25% fewer complete trajectories). Our code is available at: https://github.com/youwyouw/mirl-main.

paragraphs: Vision-language reasoning can fail before reasoning properly begins if the model describes the image incorrectly. Training based only on final-answer correctness can spend substantial computation on these unsuccessful paths and cannot clearly separate perception errors from reasoning errors. MIRL addresses both problems by treating perception and reasoning separately.

The framework uses mutual information between a generated description and the image as an inexpensive screening signal. It directs further sampling toward promising descriptions through trajectory forking. During training, independent mutual-information rewards also provide feedback for the perception stage, giving visual understanding its own optimization signal instead of relying exclusively on the final answer.

Across six vision-language reasoning benchmarks, MIRL reaches 70.22% average accuracy. The reported configuration uses 10 preliminary samples with top-6 selection and outperforms sampling 16 complete trajectories while using 25% fewer complete trajectories. These findings support checking visual grounding early: screening can improve where computation is spent, while separate perception rewards help address the ambiguity of a single correctness signal.
summary.tldr: MIRL screens visual descriptions and rewards perception separately, improving vision-language reasoning while reducing complete-trajectory sampling.

abstract: We interpret several well-known algorithms for dimensionality reduction of manifolds as kernel methods. Isomap, graph Laplacian eigenmap, and locally linear embedding (LLE) all utilize local neighborhood information to construct a global embedding of the manifold. We show how all three algorithms can be described as kernel PCA on specially constructed Gram matrices, and illustrate the similarities and differences between the algorithms with representative examples.
originalAbstract: We interpret several well-known algorithms for dimensionality reduction of manifolds as kernel methods. Isomap, graph Laplacian eigenmap, and locally linear embedding (LLE) all utilize local neighborhood information to construct a global embedding of the manifold. We show how all three algorithms can be described as kernel PCA on specially constructed Gram matrices, and illustrate the similarities and differences between the algorithms with representative examples.

paragraphs: This paper gives a shared mathematical interpretation of three methods for reducing the dimensionality of manifold data: Isomap, graph Laplacian eigenmaps, and locally linear embedding. Each method starts from relationships within local neighborhoods and uses them to construct a global embedding. The paper asks how these apparently different procedures fit into the same framework.

The central result is that all three can be described as kernel principal component analysis applied to specially constructed Gram matrices. These matrices encode the relationships used by the embedding procedure. Under this interpretation, the choice of matrix becomes the place where the distinctive behavior of each algorithm enters the common kernel framework.

Representative examples illustrate both similarities and differences among the algorithms. The contribution is a way to understand existing methods together: their common kernel formulation clarifies what they share, while their different matrix constructions retain their individual approaches to turning local information into global geometry.
summary.tldr: Isomap, Laplacian eigenmaps, and LLE can all be understood as kernel PCA with specially constructed Gram matrices.

title: A kernel view of the dimensionality reduction of manifolds

abstract: In this paper, we consider a smoothing kernel-based classification rule and propose an algorithm for optimizing the performance of the rule by learning the bandwidth of the smoothing kernel along with a data-dependent distance metric. The data-dependent distance metric is obtained by learning a function that embeds an arbitrary metric space into a Euclidean space while minimizing an upper bound on the resubstitution estimate of the error probability of the kernel classification rule. By restricting this embedding function to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, we reduce the problem to solving a semidefinite program and show the resulting kernel classification rule to be a variation of the k-nearest neighbor rule. We compare the performance of the kernel rule (using the learned data-dependent distance metric) to state-of-the-art distance metric learning algorithms (designed for k-nearest neighbor classification) on some benchmark datasets. The results show that the proposed rule has either better or as good classification accuracy as the other metric learning algorithms.

The data-dependent distance metric is obtained by learning a function that embeds an arbitrary metric space into a Euclidean space while minimizing an upper bound on the resubstitution estimate of the error probability of the kernel classification rule. By restricting this embedding function to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, we reduce the problem to solving a semidefinite program and show the resulting kernel classification rule to be a variation of the k-nearest neighbor rule. We compare the performance of the kernel rule (using the learned data-dependent distance metric) to state-of-the-art distance metric learning algorithms (designed for k-nearest neighbor classification) on some benchmark datasets. The results show that the proposed rule has either better or as good classification accuracy as the other metric learning algorithms.

paragraphs: A smoothing kernel classifier depends on both the distance between examples and the kernel's bandwidth. This paper proposes learning those choices together to improve classification. The learned distance comes from a function that maps an arbitrary metric space into a Euclidean space, making the geometry used by the classifier depend on the data.

The embedding is learned by minimizing an upper bound on the classifier's resubstitution error estimate, which evaluates error using the training examples. Restricting the embedding function to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space turns the problem into a semidefinite program. The authors also show that the resulting classification rule is a variation of the k-nearest neighbor rule.

On benchmark datasets, the proposed rule achieves accuracy that is better than or comparable to the tested state-of-the-art metric learning algorithms designed for nearest neighbor classification. These results support jointly learning the distance and smoothing behavior in the evaluated settings. The optimization objective itself concerns an upper bound on a training-based error estimate, distinct from the reported benchmark comparisons.
summary.tldr: Learning a Euclidean embedding and kernel bandwidth together yields a classifier with competitive or better accuracy in the reported metric-learning comparisons.

title: Metric embedding for kernel classification rules

abstract: Many structured prediction tasks involve complex models where inference is computationally intractable, but where it can be well approximated using a linear programming relaxation. Previous approaches for learning for structured prediction (e.g., cutting-plane, subgradient, perceptron) repeatedly make predictions for some of the data points. These approaches are computationally demanding because each prediction involves solving a linear program to optimality.We present a scalable algorithm for learning for structured prediction.The main idea is to instead solve the dual of the structured prediction loss. We formulate the learning task as a convex minimization over both the weights and the dual variables corresponding to each data point. As a result, we can begin to optimize the weights even before completely solving any of the individual prediction problems. We show how the dual variables can be efficiently optimized using coordinate descent. Our algorithm is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as stochastic subgradient and cutting-plane.

These approaches are computationally demanding because each prediction involves solving a linear program to optimality.We present a scalable algorithm for learning for structured prediction.The main idea is to instead solve the dual of the structured prediction loss. We formulate the learning task as a convex minimization over both the weights and the dual variables corresponding to each data point. We show how the dual variables can be efficiently optimized using coordinate descent. Our algorithm is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as stochastic subgradient and cutting-plane.

paragraphs: Structured prediction models can require inference that is computationally intractable, even though a linear programming relaxation provides a useful approximation. Training can still be expensive when every update requires solving one of these relaxed prediction problems completely. This paper changes how learning and approximate inference are coordinated.

The authors formulate training through the dual of the structured prediction loss. The resulting convex problem optimizes the model weights together with dual variables associated with individual examples. Because these quantities are optimized jointly, the weights can begin improving before any individual prediction problem has been solved to completion.

Coordinate descent provides an efficient way to update the dual variables. The reported algorithm is competitive with stochastic subgradient and cutting-plane methods. Its central contribution is to remove a costly dependency within the training process: learning need not wait for a fully optimized prediction at every step. The formulation allows progress on inference and progress on model fitting to proceed together.
summary.tldr: Jointly optimizing model weights and dual loss variables lets structured-prediction training progress before individual relaxed inference problems are fully solved.

title: Learning Efficiently with Approximate Inference via Dual Losses

abstract: Restricted Boltzmann machines were developed using binary stochastic hidden units. These can be generalized by replacing each binary unit by an infinite number of copies that all have the same weights but have progressively more negative biases. The learning and inference rules for these "Stepped Sigmoid Units" are unchanged. They can be approximated efficiently by noisy, rectified linear units. Compared with binary units, these units learn features that are better for object recognition on the NORB dataset and face verification on the Labeled Faces in the Wild dataset. Unlike binary units, rectified linear units preserve information about relative intensities as information travels through multiple layers of feature detectors.
originalAbstract: Restricted Boltzmann machines were developed using binary stochastic hidden units. These can be generalized by replacing each binary unit by an infinite number of copies that all have the same weights but have progressively more negative biases. The learning and inference rules for these "Stepped Sigmoid Units" are unchanged. They can be approximated efficiently by noisy, rectified linear units. Compared with binary units, these units learn features that are better for object recognition on the NORB dataset and face verification on the Labeled Faces in the Wild dataset. Unlike binary units, rectified linear units preserve information about relative intensities as information travels through multiple layers of feature detectors.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes the binary stochastic hidden units used in restricted Boltzmann machines. Its construction replaces a binary unit with infinitely many copies sharing the same weights but having increasingly negative biases. The resulting stepped sigmoid unit retains the existing learning and inference rules while allowing a richer response than a single binary unit.

The authors show that noisy rectified linear units provide an efficient approximation to these stepped sigmoid units. This connects the expanded construction to a practical computational form. The abstract also identifies a representational advantage: rectified linear units preserve relative-intensity information as signals pass through multiple layers of feature detectors.

Compared with binary units, the proposed units learn better features for object recognition on NORB and face verification on Labeled Faces in the Wild. These results support the usefulness of the changed hidden-unit representation for the two evaluated tasks. The contribution combines a derivation from replicated binary units, an efficient approximation, and evidence of improved learned features.
summary.tldr: Noisy rectified linear units efficiently approximate generalized RBM hidden units and improve learned features in the reported recognition tasks.

title: Rectified Linear Units Improve Restricted Boltzmann Machines

abstract: We introduce the nonparametric metadata dependent relational (NMDR) model, a Bayesian nonparametric extension of previous stochastic block models. The NMDR allows the entities associated with each node to have mixed membership in an unbounded collection of latent communities. Learned regression models allow these memberships to depend on, and be predicted from, arbitrary node metadata. We develop efficient MCMC algorithms for learning NMDR models from (partially observed) node relationships. Retrospective MCMC methods allow our sampler to work directly with the infinite stick-breaking representation of the NMDR, avoiding the need for finite truncations. Our results demonstrate recovery of useful latent communities from real-world social and ecological networks, and the usefulness of metadata in link prediction tasks.
