The NMDR allows the entities associated with each node to have mixed membership in an unbounded collection of latent communities. Learned regression models allow these memberships to depend on, and be predicted from, arbitrary node metadata. We develop efficient MCMC algorithms for learning NMDR models from (partially observed) node relationships. Retrospective MCMC methods allow our sampler to work directly with the infinite stick-breaking representation of the NMDR, avoiding the need for finite truncations. Our results demonstrate recovery of useful latent communities from real-world social and ecological networks, and the usefulness of metadata in link prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Network models often explain relationships through hidden communities. This paper introduces NMDR, a Bayesian nonparametric extension of stochastic block models in which each node can belong to multiple communities. The collection of possible communities is unbounded, so the model does not require a fixed finite set of community types.

Node metadata also shapes community membership. Learned regression models connect that metadata to membership patterns, allowing memberships to depend on and be predicted from information about the nodes. The authors develop efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for learning from relationships that may be only partially observed. Retrospective sampling works directly with the infinite stick-breaking representation, avoiding a finite truncation of the model.

Results on real social and ecological networks show recovery of useful latent communities and demonstrate that metadata helps with link prediction. The contribution joins relational evidence and node descriptions within one community model. Its inference method supports the unbounded representation directly, while the experiments indicate that incorporating metadata can improve the usefulness of the learned network structure.
summary.tldr: NMDR uses node metadata to predict overlapping memberships in an unbounded set of communities, with useful results for network structure and link prediction.

title: The Nonparametric Metadata Dependent Relational Model

abstract: Recent proposed subspace clustering methods first compute a self reconstruction matrix for dataset, then converted it to an affinity matrix, before input to a spectral clustering method to obtain the final clustering result. Their success is largely based on the subspace independence assumption, which, however, does not always hold for the applications with increasing number of clusters such as face clustering. In this paper, we proposes a novel reconstruction based subspace clustering method without making the subspace independence assumption. In our model, certain properties of the reconstruction matrix are explicitly characterized using the latent cluster indicators, and the affinity matrix input to the spectral clustering is built from the posterior of the cluster indicators. Evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that our method can outperform the state-of-the-arts.
originalAbstract: Recent proposed subspace clustering methods first compute a self reconstruction matrix for dataset, then converted it to an affinity matrix, before input to a spectral clustering method to obtain the final clustering result. Their success is largely based on the subspace independence assumption, which, however, does not always hold for the applications with increasing number of clusters such as face clustering. In this paper, we proposes a novel reconstruction based subspace clustering method without making the subspace independence assumption. In our model, certain properties of the reconstruction matrix are explicitly characterized using the latent cluster indicators, and the affinity matrix input to the spectral clustering is built from the posterior of the cluster indicators. Evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that our method can outperform the state-of-the-arts.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups data according to underlying subspaces. A common reconstruction-based approach first represents data points using other points, converts the resulting reconstruction matrix into pairwise affinities, and then applies spectral clustering. The paper argues that the success of such methods relies heavily on subspace independence, which may fail in applications such as face clustering as the number of groups increases.

The proposed method retains reconstruction as its starting point but does not make the subspace independence assumption. It explicitly expresses properties of the reconstruction matrix through latent cluster indicators: variables representing cluster memberships that must be inferred. This connects the reconstruction model directly to the grouping the method is trying to discover.

The affinity matrix for spectral clustering is built from the posterior distribution of those indicators. Thus, inferred cluster membership informs the similarities used in the final clustering stage. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the approach can outperform state-of-the-art alternatives, supporting the usefulness of this formulation without claiming superiority on every dataset.
summary.tldr: Latent cluster indicators guide reconstruction-based subspace clustering without assuming independent subspaces.

title: Groupwise Constrained Reconstruction for Subspace Clustering

abstract: We show that the variational representations for f-divergences currently used in the literature can be tightened. This has implications to a number of methods recently proposed based on this representation. As an example application we use our tighter representation to derive a general f-divergence estimator based on two i.i.d. samples and derive the dual program for this estimator that performs well empirically. We also point out a connection between our estimator and MMD.
originalAbstract: We show that the variational representations for f-divergences currently used in the literature can be tightened. This has implications to a number of methods recently proposed based on this representation. As an example application we use our tighter representation to derive a general f-divergence estimator based on two i.i.d. samples and derive the dual program for this estimator that performs well empirically. We also point out a connection between our estimator and MMD.

paragraphs: An f-divergence measures a discrepancy between probability distributions. Variational representations express such quantities through optimization and can serve as foundations for estimation methods. This paper shows that representations used in the literature can be tightened by restricting attention to probability measures, with implications for methods built on those representations.

The authors turn the tighter representation into a general estimator of f-divergence using two samples whose observations are independent and identically distributed. They also derive the estimator's dual optimization program. This connects the theoretical representation to a concrete estimation problem and provides an alternative optimization formulation for computing the estimate.

The dual program performs well empirically, and the authors identify a connection between their estimator and maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD. The contribution thus links a refinement in the representation of distributional discrepancy to a usable estimator and a relationship with another discrepancy measure. The reported empirical result supports the proposed estimation approach, while the tighter representation is the central theoretical advance.
summary.tldr: A tighter variational representation of f-divergences yields a sample-based estimator, an empirically effective dual program, and a connection to MMD.

title: Tighter Variational Representations of f-Divergences via Restriction to Probability Measures
